full_judgment:
This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and order dated 13-5-98 passed by the Assistant Judge, 1st Court Dhaka in Title Suit No. 134 of 1998 should not be set aside.

2. Brief facts are that; the petitioner instituted the aforesaid suit praying for a decree of permanent injunction restraining the defendant opposite parties from entering into the suit land and disturbing the peaceful possession of the plaintiff therein stating, inter alia, that the suit land, which consists of 54 decimals of land in CS Plot No. 73 of CS Khatian No. 70 of Mouza UttarAdabor PS Mohammadpur, Dhaka, was owned by Mr MS Islam who by baina dated 15-4-80 agreed to sell the suit land along with other lands to Mr Mohshahid Ali Chowdhury, the father of the plaintiff, and also received Taka 8,50;000.00 as part of the consideration money but subsequently, Mr MS Islam, while executing a deed of sale on 5-1-81 in favour of Mohshahid Ali Chowdhury and his 3 sons including the plaintiff, transferring 2.10 acres of land in respect of other lands i.e. at Plot No. 74 under Khatian No. 68 and also 10 acres of land of Plot No. 83 under Khatian No. 70 but did not execute and register the sale deed in respect of the suit land. Subsequently, Mr MS Islam changed his mind and agreed to sell the suit land to the plaintiff and then on receipt of Taka 2,50,000.00 out of total consideration amount of Taka 15,00,000.00, baina was executed on 10-12-89 and possession of the said suit land was also delivered to the plaintiff on that very date in part performance of the contract and subsequently, MS Islam received further amount of Taka 2,50,000.00 on 11-3-91 and Taka 2,00,000.00 on 29-11-92. However, the defendant opposite parties, who are miscreants and are in the habit of trespass into the properties of others for collecting money illegally from the owners, along with 4 other unknown persons, made an attempt to enter the suit land on 19-4-98 but failed due to the resistance from the plaintiff and that the plaintiff is in peaceful possession of the suit land in part performance of contract and so his possession cannot be disturbed in any manner. On the basis of the aforesaid prayer of the petitioner, the learned Assistant Judge, on 30-4-98, passed an ad interim order of injunction restraining the defendants from entering into the suit land but subsequently, on 4-5-98, in pursuance of the prayer of the opposite parties the learned Assistant Judge, modified the aforesaid order into an order directing the parties to maintain status-quo fixing 26-5-98 for hearing the matter of temporary injunction. Then on 10-5-98, the defendant-opposite parties filed an application under Order 39 rule 7 CPC praying for inspection of the suit land in order to ascertain the features of the suit property, the actual possession of the parties therein, number of structures in the suit plot, whether there are trees, plants and Rabi crops therein, whether there is an old tin shed house originally constructed by late MS Islam on the north west corner of the suit land, the learned Assistant Judge by the impugned order allowed the prayer for local inspection and being aggrieved the petitioner moved this Court and obtained the present Rule.

3. As it appears though this matter appeared in the Cause list from the date of re-opening i.e. 15-10-2000, but the learned Advocate of the petitioner did not pray for any adjournment nor he was present when this Rule was taken up for hearing in the morning hours and in the above circumstances this Court adjourned the hearing till 2-00 PM to enable the learned Advocate of the petitioner to be present during hearing but in spite of above, the learned Advocate for the petitioner failed to appear when this matter was taken up for hearing after recess. On perusal of the records this Court found that this Rule can be disposed of on point of law only. Accordingly, in consideration of the fact that this Court while issuing the Rule stayed all further proceedings of Title Suit No. 134 of 1998, I decided to hear the Rule in the absence of the learned Advocate of the petitioner. From the grounds taken in the revisional application it appears that the petitioner challenged the impugned judgment and order on the ground that in terms of Order 39 rule 7 CPC local inspection is contemplated only in cases where the suit property is in extreme danger of being wasted or damaged and so the impugned order of local inspection has been passed in utter misconception of the provision of Order 26 rule 9 and Order 39 rule 7 CPC occasioning failure of justice and the learned Assistant Judge has also not directed any points for local inspection for which a writ is to be issued to the Advocate Commissioner.

<u>4. Mr ASM Wahidul Mumin Chowdhury, the learned Advocate for the opposite party Nos. 1 and 2, relying on the cases of MM Hossain vs Mostafa Hossain reported in 40 DLR (AD) 20 and the case of Mohammed lbne Abbas vs Begum Momtaz Hossain reported in 45 DLR 421 submits that the possession of the suit land was not handed over to the plaintiff by Mr MS Islam and the plaintiff is also not in possession of the suit land in part performance of the contract as claimed by the plaintiff and so the inspection as prayed, is necessary and the learned Assistant Judge, on consideration of the documents produced before it, passed the impugned order and accordingly, no interference is at all called for Mr Chowdhury next submits that the plaintiff on one hand, claimed possession of the suit plot and, on the other hand, resisted local inspection and so he, in</u>

<u>view of the principle laid down in the case of Nur Banu vs Noor Mohammad reported in 35 DLR (AD) 182, cannot be allowed to approbate and reprobate.</u>

5. Heard the learned Advocate. In the plaint, the petitioner has asserted that on 10-12-89 Mr MS Islam, after receiving Taka 2,50,000.00 handed over the possession of the suit land to him and on 30-4-98. The learned Assistant Judge as if appears, passed an ad interim order restraining the defendant from entering the suit land but subsequently by the impugned order modified the said order and converted it into an order directing the parties to maintain status quo and the next date on 26-5-98 for hearing the matter of temporary injunction. Then on 10-5-98, the opposite parties filed an application under Order 39, rule 7 CPC, stating, inter alia, that the present suit was filed after 9 years from the execution of the alleged baina dated 10-2-89 and that the possession of the suit land was not delivered to the plaintiff petitioner on the date of the 'Baina' and it is also very unlikely that on payment only of Taka 20,000.00 out of total consideration money Taka 15,00,000.00 such possession would be delivered to the plaintiff and that the suit property being admittedly nal land and about 15-16 feet deep the defendant, after purchasing the suit property on 23-3-98 and 23-4-98, had to fill up the ditch at a cost of Taka 20,00,000.00 and thus converted the suit land into a "Baiti land" and then constructed 4-S tin sheds, Kucha structures and huts of different sizes on the suit land and inducted tenants therein and also engaged caretaker and tenants to look after the said property. In the said application under Order 39 rule 7 CPC the defendant-petitioner prayed for inspection directing the Advocate Commissioner (a) To go to the locality, i.e. suit land, with due notices to the concerned parties through their learned Advocate. (b) To ascertain the local features of the suit property. (c) To ascertain the present actual position of the suit properties and its surrounding circumstances including original nature of depth of the suit land and its present position of height in comparison with its side land. (d) to ascertain how many structures are there in the suit properties and what are their nature and character and who are in occupation, residing therein and how they are residing and what are the size of whole structures therein in the suit land where they are located to be shown in a hand sketch map if possible.

(e) To ascertain, as to whether the vacant portion of the suit land are covered by any trees and plants or Rabi crops therein, including an old tin shed house originally constructed by the said late MS Islam in the north-west corner of the suit land.

(f) To file his report with hand sketch map, etc. By the impugned order the learned Assistant Judge allowed the said prayer.

<u>6. In the revisional application the petitioner took specific ground to the effect that prayer for local inspection under Order 39, rule 7 CPC is contemplated only in case where the suit property if in extreme danger of being wasted or damaged but in the application under Order 39, rule 7 CPC filed by the plaintiff, there is no such statements to the above effect and further, the impugned order is, on face of it, wrong inasmuch as the learned Assistant Judge had not directed any points for local investigation for which writ was to be issued to the Advocate Commissioner who is to conduct the inspection and further, the application for local inspection of the suit property after modification of the order of ad interim injunction, shows the malafide of the opposite party and moreover, the impugned order has been passed in utter misconception of granting local inspection as provided under Order 26, rule 9 CPC and Order 39 rule 7 CPC. Similar point came up for consideration in the case of MM Hossain vs Mustafa Hossain reported-in 40 DLR (AD) 20 wherein on the prayer of the plaintiff, a commissioner was appointed without any notice to the defendant and then an application filed by the defendant under section 151 CPC praying for vacating the said order which being refused, the defendant moved the High Court Division but the motion was summarily rejected and then Civil Appeal No. 32 of 1986 was filed in the Appellate Division. The Appellate Division in the above decision considered the case of Amjad Ali vs Ali Hossain and another reported in 15 CWN 353 in which if was held that the power to direct inspection includes the power to direct the preparation of an inventory, if the Court is of the opinion that the preparation of the inventory is essential for the proper decision of that case but in directing an inspection and preparation of an inventory the manner should be so ordered as to cause least inconvenience to the owner.</u>

<u>7. In the case of Mahmud Ibne Abbas vs Begum Momtaz reported in 45 DLR 421 it has been held as follows:</u>

<u>"In view of the averments made by the contending parties it appears that in order to ascertain whether the deed of gift was acted upon i.e. whether possession of the land in question was delivered to the donee is a material one as because if it is found that the possession had already been delivered and the donee is in actual possession of the gifted property land then a legal question as regards the form of the suit may be taken up by the contending defendant. Under the circumstances I find that the local inspection of the gifted land as mentioned in the petition by the plaintiff- petitioner was neither irrelevant nor unnecessary. Rather, it appears that it is necessary to avoid future complication". The High Court Division accordingly, did not interfere with the order passed by the trial Court allowing the plaintiffs prayer for inspection".</u>

8. In the present case the plaintiff filed the present suit seeking permanent injunction claiming that he is in possession of the suit land in part performance of the contract and so this suit is not for declaration of title nor for recovery of possession whereas the defendants claimed that the suit land was originally nal land and they after expending Taka 20,00,000.00 converted the same into a viti land and constructed structures therein. So, it appears that prayer of the opposite parties for local inspection is within the ambit of Order 39, rule 7 CPC and the prayer is not irrelevant nor unnecessary and accordingly, the learned Assistant Judge did not commit any illegality in passing the impugned judgment and order and accordingly, no interference is called for.

In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to cost.

End.

lawyer:
Sayyid Shahid Hossain with Rani Akhter------For the Appellant. 
Rafique-ul Haque with Enayet Hossain Khan and Ziaul Haque-------For the Respondents.

Al Baraka Bank Bangladesh Ltd ------ Appellant
Vs

full_judgment:
Md Abdur Rashid J: Defendant No. 1 Al Baraka Bank presented the appeal against the decree dated 26-11-2001 passed by the Joint District Judge and First Commercial Court at Dhaka in Title Suit No.197 of 2001, which decreed the suit.

2. Respondent No.1 as plaintiff on 14-7-97 instituted Title Suit No. 208 of 97 against the appellant bank and another for a decree of declaration that the plaintiff owed no amount to said bank on account of any loan and that the plaintiff had no liability with the bank; and that so-called memorandum or deposit of title deeds dated 17-3-88 was manufactured, forged and inoperative and that the plaintiff was entitled to get back her title deed No. 788 as described in the schedule to the plaint; and also for direction for return of said title deed and for compensation of Taka 75,00,000 as damages. The suit was ultimately, renumbered as aforesaid Title Suit No. 197 of 2001.

3. Plaint case, in short, is that defendant No. 2 Shawkat Ali was proprietor of Gold Star Lines and Trans Bangla Shipping Lines. The plaintiff mortgaged her property covered by said deed as security of the loans advanced to the companies in 1987. On 17-11-88 both the loans were adjusted and on 30-7-92 defendant No.1 bank issued certificates that the loans were adjusted.

4. Meanwhile, a project profile in the name of Pan Asia, a new firm, was submitted to defendant No. 1 bank. Said property of the plaintiff was offered as collateral for the proposed project. But the project did not ultimately materialise and the plaintiff asked the defendant bank to return her document by a letter dated 17-12-92. But the bank mala fide kept her document in its custody.

5. Said bank instituted a suit in the court of Artha Rin Adalat showing said property of the plaintiff mortgaged for the loan advanced to the Coast Marine Line Ltd. It was a public limited company and one AB Siddique was the managing director of the company, The bank fraudulently created a memorandum of deposit of title deeds dated 17-3-88 and an agreement for creating further charge dated 9-3-89 behind 'the back of the plaintiff. The plaintiff never executed any such memorandum of deposit of title deeds and/or the agreement. Neither the plaintiff nor her husband was a director or a share holder of the company. She had no interest in the company. Neither the plaintiff nor her husband was connected in any way with the company.

6. The bank never informed nor obtained consent of the plaintiff before creating mortgage of her property. In spite of repeated demands, the defendant Bank did not return the deed. Hence, the plaintiff was constrained to institute the suit.

7. Denying the plaint case defendant No. 1 bank contested the suit by filing a written statement. Main defence case is that on 29-2-88 one AB Siddique Ludu applied for Bai-Muajjal facility to the bank for purchase of two ships and also for adjustment of the loan of Taka 99,50,000 and offered to mortgage the property of the plaintiff which was given in mortgage against the loans of Shawkat Ali. Defendant bank sanctioned Bai-Muajjal facility and in terms of the facility the plaintiff on 17-3-88 executed a memorandum of deposit of title deeds and deposited the original lease deed dated 28-10-66 and original deed of sale dated 22-2-73 in the bank. On 17-3-88 Mr AB Siddique Ludu also executed other charge documents. Thereafter, the plaintiff executed the agreement to create further charge on 9-3-89. The Coast Marine Line Ltd having failed to adjust the loan of Taka 1,33,70,592 the bank instituted Title Suit No. 147 of 1992 then renumbered as Title Suit No. 113 of 2000 in the 4th Court of Artha Rin Adalat at Dhaka. The plaintiff could not get back the schedule deed before adjustment of the loan of Coast Marine Line Ltd.

8. By amendment of the written statement, the defendant bank further stated that they already obtained a decree from the Artha Rin Adalat on 24-5-01 and Artha Rin Adalat found the property of the plaintiff was mortgaged to the defendant Bank. The present suit was therefore, hit by the principles of res judicata.

9. On the pleading the following issues were settled:

1. Was the suit in the present form maintainable?

2.	Was the suit bad for defect of parties?

3.	Had the plaintiff mortgaged the property covered by scheduled deed against the loan of Coast Marine Line Ltd?

4. Was the suit barred by principles of res judicata?

5. What relief the plaintiff was entitled to?

10.	In support of her case, the plaintiff examined 3 witnesses including herself while the bank examined one of its officers. Documents adduced by the plaintiff were marked Exhibit 1 to 7 while those of the defendant bank marked Exhibits A to O.

The plaintiff as PW 1 testified in support of the plaint case. She stated that she became owner in possession of the suit land by deed No. 788 dated 8-9-72 comprising of plot No.77, Road No. 24, Gulshan, Dhaka. She did not take any loan or facility from the bank. She never went to the defendant Bank. She had no account with the bank. Defendant Bank had no loan against her. She never deposited said deed in the bank.

11.	Defendant No. 2 was the son of her husband's elder brother. She gave the deed to said defendant No. 2 in trust in connection with his business. But he obtained some loan facility keeping deposit of said deed in the bank. He told her that he obtained loan in connection with his business of Gold Star Lines, and Trans Bangla Shipping Line. He was the sole proprietor of those firms. The Bank obtained a general power of attorney in respect of the loans from her and she executed and registered said power of attorney on 22-6-87 through commission. The power was given in respect of said Gold Star Lines and Trans Bangla Shipping Co only. Besides that document she did not execute any other document. Defendant No. 2 already paid off entire loan with interest to the bank. The Bank informed her by issuing two non liability certificates dated 13-7-92 Exhibit 1 and 1(ka). Defendant No. 2 gave her the certificates saying he already adjusted the loans and assured her to return the original deed. Her property was never mortgaged in respect of any other loan.

12.	Her husband Serajul Alam however, told her that her property might be given in security in respect of Pan Asia, Lines. On 17-11-88 she executed an agreement in case of any loan to be sanctioned, to said Pan Asia Lines. The Deed was not registered. Then the Project did not ultimately materialise and Pan Asia Lines was not registered with the Registrar of Joint Stock Companies. In spite of repeated demands, she did not get back her deed. On 17-12-92 she wrote to defendant bank. A copy of the letter as was received by the bank on 19-12-92 was tendered and marked as exhibit-2 and her signature thereon as Exhibit 2(ka). For not getting back the deed she suffered economically and socially and the bank caused her heavy losses by keeping the document in its custody against her consent. She suffered losses of about two crore.

13.	In cross examination, she stated she was impleaded as defendant No.4 in Title Suit No. 147 of 1992 brought by defendant No. 1 bank in the Artha Rin Adalat. After receipt of summons, she came to know about the suit. Before receipt of the summons, she had no knowledge about Coast Marine Lines Ltd. She did not mortgage any of her property against any loan of said company. There was no question to know as she had no knowledge whether the company obtained loan from the bank. She did not execute so-called memorandum of deposit of title deeds. Defendant bank had no claim or loan against her. The bank never informed her about why the bank kept her document in its custody. She did not lodge any 'Ijhar' for not returning by the bank of the deed.

14. She read up to BA. She was a housewife and her husband was doing business. They were 5 brothers, elder brother died. All brothers of her husband were doing business. AB Siddique Ludu was her husband's elder brother. He was in shipping business. She had no knowledge that AB Siddique Ludu obtained loan from the bank. Defendant No. 2 was a son of her husband's elder deceased brother. He was also in shipping business.

15. She had no knowledge that during the continuance of mortgage against the loans of Gold Star Lines and Trans Bangla Shipping Company, on 29-2-88 AB Siddique Ludu applied for Bai-Muajjal facility for Taka 99,50,000. She had no knowledge that the facility was sanctioned. She denied that before institution of the suit in 1997 and during the period of 9 years she never demanded return of the deed and that she created Exhibit 2 for the suit. She however, did not write reminder to letter dated 17-12-99. On 17-12-99 she signed her name in English. She used to sign both in Bengali and English. Her deposition was written in Bengali. She denied that the deeds dated 17-3-88 and 9-3-89 were not forged.

16. PW 2 Serajul Alam, husband of the plaintiff, deposed that the plaintiff deposited her title deed in question against the loans of Gold Star Lines and Trans Bangla Shipping Co. Shawkat Ali was the proprietor of both' firms. Shawkat Ali already paid off the loans on 17-11-88. Property was mortgaged in 1987. Defendant then issued certificates of non-liabilities in favour of Shawkat Ali on 13-7-88. Then he thought to purchase a company like Pan Asia Lines. He obtained a deed of agreement for loan against the proposed company but ultimately, did not obtain any facility. Proposed loan was also not disbursed since Pan Asia Lines ultimately was not brought into existence. He on behalf of his wife demanded return of the deed. On 17-12-92 she demanded in writing return of the deed. But the bank did not reply.

17. He stated that the property of his wife was not mortgaged in connection with the loan of Coast Marine Line Ltd. His wife was made unnecessary party because she had no connection with Coast Marine Line Ltd. He saw the signature on the Memorandum of deposit of title deed and that was not the signature of his wife. That was created by the bank. The bank withheld the deed illegally. They suffered heavy loss for want of the deed. He could not do business nor develop the land. Signature on said memorandum of deposit of title deeds did not tally with any of the signatures of his wife in the papers of the bank filed.

18. In cross-examination, he stated that they were 4 brothers alive. AB Siddique Ludu was his brother. Coast Marine Line Ltd obtained loan of Taka 99,50,000 from the defendant bank. Then he said he had no knowledge. He denied that the property of his wife was mortgaged to secure said loan of Taka 99,50,000. He had no knowledge of Title Suit No. 147 of 1992 of the 4th Court of Artha Rin Adalat. Then he said he heard that there was a suit and his wife along with others submitted written statement.

19. PW 3 Abu Bakar Siddique testified that the plaintiff was the wife of his younger brother. Coast Marine Line Ltd was a Public Ltd Company. He applied in his personal capacity for Bai-Muajjal facility for purchase of 2 ships of said company and he did not offer the property of the plaintiff against the loan proposal. Plaintiff did not deposit any document in the bank. No letter was issued sanctioning Bai-Muajjal facility. She did not execute charge documents dated 9-3-89. On 17-3-88 Shaw kat Ali mortgaged the property of the plaintiff in connection against two loans. On 17-3-88 the house was not free from liability. Then, Shaw kat Ali adjusted entire loan. On 13-7-92 he obtained non liability certificates from the defendant bank. Bai-Muajjal facility granted was not proper and he did not enjoy them. He did not request the plaintiff to mortgage the property. Showing the suit property mortgaged was false and forged.

20. Title Suit No. 147 of 1992 against Coast Marine Line Ltd was pending in the 4th Court of Artha Rin Adalat. Property of the suit was shown mortgaged there. The plaintiff was impleaded as defendant. In the written statement it was stated that the property remained mortgaged up to 17-11-88. He denied that he was the real owner of the firms of Shawkat Ali and that he got the suit instituted through the plaintiff. On 29-2-88 he applied for loan and in the application security were mentioned, that was not executed. To the question of court he replied that he proposed to mortgage one concrete built house valued at Taka 1 (one) crore and thereby nothing mentioned, his house or any particular house.

21. Azfar Ahmed testified as DW 1 on behalf of the defendant No.1 bank. He stated that the plaintiff was related to Coast Marine Line Ltd. AB Siddique was the main loanee. He took loan on behalf of Coast Marine Line Ltd. On 29-2-88 he applied for loan of Bai-Muajjal investment facility of Taka 99,00,000 for purchase of two coastal vessels. He offered to give security of the property of Gulshan of which the plaintiff was the owner. The property was mortgaged to them in respect of other loans. They sanctioned Taka 99,00,000. Mortgage property was leasehold property vide deed of lease dated 28-10-66.

22. In cross-examination, he stated that he was working in the defendant bank since 1990, after the questioned transactions. He deposed in Title Suit No. 113 of 2000 of the Fourth Court of Artha Rin Adalat. The suit property was once mortgaged. He saw the charge document of March, 1988 executed by Rina Alam. He could not say whether the property was still mortgaged on 17-11-88.

23. After sanction of a loan, charge documents, collateral security and other documents were executed, before any disbursement. Sanction letter dated 19-6-88 in favour of Coast Marine Line Ltd was issued. In sanction letter, it was not mentioned that the property of Rina Alam would be mortgaged. Coast Marine Line Ltd was a limited company. In case of loan to such limited company, a resolution of the board of directors was required. No such resolution was obtained from AB Siddique Ludu. Rina Alam was neither a share holder nor director of the company. There was no written or oral consent of Rina Alam for mortgage of her property against the loan of Coast Marine Line Ltd. It was a tradition of the bank to obtain a general power of attorney in case any loan was taken. No such power of attorney was obtained from Rina Alam. No legal notice or letter was issued to Rina Alam that her property would be sold.

24. He had no knowledge that the bank issued letter of adjustment dated 13-7-92 adjusting the loans of Shawkat in respect of Gold Star Lines and M/S Trans Bangla Shipping Lines. He could not show any consent of Rina Alam in respect of loan of Taka 99,00,000 of the BSRS. He could not show any connection or consent of Rina Alam in respect of issue of Exhibit E(2). It is true that disbursement as shown on 17-3-88 violated clause VII of sanction letter dated 19-6-88 Exhibit C. At the time the suit property was mortgaged against another loan and no letter of consent was obtained from the plaintiff for further mortgage of the property. Clause 14(ii) and (iii) of the sanction letter was not complied with. In the legal notice dated 8-6-92 for payment of loan, name of the plaintiff was not there. They did not pray for examination of the signature of Rina Alam by a handwriting expert. No one witnessed said two deeds. Those who prepared the documents did not sign. EXhibit L was not purchased in the name of the plaintiff, it was true. It was not true that signature of Rina Alam in said two questioned documents was forged. Pan Asia project did not see the light of the day for long. He had no knowledge in that respect. It was not true that the bank mala fide entered the deed of previous loans against the account of other loan.

25. These are all the oral evidence adduced by the parties.

26. On the evidence, oral and documentary, learned Joint District Judge by impugned judgment and decree decreed the suit in part and declared that loans taken on behalf of Ms Gold Star Lines and M/S Trans Bangla Shipping Lines were adjusted on 17-11-88 and further declared that memorandum of deposit of title deed dated 17-3-88 was created, forged, fraudulent and ineffective; and directed defendant No.1 bank to return schedule title deed No. 788 along with other documents to the plaintiff.

27. Mr Sayyid Shahid Hussain, learned Advocate for the appellant bank, submitted that learned Joint District Judge failed to consider the loan application Exhibit 6, sanction advice exhibit-C, original deeds of title of Rina Alam filed by the bank Exhibits H, I, and J to J(7), memorandum of deposit of title deed Exhibit E, deed to create further charge Exhibit L and oral evidence which conclusively and clearly proved that the plaintiff mortgaged the suit property to the bank again and thereby, erred in law in decreeing the suit.

28. Secondly, he submitted that after the Artha Ain Adalat found the suit property was mortgaged again, the present suit ought to be barred by principles of res judicata. In support, he cited Ms Sekendar Jute Baling Ltd vs Sonali Bank and another 1998 BLD (AD) 268; Vemlata Reddy vs Pethi Reddy, AIR 1963 SC 992, Satyadhyan Ghosal and others vs Smt. Dearjin Bibi and others, AIR 1960 SC 941; Nikunja Behari Das vs Jatindra Nath Kar, AIR 1956 Cal.613; Makhan Lal vs. Ghulam Hussain, AIR 1933 Lahore 536 and Abdulla and others v Abdul Karim and others, 20 DLR (SC) 205.

29. Mr. Rafique-ul Hoque, learned Senior Advocate, on the other hand, submitted that no issue on res judicata was framed in the Artha Rin suit and no step was taken for stay of further proceedings of the present suit pending decision of the Artha Rin suit, hence the decision of the Artha Rin Adalat will not be binding on the civil Court.

30. He submitted that the defendant bank miserably failed to prove further mortgage of same property of the plaintiff and the learned Joint District Judge therefore, did not commit any error in decreeing the suit.

31. In view of the conflicting submissions, the questions as to (a) whether the plaintiff further mortgaged her property by deposit of her title deeds and (b) whether the decree of the Artha Rin Adalat dated 24-5-2001 would act and/or operate as res judicata for the present suit are the moot issues facing us.

32.	We have perused the record as placed.

33.	As stated above, the plaintiff deposited her title deed No. 788 creating mortgage to secure the loans of Gold Star Lines and Trans Bangla Shipping Lines. Said loans were admittedly liquidated on 17-11-88. Said deed was also offered as a security against a proposed project of Pan Asia Lines. But the project did not ultimately materialise. On 13-7- 92 the bank issued two certificates stating that the loans were fully adjusted on 17-11-88, Exhibits 1 and 1(K). Then, the plaintiff on 17-12-92 wrote a letter addressed to the bank for return of her title documents, which the bank received on 19-12-92.

34. The case of the bank is that, during the continuance of the mortgage the plaintiff further mortgaged the property to secure Bai-muajjal facility for an amount of Taka 99,50,000 sanctioned to the Coast Marine Line Ltd by executing a memorandum of deposit of title deed on 17-3-88, Exhibit E. She further executed a deed of agreement for creating further charges dated 9-3-89, Exhibit L.

35. The plaintiff categorically denied to have executed any of the documents. She claimed that she never went to the bank. She never mortgaged her property to secure the loan of Coast Marine Lines Ltd.

36. Clause (f) of section 58 of the Transfer of Property Act defines mortgage by deposit of title-deeds as follows,

"Where a person delivers to a creditor or his agent documents of title to immovable property, with intent to create a security thereon, the transaction is called a mortgage by deposit of title-deeds."

37. In order to create a mortgage by deposit of title deeds,

(a) a person must deliver the deeds and (b) with intent to create a security thereon.

38. When creating mortgage by deposit of the deeds is denied, the burden is on the bank to prove that the plaintiff delivered the deeds with intent to create security. It must not also escape the notice that the schedule deed was already deposited in the bank in respect of other loans when further security on the deed was claimed to have been created on 17-3-88.

39. Defendant bank examined one of its officers who joined the bank in 1990. He had no knowledge about the execution of the memorandum of deposit of title deeds and the agreement for creating further charge. He said that he deposed on the basis of the record. So, there is practically no evidence on record to prove execution by the plaintiff of either the memorandum of deposit of title deeds or the agreement for creating further charges, exhibit E and L respectively.

40. The bank however, did not take any step to prove execution of the documents. Neither the deed writer nor anyone witnessing the execution of  the documents was examined.

41. DW 1 admitted that the bank never obtained any written or oral consent of the plaintiff in creating further charges on the deed. It neither obtained any power of attorney as it did in case of earlier loans. Nor the bank ever demanded repayment of any amount from the plaintiff. Even in the legal notice dated 8-6-92 the plaintiff was not named.

42. Now, let us see how the bank created further security on the deed of the plaintiff.

43. On 29-2-88 said AB Siddique applied for Bai-Muajjal facility. On 19-6-88 the bank issued sanction advice granting Bai-Muajjal facility to Coast Marine Lines Ltd. In the sanction letter, the property of the plaintiff was not mentioned to be mortgaged. But before issue of sanction, the bank claims that on 17-3-88 money was disbursed. DW 1 testified that after sanction, charge documents including collateral were executed. It was a limited company. Neither any resolution of the board of directors nor any power of attorney was obtained. Disbursement of loan on 17-3-88, according to DW 1, clearly violated clause VB of the sanction letter. DW 1 further stated that clauses 14(ii) and (iii) of the sanction letter were not complied with.

44. Mr Shahid submitted strenuously that if the plaintiff had not created further charge on the deeds why she did not take any step for return of the deeds. He also claimed that the copy of the letter dated 19-12-92 was created by her. In the facts and circumstances of the case, such wild suggestion is not at all accepted. It is on record that after adjustment of the loans of Gold Star Lines and Trans Bangla Shipping Lines, another project of Pan Asia Lines for purchase of two vessels from London was submitted by Serajul Alam and others and property of the plaintiff was offered as collateral. As project did not materialise, the plaintiff demanded return of her title deeds by letter dated 17-12-92 which the bank received by putting the round seal of the bank. The balk did never deny the seal. Nor any step was taken to prove the seal forged.

45. The plaintiff deposited her original deeds in trust with the bank. The bank was required to take utmost care in dealing with such security, particularly in making further charge on the deeds. Admittedly, the bank never approached the plaintiff nor obtained any consent oral or written of the plaintiff for making further charge on the document. Such conduct is not becoming with the banking ethics, customs and practice. What disturbed us most how a bank could have created without any consent of the plaintiff further security on the deed already deposited in the bank in connection with and continuance of another loan.

46. In the circumstances, we find no reason to differ with the views of the learned Joint District Judge that the plaintiff did not execute the memorandum of deposit of title deed dated 17-3-88 Exhibit E or the agreement for further charge dated 9-3-89 Exhibit Land that she did not further mortgage her property to secure the loan of Ms Coast Marine Lines Ltd. "

47. May be, when the bank failed to prove creation of further charge on the deeds, Mr Shahid submitted, mainly on the principles of res judicata just like a drowning man struggling to survive, catching a straw.

48. What is res judicata has not been defined in Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990. Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure defines res judicata.

"No Court shall try any suit or issue in which the matter directly and substantially in issue has been directly and substantially in issue in a former suit between the same parties, or between parties under whom they or any of them claim, litigating under the same title, in a court competent to try such subsequent suit or the suit in which such issue has been subsequently raised, and has been heard and finally decided by such court."

<u>49. In order to bring subsequent suit within the mischief of section 11, first and foremost requirement is that the Court in which former suit was pending and/or decided must be competent to try subsequent suit. Said Court must be of concurrent jurisdiction both in respect of pecuniary jurisdiction and subject.</u>

50. On 30-10-92 the bank instituted Title Suit No. 147 of 1992 before the Artha Rin Adalat at Dhaka and on 14-7-97 the plaintiff instituted her Title Suit No. 208 of 1997 before the Fifth Court of Subordinate Judge at Dhaka. After five years, the suit of the plaintiff was instituted. Cause of action for the suit of the plaintiff arose only when the bank refused to return the deed in question and therefore, not same as that of the suit of the bank. Relief sought for in the suits is not the same. Both suits continued side by side before two forums for a pretty good time. No step was taken by the bank either before the civil Court or Artha Rin Adalat to stay further proceedings of the subsequent suit. Reason is obvious. Neither the suit before the civil Court could be stayed pending decision of the suit before the Artha Rin Adalat nor the other way round, the suit before the Artha Rin Adalat could be stayed for the suit of the civil Court.

<u>51. Jurisdiction of Artha Rin Adalat. Artha Rin Adalat was created with particular objective, mainly for recovery of bank dues. To achieve the purpose, Artha Rin Adalat was made deemed to be a civil Court but not a full-fledged civil Court with all powers and jurisdiction of a civil Court. It is a civil Court of defined and limited jurisdiction; [Sultana Jute Mills Ltd vs Agrani Bank, 46 DLR (AD) 147]. Precisely, Artha Rin Adalat had no jurisdiction to decide the suit of the plaintiff.</u>

52. In the suit of the bank before the Artha Rin Adalat, relief was sought for a money decree of Taka 1,33,70,592 with interest and for realisation of the money by sale of mortgaged vessels and property described in the schedule to the plaint. In schedule, house property of the plaintiff was described. The suit therefore, does not appear to be a typical mortgage suit.

53. In the plaint of Artha Rin Suit, the bank just claimed that defendant No. 4, the plaintiff herein, on 17-3-88 created equitable mortgage by deposit of the title deeds of schedule property as suety. The bank did not claim that on 17-3-88 the plaintiff executed a memorandum of deposit of title deed or on 9-3-89 executed the agreement for creating further charge on the deeds in question. The defendants including the plaintiff jointly denied the claim of mortgage. The bank did not suggest any issue on such mortgage and, as such, no issue was framed by the Artha Rin Adalat. The parties, particularly the plaintiff, did not adduce all the evidence that was adduced in the present suit. In the judgment, the Adalat however, found, in so many words, that the property was mortgaged.

54. Lastly, we find learned Judge of the Artha Rin Adalat corrected his typed judgment by adding following two sentences with hand, without any initial-

“অর্থাৎ বর্তমান মোকাদ্দমার ঋণের বিপরীতে উত্ত সম্পত্তি দায়মুত্ত হয় নাই।”

“এই প্রত্যয়নপত্র দুটি তদন্ত ব্যতিরেকে দেওয়া হইয়াছে বিধায় আইনগত কোন মূল্য নাই।”

In the application made under section 151 of the Code or Civil Procedure filed by the defendants before the Artha Rin Adalat said alterations were mentioned. The bank did not deny the alterations. It further appears that on 20-5-01 the Judge. Artha Rin Adalat wrote to the District Judge for transfer of the suit from his Adalat since he was feeling embarrassed. The District Judge by his letter dated 21-5-01 rejected the prayer expressing that feeling embarrassment was not expected of a Judge. Said application was however, allowed and the property of the plaintiff was deleted from the schedule of the decree.

55. Against which, the bank already obtained a Rule Nisi moving this Division in writ jurisdiction.

56. Be that as it may, the decision of Artha Rin Adalat cannot act as res judicata to bar a suit before a Civil Court.

57. In above view of the matter, impugned judgment and decree therefore do not suffer from any illegality and infirmity. The appeal fails.

58. In the result, the appeal is dismissed with cost. Impugned judgment and decree are hereby affirmed.

59. The bank is directed to return the schedule document within seven days of receipt of this judgment.

Send down the LCR at once.

End.

parties:
Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation, and others ------ Appellant (in all the cases)
VS
Md. Abdur Rashid and others ------ Respondents
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 6th July, 2010, 27th September, 2010 and 8th October, 2009 passed by the High Court Division in Review Petition Nos. 49 of 2010, 48 of 2010, 52 of 2010 and Writ Petition No. 2331 of 2009.)
full_judgment:
Hasan Foez Siddique J: Civil Appeal Nos. 45 to 48 of 2012 have been heard together. Since all the appeals raised common points of law, they are being disposed of by this single judgment.

<u>2. The common question in these appeals is as to whether employees who opted for voluntary retirement pursuant to or in response of a special scheme floated by the Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation (BADC) would be precluded from reinstatement in their services after acceptance of their prayers for voluntary retirement and payment of retirement benefits.</u>

3. In Civil Appeal No. 45 of 2012, the respondent Nos. 1-5 filed Writ Petition No. 8872 of 2008 being aggrieved by the notification dated 26-10-2002 issued by the Secretary, Ministry of Agriculture amending Clauses 4 and 5 of the Notification No. Krirhi-5/Ma-2/98 (Part-8)/727 dated 17-11-1999 issued by the Government with regard to reorganization of BADC and office order communicated under Memo Noস্বেচ্ছা/১ক১/২০০২/২০০৩/৩৬১ dated 20-10-2002 purportedly terminating 135 employee including writ petitioners. The High Court Division made the said rule absolute holding that identical matter had been disposed of by a judgment and order dated 27-5-2008 by this Division in Civil Appeal Nos. 158- 184 of 2006 and Civil Appeal No.136 of 2007. Accordingly, the writ respondents were directed to re-instate the writ petitioners to their respective posts with all wages subject to refund of the termination benefits by the writ petitioners, if those were withdrawn by them. BADC filed Review Petition No. 49 of 2010 in the High Court Division mainly on the ground that the writ petitioners were not terminated rather they had voluntary retired from their service. The High Court Division rejected the said review petition summarily holding that the service of the petitioners were terminated in the garb of voluntary retirement. Against the said order of rejection of review petition. BADC filing leave petition, obtained leave.

4. In Civil Appeal No. 46 of 2012, the writ petitioners Md Ataur Rahman and 7 others filed Writ Petition No. 7724 of 2008 being aggrieved by the above mentioned notifications and the orders of termination from their service. The High Court Division made the said Rule absolute taking similar views. BADC filed Review Petition No. 48 of 2010 on similar grounds. The High Court Division rejected the said review petition summarily holding that the order of termination had been passed in the garb of voluntary retirement. Against the said order, BADC, filing Civil Petition for leave to Appeal, got leave. While pressing this appeal No. 46 of 2012 Mr Mahbubey Alam, learned Senior Counsel, submits that out of the 8 writ petitioners, Md Ataur Rahman, Md Abdul Hakim, Mozibor Rahman and Md Anowarul Hoque had retired from their service voluntarily and the rest were terminated. Though the rest of the writ petitioners namely, Md Mostafizur Rahman, Md Alauddin, Md Amir Hossain and Nobiul Islam have been impleaded as respondent Nos. 5-8 in this appeal but he would not press the appeal against respondent Nos.5-8. Accordingly, the appeal be dismissed in respect of the respondents No. 5, Md Mostafizur Rahman No. 6. Md Alauddin No. 7. Md Amir Hossain and No. 8. Nobiul Islam.

5. In Civil Appeal No. 47 of 2012, respondent Md Rafiqul Alam was writ petitioner No. 5 in Writ Petition No. 7682 of 2007. The said Md Rafiqul Alam and 5 others filed the aforesaid writ petition challenging the above mentioned notices and the orders of termination. Similarly, Rule was also made absolute by the High Court Division observing that since identical matter had been disposed of by this Division, the writ petitioner, were entitled to get relief in the light of the said judgment. BADC filed Review Petition No. 52 of 2010 impleading Md Rafiqul Alam, stating that he had voluntarily retired from his service. So, the matter decided by the Appellate Division was not identical so far as it relates to Md Rafiqul Alam. The High Court Division summarily rejected the said review petition by an order dated 27-9-2010. Then, BADC preferred this appeal getting leave.

6. In Civil Appeal No. 48 of 2012, the respondents were 20 in number. They filed Writ Petition No. 2331 of 2009 being aggrieved by the above mentioned notifications and the orders of termination. The High Court Division made the said Rule absolute in the light of the decision and directed to reinstate the writ petitioners in their service. Against the said judgment and order, BADC preferred this appeal getting leave. Mr Mahbubey Alam, learned Senior Counsel, submits that he would not press the appeal in respect of other respondents except respondent No. 9, Md Safiul Alam Khondoker, who had retired from service voluntarily. Accordingly, the appeal be dismissed against the other respondents except the respondent No. 9, Md Safiul Alam Khondoker.

7. Mr Mahbubey Alam, learned Senior Counsel appears on behalf of the appellants for all the appeals. On the other hand, Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, Senior Counsel appears for respondent Nos. 1-5 in Civil Appeal No. 45 of2012 and Mr Probir Neogi appears for the respondent in Civil Appeal No. 47 of2012.

8. No one appears on behalf of the respondents in other appeals.

9. Mr Mahbubey Alam, submits that the respondents, against whom he is pressing the appeals, had voluntary retired from their services and had withdrawn their financial benefits. They were not terminated from their service. After acceptance of their prayers for voluntary retirement and payment of the financial benefits, the respondents could not claim that they had been terminated from the service. The High Court Division has committed error of law in holding that the service of these respondents had been terminated in the garb of voluntary retirement.

10. Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, learned Senior Counsel appearing for the respondent Nos. 1-5 in Civil Appeal No. 45 of 2012, submits that the prayers for voluntary retirement of respondents were stayed by BADC and allowed them to continue for a considerable period thereby those prayers had been rejected by implication. By the impugned orders all the respondents had been terminated in the garb of voluntary retirement. The High Court Division rightly held so.

11. Mr Probir Neogi, appearing on behalf of the respondent in Civil Appeal No. 47 of 2012, submits that the respondent Md Rafiqul Alam initially though submitted an application for voluntary retirement but the same was not accepted and by the impugned order he had been terminated. He further submits that Rafiqul Islam did not receive any financial benefit out of same scheme of voluntary retirement like other respondents who had retired from services voluntarily. He submits that the High Court Division rightly declared the order of termination void and meanwhile BADC had reinstated him and he has been serving in BADC.

12. It appears from the materials on record that in Civil Appeal No. 45 of 2012 the respondents are 5 in number. They are I. Md Abdur Rashid, 2. Md Fazlur Rahman, 3. Solaiman Ali, 4. Md Abdur Rashid Mondal, 5. Md Jahangir Alam. Md Abdur Rashid prayed for voluntary retirement with effect from 30-9-1994. BADC, accepting the said prayer by a letter communicated under memo No. স্বেচ্ছা/১ক ১/২০০২/২০০৩/৩৬১ dated 20-10-2002, paid his retirement benefits who received 80% of the payable benefits on 23-11-2002. Respondent No.2, Md Fazlur Rahman prayed for voluntary retirement from service with effect from 30-9-1994 which was accepted by BADC on 20-10- 2002. This respondent received his entire retirement benefits of Taka 2,85,728 on 26-11-2002 under special scheme of voluntary retirement and 19-5-2003. Respondent No. 3, Solaiman Ali prayed for such voluntary retirement with effect from 30-9-1994 which was accepted on 20-10-2002. The payable financial benefits of retirement was 4,48,425. He had received Taka 3,65,120 on 23-11-2002 and Taka 16, 610 on 31-7-2004. The respondent No. 4, Md Abdur Rashid Mondal prayed for voluntary retirement from his service with effect from 30-9-1994. The payable amount against his retirement benefits was Taka 2,62,729. He received Taka 76,737 on 12-5-2003 and Taka 23,311 on 20-12-2004. Respondent No. 5, Md Jahangir Alam prayed for a voluntary retirement from service with effect from 30-9-1994 and payable amount against his retirement benefits was Taka 3,61,145. He received Taka 3,51,145 on 30-11-2002 and Taka 10,615 on 31-7-2004. Similarly, respondent No.1, Md Ataur Rahman No.2. Md Abdul Hakim, No.3. Mozibor Rahman, No.4. Md Anowarul Hoque in Civil Appeal No.46 of 20 12 filed their respective applications for voluntary retirement from services with effect from 30-9-1994. BADC assessed the payable amount of financial benefits against their services and almost all of them withdrew considerable amount out of the amounts payable under such a special scheme of voluntary retirement.

13. Mr Probir Neogi, learned counsel for the respondent Md Rafiqul Alam, in Civil Appeal No. 47 of 2012 submits that meanwhile this respondent of this appeal has been re-instated and he has been serving in BADC. After such reinstatement of respondent Md Rafiqul Alam, we are of the view that the appeal against him is tenable.

14. In Civil Appeal No. 48 of 2012, Mr Mahbubey Alam, submits that the respondent No. 9. Md Safiul Alam Khondoker had retired from his service voluntarily. From the materials on record it appears that the respondent No. 9 Md Safiul Alam Khondoker prayed form voluntary retirement from service with effect from 30-9-1994. The same was accepted on 20-10-2002. Though it appears that, on 30-10-2002, he was terminated from service but Mr Alam submits that the same was a clerical mistake. After acceptance of the prayer for voluntary retirement from service, the question of termination thereafter does not arise. It further appears from the materials produced by the appellant that he had also received a considerable amount out of the amount payable as retirement benefits.

15. BADC was said to be overstaffed. For the purpose of effective management, manpower planning was contemplated by the Ministry of Agriculture. In order to downsize the strength of staffs of BADC, the Ministry of Agricultural issued a circular communicated under Memo No. কৃষি-৫/ম-২/(অংশ-১)/৩৭৫dated 13-12-1992, the Voluntary Retirement Scheme in which some privileges had been specially offered to the employees of BADC who intended to retire from their services voluntarily. As per terms of the scheme, the employees who sought for voluntary retirement, were entitled to accept ex gratia payment as specified therein. In said circular there was a clause wherein it was specifically mentioned,

"এই ব্যবস্থা সম্পূর্ণ ঐচ্ছিক তবে, একবার অবসর গ্রহনেরইচ্ছা প্রকাশ করলে টা পরে প্রত্যাহার করা যাবে না"

In their respective applications for voluntary retirement from service, the respondents mentioned that in view of the aforesaid circular they decided to retire from service, voluntarily. Knowing fully well about the consequence of the aforesaid clause of the circular they offered their prayers. That is, admitted position is that the respondents. while working in the BADC had applied for voluntary retirement, pursuant to the scheme framed by the Ministry of Agriculture to relieve the surplus staffs, which had been accepted by the impugned orders. Since the respondents had been relieved from the duty after acceptance of their offers of voluntary retirement and special payment of retirement benefits, the rural relationship of the BADC and respondents came to an end.

<u>16. In the case of AIR India vs Nergesh Mirza, Supreme Court of India held that Government servant is not entitled to demand as of right, permission to withdraw the letter of voluntary retirement, it could only be given as a matter of grace. In the case of State of Haryana vs SK Singhal reported in (1999)4 SCC 293 Supreme Court of India observed that the cases of voluntary retirement can broadly be decided into the following categories:</u>

<u>(i) Where voluntary retirement is automatic and comes into force on the expiry of notice period,</u>

<u>(ii) When it comes into force; unless an order is passed within the notice period with holding permission; and</u>

<u>(iii) When voluntary retirement does not come to force unless permission to this effect is specifically granted by the controlling authority.</u>

<u>17. In the cases, in hand, the respondents, while working in the appellant BADC, had applied for voluntary retirement, and, thereafter, they withdrew all or considerable amounts of retirement benefits from BADC. Since the respondents had applied for voluntary retirements, such applications should be effective in view of the provision of the circular as quoted above or by the relevant law.</u>

<u>18. Mr Bhuiyan submits that since the BADC allowed the respondents to continue in service for a considerable period thereby BADC had rejected the prayers for voluntary retirement of the respondents by implication. It is not possible to accept the contention because as a general principle, one who knowingly accepts the benefits of the offer is estopped to deny the validity and binding effect of the offer and acceptance of the same. Moreover, clause 2 of the circular provides,"একবার অবসর গ্রহনের ইচ্ছা প্রকাশ করলে টা পরে প্রত্যাহার করা যাবে না"Implication may arise in consideration that statute is of something not expressly declared. He the circular quoted above provides that option once exercised shall be final. Section 9 of the Public Servant (Retirement) Act also provides so. Since the respondents accepted the ex-gratia payment, in our considered opinion, they could not have resiled there from.</u>

<u>19. In the case of Nand Keshwar Prasad vs Indian Farmers Fertilizers Co-operative Ltd. Supreme Court of India held that unless controlled by condition of service or the statutory provisions, the retirement mentioned in the letter of resignation must take effect from the date mentioned therein. The option having once been exercised the respondents could not go back on the same because the principle is that, one person may not approbate and reprobate expresses two proposition.</u>

<u>20. In view of the specific provision in the circular that,"একবার অবসর গ্রহনের ইচ্ছা প্রকাশ করলে টা পরে প্রত্যাহার করা যাবে না" which indicates as absolute terms and since that there is no provision quoted clause to withdraw prayers, we are of the view that prayers of voluntary retirements came in effect after acceptance of the prayers. The moment prayers are accepted the retirement become effective.</u>

<u>21. "Termination" and "voluntary retirement from the service" have different connotations and cannot be equated for the reasons that the termination can be termed as "naked hire and fire" rule and paralled of which was to be found only in the "Henry VIII clause". On the other hand. voluntary retirement scheme is a method used to reduce surplus staffs. Participation in the voluntary retirement plan is voluntary. It has to result in an overall reduction in the existing strength of employees. Accordingly, we are not inclined to accept the observation of the High Court Division that the respondents had been terminated in the grab of voluntary retirement. Moreover, the respondents have filed writ petitioners after about 8 years of the acceptance of their prayers and after receiving retirement benefits.</u>

<u>22. The instant process was a policy decision involving complex economic factors. The court would be slow from interfering with the economic decisions as it has been recognized that the economic expediencies lack adjudicative decision and unless the economic decision, based on economic expediencies, is demonstrated to be so violative of constitutional or legal limits. It is the administrators and legislators who are entitled to frame polices and take such administrative decisions as they think necessary in the public interest. The court should not ordinarily interfere with policy decisions, unless clearly illegal. We do not find any violation of constitutional provision or legal limits in the instant scheme.</u>

23. In view of the discussion made above Civil Appeal No. 45 of 2012 is allowed; Civil Appeal No. 46 of 2012 is allowed so far as it relates to respondent Nos. 1-4 namely (1) Md Ataur Rahman, (2) Md Abdul Hakim, (3) Mozibur Rahman and (4) Md Anwarul Haque and dismissed against the rests. Civil Appeal No. 47 of 2012 is dismissed. Civil Appeal No. 48 of 2012 is allowed so far as it relates to respondent No. 9 Md Saiful Alam Khondker and dismissed against the rests.

End.

lawyer:
Mahmudul Islam, Attorney-General instructed by Md Sajjadul Huq, Advocate-on-Record ----- For the Appellants.

parties:
Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Housing and Public Works and another ------ Appellants 
vs
Shirely Anny Ansari ------ Respondent
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 3-3-1999 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 7756 of 1997)
full_judgment:
Mahmudul Amin Choudhury J: This Civil Appeal by leave is against judgment and order dated 3-3-1999 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 7756 of 1997 making the Rule absolute.

2. Respondent as Writ Petitioner filed the aforesaid writ petition stating that she is a British national by birth and was married to Dr WA Ansari, a renowned Surgeon of erstwhile East Pakistan, Dr Ansari was given lease of a plot of land at Dhanmondi residential area which is plot No, 500-H, Road No. 8 (Old) of Plan No. 613/58 measuring an area of 14 kathas for a period of 99 years on 7-1-1960 with the option of renewal of lease. While Dr Ansari was in possession of the said plot he with proper permission constructed a one-storied building thereon. But subsequently, by a registered deed of gift dated 26-2-1965 he transferred the aforesaid land and building to his wife who is the respondent and in this way the writ petitioner became the absolute owner of the aforesaid property. It is the further case of the writ petitioner that she along with her husband Dr Ansari left for England in March 1971 leaving the house under the care of one Abdul but subsequently the Government declared the suit property as abandoned property under President's Order 16 of 1972. Coming to know of this declaration respondent appointed one Mr Habibuddin Ahmed, a retired Collector of Customs, as her constituted attorney and through this attorney she applied to the Government on 6-8-1979 for releasing the property from, the list of abandoned property but the same was rejected on 14-10-1979. Thereafter in January, 1981 the writ petitioner came to Dhaka and renewed her prayer for release of the property. She also produced her birth certificate and also other papers but in the meantime Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance 1985 was promulgated and on seeing the property in the list of abandoned property the writ petitioner filed case No 1042 of 1987 (Ka-29, Dhanmondi, Dhaka) before the Court of Settlement for releasing the property. But that petition was dismissed. Thereafter Writ Petition No. 7756 of 1997 was filed and a Rule obtained and the High Court Division then by judgment dated 3- 3-1999 made the Rule absolute and declared that the judgment of the Court of Settlement dated 18-8-1997 has been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and respondent No. 1 of the writ petition was directed to hand over physical possession of the property to the writ petitioner or her legal representative within 60 days from the date of receipt of copy of this judgment.

3. Leave was granted to consider the following:

“………………….in exercising jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution, the High Court Division committed error of law in acting, like a Court of appeal in interfering with the findings of fact arrived at by the Court of Settlement even though the Court of Settlement had not acted without jurisdiction nor made a finding on no evidence nor failed to consider any material evidence nor acted malafide."

4. Mr Mahmudul Islam, learned Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the appellants, submits that the High Court Division while disposing of the writ petition has lost sight of the fact that when a property has been enlisted as abandoned property the Government has no obligation either to deny the fact alleged by the claimant or to disclose the basis of treating the property as abandoned property. The onus is on the claimant to prove that the property is not an abandoned property. Drawing our attention to the judgment of the judgment of the Court of Settlement the learned Attorney-General contends that the respondent who claimed the property on the basis of an alleged gift failed to prove that there was actually a valid gift and the deed of gift has been acted upon. He further submits that the High Court Division while disposing of the writ petition wrongly observed that as the deed of gift is a registered one it has a presumptive value as regards its genuineness which has escaped the notice of the Court of Settlement. The Attorney-General further submits that the High Court Division committed wrong in holding that the production of the certified copy of the registered deed of gift instead of the original deed would not make much of a difference and the claim of ownership of the petitioner cannot be defeated on that count. The learned Attorney-General further submits that the High Court Division committed wrong in holding that the failure of the writ petitioner to mutate her name on its own cannot defeat the ownership of the property. It is contended that the writ petitioner-respondent failed to prove that the deed of gift has been acted upon. Mere registration of such deed is not sufficient to prove that there was a valid gift such a gift must be coupled with delivery of possession which could not be proved by the writ petitioner. It is also contended that while disposing of the writ petition the High Court Division it appears acted as a Court of appeal which is not permissible under the law.

5. Mr Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the writ petitioner-respondent, submits that in a case of gift under the Transfer of Property Act no delivery of possession is necessary. According to him, the present deed of gift is not under Mohammadan Law but under the Transfer of Property Act. He also submits that the High Court Division has not acted as an appellate Court but simply corrected the error of law committed by the Court of Settlement. He also contended that when the certified copy of the deed of gift has been produced the Court of Settlement cannot question the validity of that document. The Court of Settlement travelled beyond its jurisdiction by embarking upon an inquiry whether the deed of gift has been acted upon or not. It is contended that when the claimant succeeded in proving title over the property on the basis of a registered deed of gift the Court of Settlement can not but order releasing the property.

6. Admittedly the property belonged to Dr WA Ansari who got the lease of the property from the then Dhaka Improvement Trust for 99 years on 7-1-1960. It is also an admitted fact that with the approval of the plan by the then Dhaka Improvement Trust Dr. Ansari constructed a building on the case property. It is the definite case of the respondent that while in possession and enjoyment of the property Dr Ansari by a registered' deed of gift dated 26-2-1965 transferred the said property in favour of his Wife-writ petitioner and she became the absolute owner of the same. It is also the case of the writ petitioner that earlier in March 1971 the writ petitioner along with her husband Dr Ansari left for England leaving the house with a caretaker but subsequently after liberation of Bangladesh the property was enlisted as abandoned property. The writ petitioner filed several applications to different authorities for release of the property but without success. Then she unsuccessfully moved the First Court of Settlement, Dhaka claiming the property as her own on the basis of a gift from her husband.

From the aforesaid admitted position it appears that the case property originally belonged to Dr WA Ansari and it is the case of the respondent that he transferred the property to the respondent by a registered deed of gift in the year 1965. So claim of the respondent is on the basis of a deed of gift. The Court of Settlement it appears has found that the deed of gift is not a valid document as the same was not properly registered. The Court of Settlement found that there was no signature or LTI of Dr Ansari in the volume for registration of the deed of gift which falls short of requirement of law and that there was no evidence that Dr Ansari was exempted from appearing before the Sub-Registrar. The Court of Settlement also found that there was no evidence that the deed of gift has been acted upon.

7. As regards execution and registration of the deed of gift it appears that the Court of Settlement failed to appreciate the legal position and the facts involved in the present case. It appears from the letter of the Sub-Registrar that the deed of gift was duly executed and registered. When the competent authority has certified that the deed has been duly registered the Court of Settlement cannot question the registration. Whether the executant has signed the volume or not is the concern of the registering authority and not of the Court of Settlement. It further appears that none has challenged this registration of the deed of gift. The only duty of the Court of Settlement is to look into the claim of the respondent on the basis of this deed of gift. In such a situation the Court of Settlement very well may look into whether the deed of gift has been acted upon or not. The fate of this case depends upon this. If it is found that the deed of gift has been acted upon then the property is to be released, otherwise not.

8. Admittedly before the Court of Settlement only the certified copy of the deed of gift has been filed, no other document including mutation papers with the Dhaka Improvement Trust and the Government Revenue authority, Municipal papers etc have been filed. And no explanation has also been given for non-filing of these basic documents.

<u>9. It is well settled that in case of transfer apart from the registration of the document it must be proved that there was complete divesting of the ownership i.e. donor had voluntarily transferred the property to the donee and acceptance by him/her. It is apparent that the registration of a deed of gift is not sufficient to constitute a gift it must be coupled with delivery of possession and acceptance of the same. Admittedly the respondent is the wife of the donor and they were both living as husband and wife in the case property. In such a situation actual physical delivery of possession is impossible. It is also well settled that mere recital of delivery of possession in the deed is also not sufficient. There must be something shown to indicate the acceptance of the gift and this acceptance may be signified by an overt act such as actual taking of possession of the property or such an act by the donee as would in law amount to taking delivery of possession. Where the property is not capable of physical possession the acceptance may be shown by mutating her name in the official records, municipal papers and also with the revenue authority. It is well settled that where the donee received the deed of gift from the donor after its due execution and presented the same for registration it is sufficient indication of the acceptance of the gift. Case of the respondent is that Dr. Ansari transferred the case property to the respondent by registered deed of gift but before the Court of Settlement or before the High Court Division or even before this Court she has not produced the original deed of gift, the original lease deed of Dr Ansari, any mutation paper and any paper of revenue authority including the Municipality or any other document from which it can be found that she got implied possession of the property or that there was acceptance of the gift. It is true that where the subject matter of the gift is enjoyed jointly by the donor and the donee it is difficult to prove the actual delivery of possession but this can be proved by implied evidence i.e. by mutating the name, getting the original deed of gift and other related documents of the property. In the case before us excepting the certified copy of the deed of gift nothing has been produced.</u>

<u>10. Mr Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Advocate submits that present deed of gift is a gift under section 123 of the Transfer of Property Act and, as such, no delivery of possession is required but we fail to agree with his submission as the law on this point is very clear. The consistent view of the higher Courts of Sub-Continent is that not only a gift under Mohammadan Law but also under the Transfer of Property Act, a gift must be coupled with acceptance and delivery of possession of the property. Mere registration of such deed of gift is not at all sufficient. The Court of Settlement in the present case travelled beyond its jurisdiction holding that there was no proper registration which fact has been belied by a letter from the Sub-Registrar who is the competent authority to register such a document. Drawing our attention to the provision of sections 74 and 76 of the Evidence Act, Mr Khandker submits that as the registered document is a public document the production of the certified copy before the Court of Settlement is sufficient indication of transfer of title. Section 74 of the Evidence Act defined what are known as public documents and 76 dealt with the certified copy of such documents. We have already observed that mere registration of the deed of gift is not sufficient. Here deed of gift was registered but only the certified copy of the same has been produced which is not sufficient indication that the deed has been acted upon, something more has to be done for making a valid gift which is very much lacking in the present case Sections 74 and 76 of the Evidence Act has failed to help Mr Khandker in the matter.</u>

11. We have gone through the judgment of the High Court Division and it appears that the learned Judges of that Division based their decision only on the fact that the deed of gift is a registered one overlooking the fact that there was no indication of legal acceptance of the gift and that the same has been acted upon as required under law.

12. It is the case of the respondent that the deed of gift has been registered. The production of the original deed of gift by the donee and other documents such as mutation paper, municipal record would have indicated that the same has been acted upon. But neither the original deed of gift nor the original lease deed of Dr Ansari nor any mutation paper nor any municipal record have been produced to prove the claim of the respondent In view of the aforesaid we hold that the High Court Division misdirected itself in holding that when there was a registered deed of gift the respondent has a genuine and strong claim over the property.

13. Having given our anxious consideration to the facts and circumstances of the case and after hearing the learned Advocates of both sides we hold that the High Court Division wrongly made the Rule absolute which requires interference.

This appeal is accordingly, allowed without any order as to costs, Judgment of the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 7756 of 1997 is hereby set aside and that of the Court of Settlement restored.

End.
