<u>"Where the law making authority is of a limited or qualified character it may be necessary to examine with some strictness the substance of the legislation for the purpose of determining - what is that the legislature is really doing".</u>

<u>It is, therefore, the substance of a law and not its form that matters. If the subject-matter of a law in substance is something which is beyond the Legislature's power to legislate upon, its outward form cannot save it from the mischief of judicial review. In such cases investigation may be held to find out whether what has been made is in fact within the power of the Legislature. For the purpose of this investigation, Court can examine the effect of the legislation and take into consideration its object, purpose and design. (Attorney General for Alberta Vs. Attorney General for Canada, 1939 AC 117).</u>

38. Reading the Repeal Act as a whole we find that it has repealed the Upazila Parishad Ordinance (No. 59 of 1982) and abolished the Upazila Parishads created there under. Consequent on the abolition of the Parishads certain provisions were also made in the Repeal Act, such as, assets of the Parishads shall vest in the Government who shall also accept the liabilities of the Parishads; litigations filed by and against the parishads and pending at the time of the Repeal Act shall be regarded as litigations filed by and against the government; officers and employees of the Parishads shall stand transferred to the Government, etc. We do not find any wrong in these provisions made consequent to the repeal of the parent law. The observation made by one of the two learned Judges of the High Court Division that the assets of one abolished local body can be vested only in another local body and not in the Government is not correct. Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed, however, contends that "if only the rights, powers authorities and privileges accrued or acquired before the abolition of the Parishads were intended to be vested in the government, then a language similar to section 6(c) of the General Clauses Act ought to have been used; but the language of sec. 2(2)(kha) of the Repeal Act cannot be construed to limit the vesting to accrued or acquired "rights, powers, authorities and privileges". In fact the legislative intent behind the repeal, he concludes, is to provide for continued functioning of the abolished Parishads under the administrative direction of the government. Learned Counsel has in this connection referred to two executive Instructions of the government to the Upazila Nirbahi Officers which tend to show that the Government officers are continuing the functions of the abolished Parishads.

39. Learned Attorney-General, refuting this contention, has referred to about a dozen Executive Instructions of the Government issued to the Upazila Nirbahi Officers and other officers posted in the Upazila head-quarters to show that the Upazila Parishads as "body corporate" have been totally abolished, that all officers and employees of the Parishads, who were in fact officers and employees of the Government but were "deemed to be on deputation to the Parishads" have been reverted to their respective Ministries, Departments and Directorates and are now working directly under their immediate superiors posted at the District Head-quarters, drawing their salaries from the budgetary allocations of the respective Ministries. He has explained that in the transition period, the Upazila Nirbahi Officer, who is the senior most among officers of the government posted to the Upazila administration has been directed by the government to coordinate and supervise the various functions and affairs of the government consequent on the abolition of the Parishad. The Nirbahi Officer, along with officers of other Government Departments, has been running the affairs of Government and not of any corporate body like the defunct Parishad.

<u>40. It appears to us that the legislative drafting of section 2(2)(kha), particularly the words in Bengali "rights, powers, authorities and privileges of the abolished Parishads" has apparently created an impression that those attributes of the Parishads have remained to be enjoyed by the Government. If these words are deleted then no confusion will be left. Upon consideration of the entire Repeal Act we do not find any substance in the contention that it is a colourable legislation. While dealing with the question as to whether the Upazila is an administrative unit we have found that it is not, and as such, an essential constitutional requirement for the Upazila Parishad to be a local government is not fulfilled. We have also found that the Upazila Parishad is not also wholly an elected body. This Parishad is therefore not a local government under the Constitution. Abolition of such a body violates no provision of the Constitution so as to attract the relief under Article 102 of the Constitution.</u>

<u>41. In view of the discussions above it is decided as follows:</u>

<u>i) On construction of Articles 59 and 60, read with Articles 9 and 11 of the Constitution and considering the origin, growth and development of Local Government Institutions at different levels of the Administration over one and a half centuries, it is found that Local Government is an integral part of the democratic polity of the country. The system of Local Government Institutions may be altered, re-organised or re-structured, and their powers and functions may be enlarged or curtailed by Act of Parliament, but the system as a whole cannot be abolished.</u>

<u>ii) For an Institution to be a Local Government under the Constitution, two requirements are to be fulfilled. One is that a Local Government is constituted in an "administrative unit", and the other is that the Local Government is entrusted to a body composed of elected persons.</u>

<u>iii) An "administrative unit", as defined in Article 152(1), is a "district or other area designated by law for the purposes of Article 59". In the case of a district, no designation is necessary, but it is necessary in all other cases as was done in the case of unions and municipalities by Act IX of 1973- The Bangladesh Local Government (Union Parishad and Paurashava) (Amendment) Act, 1973 before deletion of Articles 59 and 60 by Act II of 1975.</u>

<u>iv) An Upazila Parishad established by Ordinance No. 59 of 1982, as it stood amended by Ordinance No. 33 of 1983, is not a Local Government within the meaning of Article 59. This Parishad has been lawfully abolished by the impugned Ordinance No. 37 of 1991, which has been later on made an Act, Act No. 2 of 1992. These are valid laws and not ultra vires the Constitution except the words “অধিকার ক্ষমতা, কর্তৃত্ব, সুবিধাদি” in sub-section (2) Kha) of section 2 of the said Ordinance/ Act.</u>

<u>But there are other local bodies constituted by, and functioning under different statutes. With the re-appearance of Articles 59 and 60 with effect from 18 September 1991 on which date the Twelfth Amendment of the Constitution was made, these local bodies shall have to be updated in conformity with Articles 59 and 60 read with Article 152(1) for the lawful functioning of the said local bodies. The areas in which these bodies other than the Zilla Parishads have been constituted shall have to be designated as administrative units by amending these statutes. Designation afresh of the unions and municipalities is also necessary in view of the fact that Act No. IX of 1973, along with the President's Order No. 22 of 1973. was itself repealed by Ordinance No. XC of 1976-Local Government Ordinance 1976 in the case of Unions and by Paurashava Ordinance, 1977-Ordinance No. XXVI of 1977-in the case of municipalities. Required designations by amending the relevant statutes with effect from the date on which the Twelfth Amendment of the Constitution was made should be provided as soon as possible-in any case within a period not exceeding four months from date.</u>

<u>vi) The other constitutional requirement for these local bodies is that they shall be entrusted to bodies "composed of persons elected in accordance with law". The existing local bodies are, therefore, required to be brought in line with Article 59 by replacing the non-elected persons by election keeping in view the provision for special representation under Article 9. Necessary action in this respect should be taken as soon as possible-in any case within a period not exceeding six months from date. In the suggested amending statutes, all actions taken by the local bodies concerned since 18 September 1991 should be ratified.</u>

In the result, both the appeals are dismissed without any cost. The leave petition is also dismissed.

MH Rahman J : I agree. I have got nothing to add.

ATM Afzal J: To think of writing anything further, after having perused the main judgment of my Lord the Chief Justice and those of my brothers Mustafa Kamal and Latifur Rahman H, is very likely to incur the ordinary human folly of repetition. But then it is human failing again which prompts me to make some observation on one or two topical matters.

44. Upazila Parishad, a tier of local Government at the upazila/thana level has been abolished by the impugned legislation, namely, the Local Government (Upazila Parishad and Upazila Administration Re-organisation) (Repeal) Ordinance, 1991 (Ordinance No. 37 of 1991), subsequently made into an Act, Act No.2 of 1992. This repealing Ordinance! Act indeed repealed the Local Government (Upazila Parishad and Upazila Administration Re-organisation) Ordinance, 1982 (LIX of 1982) under which the administration at the thana/later on called, Upazila level was re-organised and Upazila Parishad constituted.

<u>45. The repealed Ordinance is a relic of the erstwhile Martial Law regime and so is the abolished local Government i.e., Upazila Parishad. It may be of some interest to reflect that the precursor of the Upazila Parish ad was Thana Council which again was conceived during a Martial Law period and constituted under the Basic Democracies Order, 1959 promulgated by Field Marshal Mohammad Ayub Khan. It is of historical importance which should be mentioned that in the history of the evolution of local Government in this country over a period of more than a century and half which has been minutely delineated in the judgment of the learned Chief Justice there had never been a local Government at the thana level until it was introduced during the first Martial Law period in the then Pakistan as mentioned above. This local Government tier is thus a by product of the Martial Law era.</u>

<u>46. Now, a democratically elected Government has done away with this tier upon finding that "the Upazila system itself was liable for drainage of Government money productive activities which negated the welfare the people and the Upazila Parishads were not economically viable as they were more dependant on Government allocation rather than earning revenue from their own sources" (vide affidavit-in-opposition of the respondents). In a further affidavit before this court it has been stated that after the enactment of the repealing Ordinance on 23.11.1991, a high level Local Government Review Commission was constituted by the Government to review and study the local government of Bangladesh and recommend a suitable, effective, responsible and accountable Local Government structure for Bangladesh.</u>

47. It has been rightly asserted by the respondents, and no learned Counsel has disputed it, that the constitution of Local Government Bodies and the tiers thereof have undergone changes from time to time since the Bengal Local Self Government Act, 1885 (Bengal Act III of 1885) was enacted, that such changes were made in exercise of Law-making power either by Act or by Ordinance or by President's Order and that thus the constitution and the tiers of local Government Bodies were always dependent on the policy of the respective Governments of the day.

48. The question of vires of the impugned Ordinance/Act was raised on the ground of inconsistency mainly with Articles 9, 11,59 and 60 of the Constitution. Article 9 which provides that the State shall encourage local Government institutions composed of representatives of the areas concerned etc, it is interesting to note, was not there in the original constitution but was again a contribution of a Martial Law regime, the same having been incorporated by Proclamations Order No.1 of 1977. Articles 59 and 60 and later part of Article 11 which speak of Local Government and peoples' participation in administration, although there in the original Constitution, were deleted with effect from 25 January 1975 by Act no II of 1975 (Fourth Amendment) and they remained in exile until brought back by Act No. XXVIII of 1991 (Twelfth Amendment) with affect from 18.9.91.

49. In this background, we were called upon to consider the challenge as to the vires of the impugned Ordinance/Act made by Mr. Amirul Islam and Dr. Kamal Hossain. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, learned counsel for one of the appellants, however, did not impugn the Ordinance/Act wholesale. He frankly submitted that the repealing Ordinance/Act would have been unexceptionable if only the অধিকার, ক্ষমতা, কর্তৃত্ব ও সুবিধাদি of the বিলুপ্ত উপজেলা পরিষদ were not vested in the Government as provided in section 2 (2)(Kha) thereof. He conceded that the Government's power to reorganise, re-structure and re-model the local Government institutions in the light of current experience and needs of the society cannot be disputed and to that end the abolition of a tier of local Government (here Upazila Parishad) cannot be said to offend any provision of the Constitution. If it were a repeal simpliciter of the (repealed) Upazila Ordinance (LIX of 1982) without the aforesaid offending provision, there would have been no valid cause of action for the appellants, Mr. Ahmed submitted.

50. I would like to record my appreciation for the fair and bold stand taken by Mr. Ahmed. Indeed he has summed up the position in law correctly.

51. As to his submission that by the aforesaid provision in section 2(2)(Kha), there was a covert attempt to continue the Upazila Parishad through the Government servants in violation of the mandate in Article 59 that local Government should be entrusted to elected bodies, even though the repealing Ordinance/Act professed merely to abolish the Upazila Parishad and thus the same was a colourable legislation. I think there is not much to add after what has been stated in the judgments of the learned Chief Justice and Mustafa Kamal J. Mr. Ahmed is right in his contention that the provisions of Articles 59 and 60 are limitations on the plenary legislative power of the Parliament in the field of Local Government.

<u>52. The contention of the learned Attorney-General that the Legislature may without designating an area as an administrative unit for the purpose of Article 59 in exercise of its plenary legislative power (Article 65) establish local Government is mischievous as it would amount to defying the mandate of Articles 59 and 60 which cannot be permitted. The argument, therefore, must be rejected.</u>

53. The vesting of অধিকার, ক্ষমতা etc, of the বিলুপ্ত উপজেলা পরিষদ in the Government as provided in section 2(2)(Kha) of the repealing Ordinance/Act was apparently made as the draftsman blindly followed and copied the usual sections in case of a repeal without understanding that in the present case there was no successor local Government to be vested with the powers, etc. of the abolished local Government. A reference to section 66 of the repealed Upazila Ordinance (LIX of 1982) will show that after abolition of the Thana Parishad, provision was made in sub-section 2(b) that "all assets, rights, powers, authorities and privileges, and all property ........................... of the abolished Parishad .................. shall stand transferred to and vest in the (Upazila) Parishad". In contrast it will be seen that when the Thana Council was dissolved under PO No.7 of 1972 and no provision was made for any kind of local Government at that level it was only provided in Article 5(b) thereof that "the assests and liabilities of a dissolved Thana Council shall vest in the Zilla Board concerned and the employees of such Thana Council shall be deemed to be the employees of such Zilla Board".

54. There was no necessity of vesting in the Government the rights, powers, authorities and privileges of the abolished Upazila Parishad and it clearly shows a lack of understanding of the powers of the Central Government vis-a-vis a Local Government, William Valenta in his book, "Local Government Law (American case book series) page 2 points out that "local Governments are not true sovereign governments, but political creatures and subdivisions of sovereign state governments. As such they possess no independent sovereign powers or authority, save those delegated to them by state constitutions and laws. In brief, they remain subject to the sovereign authority of the national and state governments" Indeed the purpose of the repealed Ordinance was to transfer some powers and functions of the Government to the Upazila Parishads. These were called "transferred subjects". When the Upazila Parishad was abolished by the repealing Ordinance/ Act, a fortiori those subjects reverted back to the Government and the whole field came to be occupied by it.

55. As to the larger question raised by the other learned Counsels, Mr. Islam and Dr. Hossain, that the repealing Ordinance/Act is ultra vires the Constitution being inconsistent with Articles 9, II, 59 and 60, it has been concurrently found by the learned Chief Justice and Mustafa Kamal J., with which I agree, that the Upazila Parishad not being a local Government within the meaning of Article 59, the abolition of such a body violates no provision of the Constitution. I would add that even if it were a local Government in terms of Article 59 even then the abolition thereof in the circumstances and as averred by the Government cannot be said to be violative of any provision of the Constitution. Upazila Parishad may not have been local Government strictly in terms of Article 59 but then it cannot be denied that it has all the attributes of a local Government. Mr. Amirul Islam laid great emphasis on the long historical background of the evolution and existence of local Government in the body polity of this country to impress upon us that the Constitution in its various provisions not only recognised this historical fact but also recommended for establishment of local Government as a part of the democratic fabric of the State.

<u>56. Accepting that the Upazila Parishad was a local Government and the Constitution provides for promotion of such local Government, can it be said that the abolition thereof has offended any provision of the Constitution. In the beginning of this judgment it has been noticed that the tiers of local Government had never been static and the Constitution and tiers of local Government depended on the legislative policy of the Government in office. It has also been noticed that the Government found the Upazila system not a viable one and set up a high level review 'commission to recommend a suitable, effective, responsible and accountable local Government structure for Bangladesh. Therefore, it may be said that by enacting the repealing Ordinance / Act, the Government has taken one step backward only to take more worthy steps (as professed) forward in the matter of local Government, As far as the policy behind such move is concerned it cannot be disputed that the same cannot be a matter for the Court to enter into. The system of local Government as such has not been done away with for good but a review has been undertaken to evolve a better system dismantling a tier at the thana level. I do not see therefore how it is inconsistent with Article 9. As for inconsistency with Article 11 that the repealing Ordinance! Act has denied participation by the people through their elected representatives in the Upazila Administration, the question does not arise because the Upazila (as an administrative unit) itself has been abolished and thus there cannot be any participation by the people the administration qua the Upazila.</u>

<u>57. There is no mandate in Article 59 that the legislature must designate any particular area as an administrative unit for the purpose of Article 59 or that the legislature must maintain a tier of local Government at the Thana level or in any particular area. There is no constitutional limitation in Article 59 that the legislature cannot abolish a local government of a particular tier if it is considered necessary. It cannot be disputed that the legislature has plenary power to repeal any law including one dealing with local Government. Thus viewed I do not find any inconsistency with any provision of the Constitution.</u>

58. Naimuddin J. in his judgment found that the Upazila Parishad was not a local Government institution within the meaning of Articles 59 and 9 of the Constitution and as such Article 9 cannot be invoked for declaring the repealing Ordinance/Act void under Article 7(2) on the ground of inconsistency with Article 9. He has not also found that the impugned Ordinance/Act is in conflict with any other provision of Part II of the Constitution containing Fundamental Principles of State Policy. That being so, it was wholly unnecessary to decide whether in view of the Provision in sub-article (2) of Article 8 that the principles set out in Part II shall not be judicially enforceable, any legislative act which is in direct conflict with and passed in flagrant violation of the provisions of Part II can be declared void under Article 7(2). Having answered this hypothetical question in the affirmative after taking hypothetical facts into consideration in a lengthy discussion, the learned Judge addressed himself to the real question thus;

"Consequently, if it is found that the impugned repealing Ordinance is violative of Article 9 of the Constitution it is liable to be struck down as void in view of Article 7(2) of the Constitution".

<u>59. Then the finding was made that the repealing Ordinance was not violative of Article 9 with which we have agreed. Therefore the broad decision that a law can be declared void in case of a conflict with any provision of Part II of the Constitution was uncalled for and made on hypothetical facts. This as a rule, the Courts always abhor. The Court does not answer merely academic question but confines itself only to the point/points which are strictly necessary to be decided for the disposal of the matter before it this should be more so when Constitutional questions are involved and the Court should be ever discreet in such matters. Unlike a civil suit, the practice in Constitutional cases has always been that if the matter can be decided by deciding one issue only no other point need be decided.</u>

Finally, I wish to express my full agreement with the main judgment prepared by the learned Chief Justice.

Mustafa Kamal J : In concurring with the judgment delivered by the learned Chief Justice, I would like to express my opinion on the issues involved, without duplicating the facts and without re-stating the history of local government which have been well-covered in his Lordship's judgment.

61. The debate centered round a repealing legislation-Ordinance No. XXXVII of 1991- shortly the Repealing Ordinance, later on made an Act-Act No. II of 1992, shortly the Repealing Act. The repealed legislation is Ordinance No. LIX of 1982, shortly the Repealed Ordinance.

Three broad questions, the first (i) Is the Repealing Ordinance/Act wholly or in part inconsistent with Articles 59 and 60 of the Constitution and is thus void either wholly or to the extent of the inconsistency under Article 7(2) of the Constitution?

62. Mr. Amirul Islam argued that the Repealing Ordinance/Act in its totality is inconsistent with Articles 59 and 60 of the Constitution. It destroys the elected part of the body. The Upazila exists as a territorial unit, a unit of administration. But the powers, authority, functions and privileges of dissolved Upazila Parishad are vested in the Government. In the garb of a repeal, it is a re-enactment and recreation of a local government to be run by an (unrepresentative body. Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed submitted that only the words ”অধিকার, ক্ষমতা, কর্তৃত্ব ও সুদিধাদি”  occurring in sub-section (2) of section 2 of the Repealing Ordinance/Act is inconsistent with Articles 59 and 60. He submits that if only the rights, powers, authorities and privileges accrued or acquired before the abolition of Upazila Parishad were intended to be vested in the Government, then a language similar to section 8(c) of the General Clauses Act ought to have been used. But the vesting in section 2(2) goes much beyond accrued or acquired rights. The Repealing Ordinance continues the functioning of the abolished Parishads under the administrative directions of the Government. It is thus a colourable piece of legislation. The learned Attorney-General replied that the Repealed Ordinance/Act was not a Local Government within the meaning of Article 59 as Upazila was not designated as an administrative unit for the purposes of Article 59 and so its abolition by the Repealing Ordinance/Act is not inconsistent with the provisions of Articles 59 and 60. He further submits that both the intention and working of the Repealed Ordinance are the abolition of Upazila system altogether and so the question of colourable legislation does not arise.

The second question

(ii) Is the Repealing Ordinance/Act inconsistent with Articles 9 and 11 of the Constitution and if so, can it be declared void on that ground under Article 7(2) of the Constitution?

63. Mr. Amirul Islam submitted that the Repealing Ordinance/Act is liable to be declared void wholly, first, for being violative of the Preamble of the Constitution and secondly, for being inconsistent with, Articles 9 and 11. He submits that the Fundamental Principles of State Policy may not be "judicially enforceable" but inconsistency therewith renders a law liable to be declared void under Article 7(2), there being a distinction between "enforce- ability" and "inconsistency". Dr. Kamal Hossain submits that a law which negates a clear directive of the Fundamental Principles of State Policy is liable to be declared void as being inconsistent with the Constitution. The learned Attorney-General submits that a law is not liable to be declared void on the ground of inconsistency with the Fundamental Principles of State Policy, that Article 8(2) of the Constitution is an exception to Article 7(2) and that to declare a law as void is another way of enforcing a different state of things so that there is no real distinction between "enforceability" and "inconsistency" .

The third question

(iii) Was the Repealing Ordinance/Act validly passed under the Ordinance-making power of the President under Article 93 of the Constitution?

64.	 Dr. Kamal Hossain submits that the Repealing Ordinance/Act is ultra vires the President and unconstitutional since Article 93 did not empower the making of the impugned Ordinance for the following reasons:

(a) An organic law providing for a vital aspect of the structure of Government cannot be made by an Ordinance, circumventing the Parliament;

(b) No facts have been presented by the Government to show that circumstances existed which rendered immediate legislation necessary;

(c) The Repealing Ordinance has circumvented the law-making procedure of the Parliament.

65. The learned Attorney-General replied that the appellants have not been able to lay any acceptable foundation to hold that no satisfaction existed for promulgating the Ordinance. Since the Repealing Ordinance has been enacted into a Repealing Act, this submission has lost its validity, he further submits.

66. On the first question:

Articles 9, 11, 59 and 60 of the Constitution are unique and several conclusions can be drawn from them:

First, the constitutional provisions on local government, namely, Articles 9, 11, 59 and 60 mark out the Constitution of Bangladesh as clearly distinctive from other Constitutions of the world. No Constitution contains any definitive provision on local government. In England the local government units, unlike the central government, are not products of constitutional design, but of historical development. Same is the case in the USA and India. In this sub-continent too local government developed along historical lines without following any constitutional pattern. It is the Constitution of Bangladesh which for the first time devised an integrated scheme of local government within a constitutional pattern. This is a most distinctive and unique feature of the Constitution of Bangladesh.

<u>67. Secondly, the words "Local Government have not been defined in the Constitution, nor does the Constitution require any organ of the State to create a new a local government, as it does in respect of a President-"There shall be a President of Bangladesh ........... (Article 48), or a Parliament-</u>

<u>"There shall be a Parliament for Bangladesh 	"</u>

<u>(Article 65) or a Supreme Court-"There shall be a Supreme Court of Bangladesh ............................(Article 94) etc. In the absence of any definition and in the absence of any directive to create a local government afresh, the Constitution will be presumed to have referred to the already-known concept and institution of and the existing legislations on local government. Local government, as a concept and as an institution, was already known to have possessed certain common characteristics, namely, local elections, procedure for public accountability, independent and substantial sources of income clear areas for independent action and certainty of powers and duties and the conditions under which they would be exercised. On the date of coming into force of the Constitution, there were 3 statutes on local government viz, PO No. 7 of 1972, as amended up-to-date and so much of the Basic Democracies Order, 1959 and the Municipal Administration Ordinance, 1960 which were not inconsistent with PO No.7 of 1972. So far as those prevalent legislations are concerned, Article 149 of the Constitution provided as follows:</u>

<u>"149. Subject to the provisions of this Constitution all existing laws shall continue to have effect but may be amended or repealed by law made under this Constitution."</u>

<u>Article 152(1) defined "existing law" as follows:</u>

<u>"existing law" means any law in force in, or in any part of, the territory of Bangladesh immediately before the commencement of this Constitution, whether or not it has been brought into operation;"</u>

68. If Articles 59 and 60 are read with Article 149 and Article 152(1) as above, it clearly means that all existing laws on local government, if they are meant to be continued, have to be brought in conformity with Articles 11, 59 and 60 of the Constitution so that the laws may operate "subject to the Constitution", or else those parts of the existing laws on local government which are specifically inconsistent with Articles 59 and 60 stand the risk of being declared void under Article 7 (2).

<u>69. Thirdly, to the extent that Articles 59 and 60 prescribe manner and method of establishing local government, its composition, powers and functions including power of local taxation, the plenary legislative power of Parliament to enact laws on local government is restricted pro tanto. The learned Attorney-General submits that the plenary power still remains unaffected. I cannot conceive of a local government existing in terms of Articles 59 and 60 and another outside of it That will make a mockery of Articles 59 and 60 and will be in direct conflict with Article 7(1) of the Constitution, namely, "All powers in the Republic belong to the people, and their exercise on behalf of the people shall be effected only under, and by the authority of, this Constitution". If Parliament has to pass a local government legislation, it has to conform to Articles 59 and 60, read with Article 152(1). With Articles 59 and 60 in the Constitution local government legislation became very much a subject- matter of legislation within the terms of the Constitution. Parliament is not free to legislate on local government ignoring Articles 59 and 60.</u>

70. After the Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act, 1975, passed on 25.1.75, deleted Chapter III of Part IV, and omitted the words "and in which effective participation by the people through their elected representatives in administration at all levels shall be ensured" from Article II, local government legislation was relegated to the realm of ordinary legislation unrelated to constitutional provisions and / its fate was left to historical development as in other countries. From its high pedestal of being a legislation within a constitutional mandate, local government legislation became a subject-matter of wanton experimentation. With the restoration of Articles 59 and 60 and the omitted portion of Article II by the Constitution (Twelfth Amendment) Act, 1991 on 18.9.91, the constitutional position is now the same as when the Constitution of Bangladesh came into force on 16.12.72. All existing local government legislations must confono to Articles 59 and 60 with effect from 18.9.91, or else those parts of them which are inconsistent with Articles 59 and 60 stand the risk of being declared void under Article 7(2).

<u>71. Fourthly, the first step that has to be taken to bring a local government law in conformity with Article 59 is that Parliament will have to designate by law administrative units of the Republic where it will either continue the existing local government institutions or create new ones. The term "administrative unit" is a term of the Constitution having a definite meaning in Article 152(1). A designation by law for the purposes of Article 59 is necessary in order to create an "administrative unit". But after designating an area as an "administrative unit", Parliament is not obliged to set up a local government therein. The Constitution does not mandatorily require Parliament to do so. It does not say "There shall be a Local Government in every administrative unit of the Republic". Article 59 only says, "Local Government in very administrative unit of the Republic" i.e., if and when a local government is set up in an administrative unit. Article 59 does not mean conversely that local government in areas which are not designated as administrative units may be entrusted to bodies composed of persons to be decided by Parliament, elected or nominated. That will be colourable legislation.</u>

72. Fifthly, from a combined reading of the Preamble, Articles 7, 9, 11, 59 and 60 of the Constitution it is clear that the makers of the Constitution devised a scheme of total democracy, both at the centre and at the level of local government. The Preamble declares democracy to be a fundamental principle of the Constitution. Article 7(1) says that all powers in the Republic belong to the people and Article 11 proclaims that "the Republic shall be a democracy". Various autocratic regimes at various times vigorously persisted with the idea of an unrepresentative national government at the Centre but waxed eloquent on grassroot-level democracy solely for the purpose of building up a power base. The makers of the Constitution wanted no such half-way house between autocracy and democracy. The choice was clearly for a fully democratic constitutional pattern, both at the national level and at the local level. And there lies the second step. Local Government "shall be entrusted to bodies, composed of persons elected in accordance with law". Special representation may be given to "peasants, workers and women", as enjoined by Article 9, but not at the cost of robbing the local government institutions of their elected, hence representative character.

<u>73. Lastly, the structure of local government was left fully and completely in the hands of Parliament No one can claim a vested right in any particular form or in any particular number of tiers of local government. Within the framework of Articles 59 and 60 Parliament retains the power of continually re-organising, re-structuring and re-modelling the local government institutions in the light of experiences gained to meet the changing needs of changing times. It is to be remembered however that local government is a part of the constitutional system and therefore Chapter III of Part IV of the Constitution containing Articles 59 and 60 cannot ever be kept as a dead letter. Local Government cannot be abolished altogether. It must exist in some form, in some tier or tiers at any given point of time to give a meaning to Chapter III of Part IV and to justify its rationale, validity and existence. It is not a mere adornment in the Constitution.</u>

74. Designation by law:

Article 152(1) defines "administrative unit" as follows:

"administrative unit" means a district or other area designated by law for the purposes of article 59."

The Bengali version is as follows:

“প্রশাসনিক একাংশ” অর্থ জেলা কিংবা এই সংবিধানের ৫৯ অনুচ্ছেদের উদ্দেশ্যসাধনকল্পে আইনের দ্বারা অভিহিত অন্য কোন এলাকা।”

Mr. Amirul Islam vehemently argued that no specific and express designation by law is necessary to create an "administrative unit". If a legislation answers the characteristics of a local government with reference to a clear territory or area, powers and functions, then designation will be implied. The Repealed Ordinance, he submits, conferring local government powers and functions on a clearly demarcated area, namely, an Upazila, sufficiently answers the requirement of designation under Article 59 read with Article 152(1).

<u>75. This interpretation of the words "designation by law" is supported by some other provisions of the Constitution, containing the word 'designation'. Article 52(2) of the Constitution says that "the conduct of the President may be referred by Parliament to any court, tribunal or body appointed or designated by parliament for the investigation of a charge under this article". The designation by Parliament can never be by implication. It must be specific, volitional and definite. Sometimes the Constitution itself makes the designation, see Article 65(2), the members (of Parliament) "shall be designated as Members of Parliament". Similarly when the Constitution requires designation by law for the purposes of Article 59, the law must so designate expressly, unequivocally and directly, mentioning the purpose for which the designation is being made. There cannot be any designation by implication. As the Repealed Ordinance never designated Upazila as an administrative unit, it was not a local government within the meaning of Article 59.</u>

76. Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed submits that Article 152(1) does not require a district to be designated by law, for a district stands designated by Article 152(1) itself, as a combined reading of both the English and Bengali texts of Article 152(1) will reveal. Also, no designation is necessary in the case of areas within a district like union, municipalities, corporations, etc., as those areas are covered by a district which is already designated. It is only when two or more districts or an area bigger than a district are contemplated to be administrative units that designation is necessary, he submits. It his submission is correct then Upazila need not be designated by any law at all.

77. The learned Attorney-General submits that designation is necessary not only in the case of a district but also in the case of "other area", i.e., area other than a district, whether it is within the district or outside of it or whether it is bigger than a district or smaller.

78. It appears to me that unlike the Bengali text, the English text leaves room for some controversy as to whether "designated by law for the purposes of article 59" qualify both "a district" and "other area" or only the words "other area". The Bengali text suffers from no ambivalence. Proviso to Article 153(3) of the Constitution provides that "in the event of conflict between the Bengali and the English text, the Bengali text shall prevail". The Bengali text clearly designates district as an administrative unit, only the "other areas" are required to be designated by law for the purposes of Article 59. This interpretation is not only in consonance with the plain meaning of the Bengali text, but also stands to reason. If both a district and other area are required to be designated by law for the purposes of Article 59, then the word "a district" is superfluous, 'any area' would have sufficed. We shall not give an interpretation to the text of the Constitution which renders any word of it a surplusage. Furthermore, the word 'district' was not unknown to the makers of the Constitution, as the District Act, 1838, already familiarised the term. It enables creation of a new district in any part of Bangladesh and alteration of the limits of the existing districts. Article 152(1) even uses the words "District Judge" while defining "judicial service". A district, therefore, stands already designated by the Constitution and the words "designated by law for the purposes of Article 59" refer only to the words "other area".

79. But "other area" needs to be designated by law, be it within a district or a combination of districts, the reason being that a district is designated by the Constitution as a whole and the word 'bodies' in Article 59 refers to more than one body at the particular unit level. When a separate local government is set up in part of a district, say a Union or Paurashava or Corporation, a part of the territory of a district is carved out to give the local government institution a separate, distinct and independent legal entity. It will be a union-level or Pourashava-level or Corporation-level body, limited to the area earmarked for it and it will not be a district-level body at all. It needs designation to make it an administrative unit.

80. In any view of the matter Ordinance No. LIX of 1982 which was repealed by the Repealing Ordinance, having not designated Upazila as an administrative unit for the purposes of Article 59 was not a local government in terms of Article 59. Parliament has the power to abolish altogether a local government which is not a local government within the meaning of Article 59. If Parliament has to continue that type of local government, it has to bring that local government in conformity with Articles 59 and 60.

Legislative Practice :

On the date of coming into force of the Constitution bureaucratisation of local government institutions was complete. There was no semblance of any representative local government institution anywhere in any of the rural and urban areas and it was quickly realised that such state of affairs would attract the mischief of Article 7(2) of the Constitution, namely, " ..... .if any other law is inconsistent with this Constitution that other law shall, to the extent of the inconsistency, be void." By the Bangladesh Local Government (Union Parishad and Paurashava) Order, 1973, PO No. 22 of 1973, promulgated on 22.3.73, a two-tier elected local government, namely, a Union Parishad at the rural level and a Paurashava at the urban level was sought to be established. The first paragraph of the Preamble of PO No. 22 of 1973 was as follows :

"Whereas Article 59 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh provides, inter alia that Local Government shall be entrusted to bodies, composed of persons elected in accordance with law;"

There was, however, no designation of unions and municipalities as administrative unit, as required by Article 152(1) of the Constitution.

81. It was the impression of all the learned Counsels for the appellants as well as of the learned Attorney-General that there PO No. 22 of 1973 rested and that there was no designation of unions and municipalities as administrative units in the said legislation.

82. Much to our surprise we find that by way of amendment of PO No. 22 of 1973 the Parliament enacted the Bangladesh Local Government (Union Parishad and Paurashava) (Amendment) Act 1973, Act No. IX of 1973, giving it a retrospective effect from 22.3.73 wherein it introduced Article 2C in PO No. 22 of 1973 as follows:

"2C. The unions and municipalities shall be administrative units within their respective areas for the purposes of Article 59 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh".

It is indeed surprising, no less regrettable, that this important piece of legislation which throws light on legislative practice escaped the notice of the learned Counsels of both sides. Much of their arguments were based upon the provisions of PO No. 22 of 1973 but Article 2C introduced by Act IX of 1973 robs them of their validity and relevance. In Article 2C Unions and Municipalities were clearly and specifically designated as "administrative units" for the purposes of Article 59, but the Zillas or Districts and the Thanas were not so designated. The learned Attorney-General argued that a Thana continued to be administered as a local government by Administrators from 9.9.72 to 18.5.76 (when Thana Parishads were established by Thana Parishads Ordinance 1976, Ordinance No. XXXII of 1976) designation an as an unrepresentative body. This was to him yet another example of a permissible local government institution outside of the framework of Articles 59 and 60. The answer is that a Thana existed no doubt as an undesignated and unrepresentative local government upto 18.5.76, but the permissibility of its existence was not tested in a court of law, as long as Articles 11, 59 and 60 of the Constitution were in full force. Prevalence is not synonymous with constitutionality.

83. During the period from 16.12.72 to 25.1. 75, when Articles 11, 59 and 60 of the Constitution were in full force, Parliament also passed the Dacca Municipal Corporation Act, 1974 (Act No. LVI of 1974) on 29.7.74, providing for constitution of a Municipal Corporation for municipal administration of the City of Dacca (as Dhaka was then spell) with 72 elected Commissioners and elected Mayor and Deputy Mayors. The city area was not designated afresh as an "administrative unit", presumably because "municipalities" "within their respective areas" were already designated as "administrative units" for the purposes of Article 59 of the Constitution by Article 2C of PO No. 22 1973. However, Act No. LVI of 1974 was to come into force on a date to be appointed by the Government and the day never came. The city of Dhaka continued to be a Paurashava,

Not quite a total repeal :

The Repealing Ordinance in its totality abolishes the Upazila Parishad altogether and without dilating on the actual working of the Repealing Ordinance, I would say that its short contents are unexceptionable, except for the words  “অধিকার, ক্ষমতা, কর্তৃত্ব ও সুদিধাদি” in section 2(2)(Kha) thereof which are in violation of Articles 59 and 60 of the Constitution. It is not a colourable piece of legislation as Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed submits, but the faulty draftsmanship certainly suggests that the Government has been vested with the continuing authority, powers, functions and privileges of a dissolved Upazila Parishad, Although Upazila Parish ad is not a local government within the meaning of Article 59, but its powers, functions, privileges, etc. are certainly those of a local government as described in Articles 59(2) and 60.

With the re-appearance of Articles 59 and 60 in the Constitution, the Government or for that matter, any person or body, not elected in the area according to law, cannot upon abolition of a local government tier, take over the authority, powers, functions and privileges of a local government institution of that tier even for a temporary period or as a stop-gap arrangement. The abolition must mean a total abolition. Those powers, functions, etc. which the Central Government ceded to Upazila Parishad for purposes of forming a local government will eventually go back to the Government upon its abolition, but the Government will exercise those powers, functions, etc. as governmental powers, not as powers, functions, etc. belonging to the erstwhile Parishad or a local government. This was a draftsman's error for which Parliament cannot be accused of making a colourable legislation.

<u>84. My answer to the first question is therefore affirmative partly. On the second question Article 7(2) provides that this Constitution is, as the solemn expression of the will of the people, the supreme law of the Republic, and if any other law is inconsistent with this Constitution that other  law, to the extent of the inconsistency, be void. Therefore, this Constitution taken as a whole is a law, albeit the supreme law and by "any other law" and "that other law" the Constitution refers to the definition of "law" in Article 152(1), including a constitutional amendment. It is the Law of the Constitution itself that the fundamental principles of state policy are not laws themselves but "principles". To equate "principles" with "laws" is to go against the Law of the Constitution itself. These principles shall be applied by the State in the making of laws, i.e., principles of policy will serve as a beacon of light in the making of laws, shall be a guide to the interpretation of the Constitution and of the other laws of Bangladesh, and shall form the basis of the work of the State and of its citizens. Not being laws, these principles shall not be judicially enforceable.</u>

<u>85. There the Constitution rests. It does not say, as it says in Article 26 in respect of fundamental rights :</u>

<u>"26(1). All existing law inconsistent with the provisions of this Part shall, to the extent of such inconsistency, become void on the commencement of this Constitution.</u>

<u>(2) The State shall not make any law inconsistent with any provisions of this Part, and any law so made shall, to the extent of such inconsistency, be void.</u>

<u>(3) There being no specific provisions in the Constitution providing laws inconsistent with fundamental principles of state policy to be void, the learned Counsels for the appellants have fallen back upon Article 7(2) and have urged for acceptance of an intrepretation which will bring Fundamental Principles of State Policy at par with Fundamental Rights in so far as voidability is concerned. The submission is unacceptable, because, first, the makers of the Constitution did not lack in expression if they so meant it. Provisions analogous to Article 26 could have been inserted in Part II as well. The omission is deliberate and calculated. Secondly, Article 8(2) proclaims the fundamental principles of State Policy as "principles", not "laws" and that is the mandate of this Constitution. Article 7(2) cannot be interpreted to mean that if any other law is inconsistent with the "principles" mentioned in Part II then that other law to the extent of the inconsistency, will be void. The Constitution is the supreme law and if the supreme law prescribes "principles" not "laws", and directs the use of these principles in certain specific manner, then the other law cannot be made void on the ground of inconsistency with these principles. It is argued that Articles 9 and 11 are provisions of the Constitution and if any other law is inconsistent with these provisions, then it will be void. Article 7(2) says "this Constitution", not "provisions of the Constitution", which expression the Constitution uses in some other places. The use of the words "this Constitution" and not "provisions of the Constitution" is also deliberate.</u>

86. A hypothetical question has been posed. Parliament passes a law which glaringly violates and flouts a fundamental principle of State policy, and if its vires is challenged solely on the ground of inconsistency with that principle and on no other ground whatsoever, will the High Court Division declare or not declare the law void ? It is a madness scenario. The learned Counsels could not show any such legislation in this sub-continent, but suppose, Parliament is struck with such madness, is the High Court Division in its writ jurisdiction the only light at the end of the tunnel ? What does public opinion political party and election do if Parliament goes berserk?

87. In answering the second question I have not examined whether the Repealing Ordinance/Act is inconsistent with Articles 9 and 11 or not, in view of my negative answer to the last part of the question and in view of the fact that I have already found a part of the Repealing Ordinance/Act inconsistent with Articles 59 and 60.

On the third question

The Repealing Ordinance having been made into an Act of Parliament the question raised is now academic and may be considered in an appropriate case.

Latifur Rahman J : Agreeing with the judgment of my Lord the Chief Justice, I like to add few words in this case, as an elaborate argument has been made from the Bar with regard to the concept of Local Government, existence of Local Government Institutions in Bangladesh since British time and the Constitutional validity of the Repealing Ordinance as it violates the provision of Articles 9, 11,59 and 60 of our Constitution.

89. In these appeals, the appellants who were elected as Chairmen of Upazila Parishads in the last Election held on March, 1989 have challenged the vires of the Local Government (Upazila Parishad and Upazila Administration Re-Organization) (Repeal) Ordinance, 1991 (Ordinance No. XXXVII of 1991), (now Act II of 1992), hereinafter called the Repealing Ordinance, whereby the Local Government (Upazila Parishad and Upazila Re-Organization) Ordinance, 1982 being Ordinance LIX of 1982, hereinafter called the Upazila Ordinance was repealed.

90. The factual contentions of these appellants are that, they were elected on the basis of adult franchise as Chairmen of Upazila Parishads for a term of 5 years and before completion of their terms the present Government repealed the said Upazila Ordinance by the Repealing Ordinance, thereby removing the appellants from their elected office as Chairmen of Upazila Parishads.

91. The legal contentions of the appellants are that, the Government by virtue of the Reapealing Ordinance has violated the provisions of Articles 9, 11, 59 and 60 of the Constitution and as such the same is liable to be declared as void by virtue of Article 7(2) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh.

92. Mr. Amirul Islam, learned Advocate appearing for the appellant in Civil Appeal No.4 of 1992, has argued two points for our consideration.

93. Firstly. he submits that Article 9 of the Constitution postulates promotion of Local Government Institutions and Article 11 contemplates democracy and effective participation by the people through their elected representatives in administration at all levels and the appellants being elected representatives of the people in the Local Government Institution, the promulgation of the impugned Repealing Ordinance violates Articles 9 and 11 of the Constitution and as such the Repealing Ordinance is liable to be struck down as void in view of Article 7(2) of the Constitution.

94. Secondly, he argues that the Reapealing Ordinance is expressly and clearly violative of Articles 59 and 60 of the Constitution inasmuch as by abolishing the local Government Institutions at Upazila levels, the impugned Ordinance has clearly violated the mandate of Article 59 providing Local Government in every Administrative Unit of the Republic and hence the Ordinance is liable to be declared as void under Article 7(2) of the Constitution.

95. Before adverting to the arguments of Mr. Amirul Islam who mainly argued in this case on behalf of the appellants, I like to trace out in brief, the historical background of Local government Institutions with special reference to the Upazila Ordinance as promulgated by the Chief Martial Law Administrator in 1982.

96. Concept of Local Government-In the concept of political philosophy "Local Government" means self-administration (in local affairs) in cities, towns, villages and the like, as opposed to national or central Government. It is undeniable that for effective working of democracy such local Government institutions were elected in grass-root levels and at various tiers in various countries of the world as Governmental units. To-day, political activity is present everywhere, amongst the citizens of a country as in capital, towns and villages. Political activities are mixed up with countless daily activities, economic, social, religious, educational and others and these are all inter-dependent When we speak of political activity we are bringing in the concept of a unit of the Government in the nation itself, and also in each separate city, town, village and other distinct local Government entity. In these areas a unit of Government may be established by a distinct residential population occupying a definite land area by elected representatives of the people and defined for the purpose as a separate local Government.

97. History of Local Self Government in British-India

If we trace back the historical background of the local Government Institutions in the Sub-continent during the British regime, then we find that such political activity units were set up on smaller scale in villages and towns. The Bengal Local Government Act of 1885 (Bengal Act III of 1885)empowered the Provincial Government to establish District Board for every District and a local Board in any Sub-Division or pan of the Sub-Division or in any two or more Sub-Divisions combined. Thus under that Act District Boards and Local Boards were introduced in our country in the Sub-continent. Thereafter came The Bengal Village Self-Government Act, 1919 (Bengal Act of 1919) which gave power-to the Provincial Government to declare local area to be Union Board where every male person of the full age of 21 years living within the Union were entitled to vote at an election of the members of the Union Board and those members could elect the President of the Union Board who presided over the Board. Thus, it is found that in British time the local Government institutions such as Union Boards and District Boards were in existence in our country as a measure of self-government

98. History of Local Government in Pakistan time-After partition of the Sub-continent and creation of Pakistan these two local government institutions at Union and District levels were in practice till promulgation of Basic Democracies Order, 1959, whereby it provided for four tiers of local councils, namely, Union Council, Thana Council, District Council and Divisional Council in the then East Pakistan (now Bangladesh). According to this Order, a Thana Council consisted of representative members, official and appointed members as might be fixed by the Commissioner. The new development that we find in this Order is the emergence of Thana Council and Divisional Council as new local Governments in the Thana and in the Division along with the local self-governments that were in existence in the Union and in the District.

99. Local Government after emergence of Bangladesh and its main features in pre Constitution and post Constitution period.

Bangladesh Local Councils and Municipal Committees (Dissolution and Administration) Order 1972 (PO 7n2) dissolved all local Councils and Municipal Committees and a Union Council was called Union Panchayet, a town committee was called as Sahar Committee, and a Municipal Committee was called Paurashava. The Bangladesh Local Government (Union Parishad and Paurashava) Order, 1973 (PO 22 of 1973) was promulgated on 22.3.1973 wherein Union Panchayet was called Union Parishad and Union Parishads and Paurashavas were created throughout Bangladesh in accordance with the various provisions of that Order. In 1976 Local Government Ordinance, 1976 (Ordinance No. XC of 1976), was promulgated providing for the constitution of local government bodies in rural areas and to consolidate and amend certain laws relating to local government in such areas. A salient feature of this Ordinance was that there would be a Union Parishad for a Union, Thana Parishad for a Police Station and a Zilla Parishad for a District. It may be mentioned that Thana Council was first constituted by the Basic Democracies Order, 1959 and then Thana Parishad was constituted by Ordinance No. XC of 1976. The Sub-Divisional Officer was the ex-officio chairman of the Thana Council as well as the Thana Parishad. So the office of the Chairman of the Thana Council and the Thana Parishad was not an elective office. Before coming into force of the Ordinance XC of 1976 Thana Parish ads were constituted by Ordinance No. XXXII of 1976. In 1982 the Local Government (Thana Parishad and Thana Administration Re-Organization) Ordinance, 1982 (Ordinance LIX of 1982) was promulgated. By section 2A of Ordinance LIX of 1982, the Government declared by notification in the official gazette any areas specified therein to be a Upazila for the purpose of this Ordinance. This Ordinance provided for the first time that the Chairman of the Upazila Parishad would be elected by direct election. Thus, it is found that the posts of office of Chairman of Upazila Parishad was never before an elective office. The Upazila Parishad even under Ordinance LIX of 1982, as amended from time to time existed of elected members, officials members and nominated members. It was also provided in the Ordinance that till such time a Chairman was elected, the Upazila Nirbahi Officer or any other person nominated by the Government would act as Chairman. This Upazila Ordinance was ultimately repealed by the Repealing Ordinance and the Upazila Parishad was abolished.

100. It will be worthwhile to refer herein-below, the legislative purpose of enacting Ordinance LIX of 1982 which was promulgated by the Chief Martial Law Administrator in pursuance of the proclamation of the 24th March, 1982 after usurpation of power by the Chief Martial Law Administrator. The resolution dated 23rd October, 1982 which was published in the Bangladesh Gazette Extraordinary gives a background as to the decision of the Government to organize the Administration at the Thana level which was termed Upazila in the Ordinance at that time. From the resolution it is abundantly clear that under the Re-Organization set up Thana was called Upazila and it would be the focal point of all administrative activities. The Basic purpose was to recognise the Administration at Thana and thereafter to transfer responsibility for all development activities at the Upazila which was a Thana previously. The Government retained the direct responsibility for regulatory function and major development activities of national and regional level and education, health, family planning and all other allied subjects relating to the development of the Upazilas were entrusted to the Upazila Parishad. It is to be clearly borne in mind that soon after taking over power, the Chief Martial Law Administrator thought of decentralising the Administration and with that end in view, the Supreme Court High Court Division at Dhaka was decentralised at District levels and the Courts functioned till the decision of the case famously known as Constitution 8th Amendment Case. The concept of Upazila Parishad of the Chief Martial Law Administrator could not be implemented through election at Upazila levels due to stiff opposition from the major political parties as the parties demanded Parliamentary Election to be held after withdrawal of Martial Law. The Upazila Polls was, however, held on 9th May, 1985 and the second polls to the Upazila was held in May, 1989 in which these appellants were elected as Chairmen. In this Scheme, 464 Upazilas were created, and to my mind it appears that the scheme of creation of Upazilas was more a matter of strengthening and mobilising the strength of the Martial Law Administrator. The scheme of decentralisation of the Administration at Upazila levels was ushered in transferring development activities to Upazilas, thereby creating local Government in Upazila levels.

101. With regard to Mr. Amirul Islam's first point it may be pointed out that Part II of our Constitution (Articles 8-25) provides the fundamental principles of State Policy. In this case, we are concerned with two relevant fundamental principles of State Policy namely, Articles 9 and 11, Article 9 reads as follows:

"The State shall encourage local Government institutions composed of representatives of the areas concerned and in such institutions special representation shall be given, as far as possible, to peasants, workers and women."

Article 11 reads as follows:

"The Republic shall be a democracy in which human rights and freedoms and respect for the dignity and worth of the human person shall be guaranteed, and in which effective participation by the people through their elected representatives in administration at all levels shall be ensured."

These above fundamental principles of State policy are in the nature of instrument of instructions to the Government to implement these principles by legislation so that the nation as a whole can achieve certain ultimate ends by the actions of the Government. It is to be borne in mind here that so long the State does not legislate on these fundamental principles of State Policy as laid down in Part II of the Constitution these principles cannot be termed as law. Presently, I will refer to Article 8 (2) of the Constitution which reads as follows:

"The principles set out in this Part shall be fundamental to the governance of Bangladesh, shall be applied by the State in the making of laws, shall be a guide to the interpretation of the Constitution and of the other laws of Bangladesh, and shall form the basis of the work of the State and of its citizens, but shall not be judicially enforceable."

From this Article it is clear that all these principles as contained in this Part:

(i) shall be fundamental to the governance of Bangladesh;

(ii) shall be applied by the State in the making of laws;

(iii) be a guide to the interpretation of the Constitution and of the other laws of Bangladesh;

(iv) shall form the basis of the work of the State and of its citizens;

(v) but all these principles set out in this part shall not be judicially enforceable.

Thus, this Sub-Article (2) of Article 8 of the Constitution clearly says the purpose and intent of these fundamental principles of State policy and at the same time it speaks that those principles shall not be judicially enforceable. Keeping this in mind, we are to consider Article 7(2) of our Constitution. Article 7 of our Constitution speaks of supremacy of the Constitution. As a matter of fact, it is needless to say, that even without this Article the Constitution is the supreme law of the land and all other laws are subordinate to the Constitution. In Article 152 of the Constitution law has been defined as "law means any Act, ordinance, order, rule, regulation, bye-law, notification or other legal instrument, and any custom or usage, having the force of law in Bangladesh." Sub-Article (2) of Article 7 speaks that, "If any other law is inconsistent with this Constitution that other law shall, to the extent of the inconsistency, be void." From this Article 7 of the Constitution it is evident that this Constitution is the supreme organic law of Bangladesh and all the three organs of the State namely, the legislature which makes laws, executive which executes the same and judiciary which interprets the Constitution and the laws made by the legislature, derive their authority from this Constitution. Hence, all these organs of the State must act in accordance with the Constitutional mandate and no organ is to transgress on the domain of the other organ and in case of such interference it is the judiciary no doubt which will ultimately declare the law which is inconsistent with the Constitution as void to the extent of its inconsistency.

<u>102. Now let us see how Articles 9, 11 and 7(2) of the Constitution can be interpreted keeping in view the principle of Constitutional interpretation of all these constitutional provisions. It is to be kept in mind that every part of our Constitution from the preamble to the last schedule is the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. Every provision of the Constitution is essential and all these provisions must exist in harmony and there cannot be any conflict between any provision of the Constitution and no provision will be subordinate to the other. In interpreting these various provisions of the Constitution, the construction of one part will throw light on the other part and the construction must hold a balance between all the parts of the Constitution and one part of the Constitution must be complementary and supplementary to the other part. As a matter of fact, it is to be presumed that all the provisions are harmonious and by no stretch of imagination one provision of the Constitution can be in conflict with the other as the framers of a written Constitution can never intend for such conflict and anomaly. What Mr. Amirul Islam argued is, to my mind, really a matter of implied limitation. He wants to argue that in view of Article 7(2) of the Constitution the Repealing Ordinance can be declared as void as impliedly, it violates Articles 9 and 11. In interpreting a written Constitution no implication can be made. Such a method of construction would defeat the intention of the Constitution. Implied limitation cannot be applied in our Constitution which is a written Constitution, as expressly Article 8(2) speaks of non-enforceability of the Articles contained in Part II of the Constitution. Further, Article 7(2) speaks of law being inconsistent with the Constitution, but these principles as set out in Part II, particularly, Articles 9 and 11 with which we are concerned are not laws and as such no individual can come to a court of law on the plea that his legal right has been violated. Further, the word 'void' as used in Article 7(2) is also very significant, as because an existing law can only be declared void if this is inconsistent with the Constitution. Mr. Amirul Islam while arguing wanted to make a distinction between these- two terms "void" and "enforceable" as contained in our Constitution. But it appears to me that in the context of the present case, the distinction between the terms 'void' and 'enforceable' are not of much importance as Article 8(2) of the Constitution clearly contemplates that the fundamental principles of State Policy are not enforceable in a court of law and the appellants have no justiciable rights in their favour. The distinction as drawn by the learned Advocate is only superficial and indirectly he is seeking for enforceability which is precluded by this Article. Further, there being no violation of law, such a declaration that the Repealing law is void under Article 7(2) of the Constitution cannot be sought for.</u>

103. It is true that in the Indian Constitution there is no corresponding Article like Article 7 of our Constitution, but for that we can only say, that this is an unique .feature in our Constitution contained in Part I of the Constitution which recognized people as the source of all powers in the Republic as it is evident that the people of Bangladesh proclaimed independence on the 26th day of March, 1971 through a historic war for national independence. An argument on Article 7(2) of the Constitution as argued by all the learned Advocates of the appellants touching on the spirit of the Constitution is very attractive for it has a powerful appeal to sentiment and emotion. But a constitutional law has to gather the spirit of the Constitution from the language of the Constitution. What one may believe or think to be the spirit of the Constitution cannot prevail if the language of the Constitution does not support that view.

104. Thus I hold that Articles 7(2) and 8(2) co-exist harmoniously and the learned Advocate in an indirect manner is only trying to get a declaration of voidability which is not contemplated under the Constitution.

105. From Article 8(2) of the Constitution it is clearly found that fundamental principles of state policy are not justiciable, in other words, the courts cannot compel the Government to carry out any fundamental principles unless that is implemented by appropriate legislation. The Indian decisions that has been referred before us relating to enforcement of fundamental rights are mixed up with directive principles of state policy, wherein the fundamental rights are enforceable by Articles 32, 226(1) of the Indian Constitution and the courts are bound to declare as void any law which is inconsistent with any of the fundamental rights. But the court cannot declare as void any law on the ground that it contravenes any of the directives. Thus, in the Indian jurisdiction in case of conflict between fundamental rights and the directive principles of state policy the former shall prevail. The decisions of Indian Jurisdiction are not of much help to us in this case.

106. A little analysis of Article 26 in Part III of the Constitution dealing with fundamental rights will also help us in understanding Article 7(2). Article 26 of the Constitution reads as follows:

"26. (1) All existing law inconsistent with the provisions of this Part shall, to the extent of such inconsistency, become void on the- commencement of this Constitution.

<u>(2) The State shall not make any law inconsistent with any provisions of this Part, and any law so made shall, to the extent of such inconsistency, be void.</u>"

Thus, we find that laws inconsistent with fundamental rights shall be void and the State shall not make any law inconsistent with any provision of Part III which contains fundamental rights. So the term 'void' is referable to law and making of the law and it cannot have any meaning with respect to enforcement of law. Article 102(1) of the Constitution speaks of enforcement of any of the fundamental rights conferred by Part III of the Constitution on an application by an aggrieved person. Article 102(2) gives the power of the High Court Division to issue certain orders and directions in the nature of mandamus, prohibition, habeas corpus and quo warranto, Hence, it is difficult to accept the submission of the learned Advocate that under Article 7(2), the fundamental principles of State Policy which are not laws can be declared void.

<u>107. Now taking up the second point of the learned Advocate for the appellant, it may be mentioned that in our Constitution, Part IV (The Executive) contains Chapter Ill-Local Government We have already referred earlier that local Government is meant for successful working of the democracy and with that objectives in view the framers of the Constitution embodied Articles 9 and 11 which encourage local Government' institutions and participation of people through their elected representatives.</u>

<u>Article 59(1) reads as follows:</u>

<u>"59(1) Local Government in every administrative unit of the Republic shall be entrusted to bodies, composed of persons elected in accordance with law."</u>

<u>The above Article shows that the local Government bodies will be composed of elected representative in every administrative unit of the Republic. From the history of the local Government as detailed herein above, we have found that in British India Local Government existed in Union and District. In Pakistan and after liberation, local Government also existed in Thana (police Station) along with the union and the District. Thus Thana as an unit of the administration for the purpose of local, Government was in practice both in pre-constitution and post-constitution period. The language of Article 59 clearly says that local Government need not be created under the Constitutional mandate as this Article does not create local Government. This Article speaks of composition of local Government in every administrative unit of the Republic. It may be mentioned that the Government in its plenary legislative power can create local Government and can also abolish local Government in various tiers. This power of the Parliament cannot be questioned.</u>

<u>Now the relevant question for our consideration is, whether the Parliament can abolish the Upazila Parishad Ordinance by the Repealing Ordinance. The Parliament is vested with the legislative power of the Republic subject to the provision of this Constitution. This power is also not denied by the learned Advocates for the appellants. Thus, the Upazila Parishad Ordinance could be validly repealed by the Repealing Ordinance.</u>

<u>108. The pertinent question now remains to be decided is, whether in the touchstone of Article 7 (2), the Repealing Ordinance can be declared void as because it violates Articles 59 and 60 of the Constitution. Reading Articles 59 and 152(1) of the Constitution together, I find that Upazila Parishad established under Ordinance No. 59 of 1982 cannot be termed a local Government within the meaning of Article 59 of the Constitution as the Upazila which is admittedly not a district has not been designated as 'an administrative unit' by law for the purpose of Article 59. Upazila being not an administrative unit within the meaning of Article 152(1) of the Constitution it is not a local Government under Article 59 of the Constitution. The designation as an administrative unit is a constitutional requirement and without such designation the Upazila cannot assume the character, nature and function of a local Government under the Constitution. The Upazila Parishad which was in existence at the time of promulgation of the Repealing Ordinance was also not composed of elected persons. Article 60 speaks that the parliament by law may confer powers on the local Government composed under Article 59. Since there is no violation of Article 59, the question of violation of Article 60 does not at all arise in the present case.</u>

109. Dr. Kamal Hossain, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant in Civil Appeal No.3 of 1992, submits that though Article 93 of the Constitution empowers the President to promulgate an Ordinance when the Parliament stands dissolved or is not in session, but Article 93 was applied in the present case wrongly without any valid purpose and satisfaction of the President by disregarding the parliamentary procedures by which legislation was made by the President in his ordinance making power on an organic law. The learned advocate has also cited some decisions of Indian jurisdiction for our consideration in this case.

110. With regard to Dr. Kamal Hossain's argument on Article 93 of the Constitution relating to the Ordinance making power of the President, suffice to say that the impugned Ordinance having been replaced by Act II of 1992, much of the efficacy with regard to the argument of the learned Advocate touching on the satisfaction of the President and that the Ordinance was unnecessary and wrongly promulgated has become irrelevant for our consideration.
