Since the Ordinance has already been made an Act of Parliament, the question of its validity has become academic and we need not express any opinion in this case.

111. We can only say that President under our Constitution is only a Constitutional head and normally he acts in all matters including the promulgation of an Ordinance on the advice of the Prime Minister as contemplated under Article 48(3) of the Constitution. Further, what advice was tendered by the Prime Minister cannot be enquired into in any Court Dr. Kamal Hossain's main argument was on the Parliamentary safe-guard against Ordinance making power of the President. It appears that in the present case the Government legislated by an Ordinance instead of by an Act of Parliament, and it makes no difference at all because it is to be presumed that the ordinance was promulgated by the advice of the Prime Minister who is the leader of the majority party in the Parliament. It is true that the present Government has a clear majority in Parliament, and without making an Ordinance if a bill would have been introduced in the House that would have no doubt given to all the members of the Parliament a detailed opportunity of considering the 'pros and cons' of the proposed Ordinance through consultations and deliberations by its members. Be that as it may, in the present case the Ordinance has already been passed by the legislature into an Act. Thus the argument with regard to the parliamentary safe-guard and the possibility of abusing the power cannot hold good in the facts of the present case.

112. Dr. Kamal Hossain, cited the case of Laxmikalta Vs. Union of India, reported in AIR 1987 (SC) 232. That is a case where some new directions were given by the Supreme Court for the difficulties faced in implementing the directions given earlier in the same case, reported in AIR 1984 (SC) 469. That case considered Fundamental rights under Articles 15 and 24 and Directive principles of state policy under Article 39. Thus, this reported decision relating to adoption of Indian children by Foreigners has no application in the fact of the present case. The next case cited by the learned advocate is the case of Sheela Barse Vs. State of Moharastra, AIR 1983 (SC) 378. That was also a case relating to Fundamental rights and Directive principles of State policy. The case of Mukesh Adllani Vs. State of Madhya Pradesh, AIR 1985 (SC) 1365 arose on the basis of a letter written by an Advocate to one on the Judges of the Supreme Court depicting the horrid plight of the bonded labour working in stone quarries at Raisen in Madhya Pradesh. That case was disposed of by the Supreme Court holding that no labourer can be paid less than the minimum wages as contemplated under the Minimum Wages Act. The ratio of the above decisions are of no relevance for our purpose in the present case.

113. With regard to Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed's argument that the impugned legislation is a colourable legislation, suffice it to say that in determining the Constitutionality of the Repealing Ordinance this Court cannot be called upon to embark -on an enquiry into public policy or investigate into question of political wisdom or even upon motives of the legislature in enacting the Ordinance, if it is found that the legislature is competent to legislate on the subject without infringing any provisions of the Constitution.

<u>114. The learned Advocate cited the case of KC Gajpati Narayan Vs. State of Orissa reported in AIR 1953(SC) 375, where the doctrine of colourable legislation is based on the maxim that one cannot do indirectly what he cannot do directly. In Paragraph 18 of that decision, their Lordships of the Supreme Court of India have clearly spelt out the doctrine of colourable legislation by giving emphasis on the competency of the legislature to pass a particular law. In our case it is admitted by Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed that the Parliament has the competency to pass the impugned Repealing Ordinance. This being the legal position, the argument of the learned Advocate as to the challenge of this Repealing Ordinance as colourable is untenable in law.</u>

<u>Before parting with the case, I need to say a word as to the interpretation of Articles 7(2), 8(2) and 9 of the Constitution by Naimuddin Ahmed J. The learned Judge in his judgment observed as follows:</u>

<u>"Consequently, if it is found that impugned repealing ordinance is violative of Article 9 of the Constitution, it is liable to be struck down as void in view of Article 7(2) of the Constitution. "</u>

<u>This observation cannot hold good in interpreting the Constitutional provisions as indicated herein above. I must say that in dealing with Constitutional. Provisions the court is not allowed to take hypothetical questions as has been posed by the learned Judge and has answered them like an academician. The learned Judge has made some quotations from Text Books on various Constitutional law of some renowned scholars. Abstract theoretical questions are not to be decided by any court as those ate of only academic importance. It is no doubt true that these fundamental principles of State Policy as contained in our Constitution have been declared "to be fundamental to the governance of Bangladesh shall be applied by the State in making of the laws", but we will normally hold that the State will not make a law contrary to the fundamental principles of State Policy. But even then if a law is made by ignoring these fundamental principles of State policy, the Government will have to answer and face the people who elect them. So, by taking a hypothetical question and on an interpretation of Article 9, the learned Judge ought not to have ventured to strike down the Repealing Ordinance as void under Article 7(2) of the Constitution in the face of clear constitutional mandate of Article 8(2).</u>

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and decree dated 15th July, 1985 passed by the High Court Division, Barisal Bench in Second Appeal No. 295 of 1969).
full_judgment:
MH Rahman, J. : Respondents filed Title suit No. 21 of 1966 for a declaration that the order dated 17th December, 1963 of the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev) Bakerganj passed in Case No. 1 of 1962-63 under the provisions of Transfer of Agricultural Land Act 1951 (Act XXXIII of 1951) hereinafter referred to, in brief, as the Act, was illegal, without jurisdiction and not binding upon them, By that order the Government forfeited the suit land plaintiff No. 1 claimed to have auction purchased in Rent Execution Case No. 533 of 1933 in the benami of Krishna Lal Kundu, father of plaintiff No. 2 The plaintiffs case is that after the auction purchase plaintiff No. 1 leased out some portion of the suit holding to Afser Ali Akon and others on 2nd May, 1939 on receipt of kabuliyat from them. He got an ex parte decree in Rent Suit No. 952 of 1948 in the Fourth Court of Munsif, Patuakhali, for realisation of arrear rent, against Afsar Ali Akon and others, and in that suit plaintiff No. 2 was impleaded as a proforma-defendant as his father Krishna Lal Kundu was not then alive. As the disputed lands were recorded in the name of his benamder, plaintiff No. 1 obtained a deed of release, Ext. 7 from plaintiff No. 2, the only heir of Krishna Lal. But by the impugned order the Additional Deputy Commissioner, Barisal treated the deed of release as a deed of transfer, forfeited the disputed 4.19 acres of land of the deed, and imposed a fine of Tk. 100.00 on plaintiff No. 2 under the provisions of Act XXXIII of 1951 for transferring land in excess of 10 standard bighas.

2. The Government, appellant before us, contested the suit asserting, inter alia, that Krishna Lal Kundu was the real auction-purchaser of the suit property and not a benamder, that the so-called deed of release was in fact a deed of transfer; and that as plaintiff No. 2 in contravention of section 3 of the Act transferred more than 10 big has of land without permission of the Collector the impugned order was rightly passed.

<u>3. The trial Court decreed the suit. Relying on Abdul Gafur Sardar and ors. Vs. Wazed AIi Talukdar and another, 19 DLR 33 (37) wherein it is observed that "the Mukti-patra cannot confer the title on any party unless it is supported by a registered deed of transfer-kabala or gift" the trial Court held that the deed of release was not a document of transfer and that plaintiff No. 1 was the real owner of the property. The Appellate Court, however, reversed that decision. It disbelieved the case of benami on a detailed considerations of matters involved in the case. There was no evidence as to the necessity of the benami purchase. The plaintiffs did not produce the original document, namely, the sale certificate. The kabuliyat, Ext. 1, by Afsar and others, was executed on 2nd May, 1939 in favour of Krishna Lal Kundu indicating that even in 1939 the plaintiff was not acknowledged as the real owner of the lands. Exhibits-2 series show that some land was recorded in the name of Afsar. From 1931, the year of auction purchase, till 1948, the year plaintiff No. 2 obtained the ex parte decree in the rent suit against Afsar and others, impleading plaintiff No. 2 as a proforma-defendant, there was nothing to show that the lands were acquired by plaintiff No. 1. The assertions of the plaintiffs in the plaint and in the release are at variance. In the release it is stated that plaintiff No. 2 was the benamder, but the plaint indicated that plaintiff No. 2's father Krishna Lal was the benamder. In the plaint it was stated that plaintiff No. 1 was the real auction purchaser, but Exhibit-A, the written objection filed by plaintiff No. 2 before the Additional Deputy Commissioner, showed that the father of plaintiff No. 1 was the auction-purchaser. Plaintiff No. 1 and his father could not be the auction-purchaser at one and the same time as much as plaintiff No. 2 and his father could not be the benamder at the same time. The land acquired in rent execution case in 1931 was far in excess of the suit land, and plaintiff No. 1 did not take the deed of release in respect of the entire suit land claimed to have been purchased by him. The Appellate Court construed the release as an instrument of transfer.</u>

4. The High Court Division restored the judgment and decree of the trial Court In spite of its finding that plaintiff No. 1's case of leasing out a portion of the disputed holding to Afsar Ali Akon and others was not supported by the kabuliyat as it was executed in favour of Krishna Lal Kundu, it abruptly held that the ex parte rent decree, obtained by plaintiff No.1 in Rent Suit No. 952 of 1948 against the heirs of Afser Ali Akon in respect of that Kol-raiyati holding mentioned in the kabuliyat amply proved that long before the Act came into being, plaintiff No. 1, asserting his right as an auction purchaser, possessed the disputed land and that he was not required to make any purchase from plaintiff No. 2 and that the release was a simple deed acknowledging the claims of plaintiff No. 1 and not a deed of transfer. The High Court Division, however, did not set aside the finding of the Appellate Court that Krishna Lal Kundu was not the benamder of plaintiff No. 1.

The question of benami auction-purchase was raised and hotly contested before the trial Court. The appellate Court's finding in this regard can not be termed as irrelevant It was a material finding though no issue was framed on that point before the trial Court The High Court Division was clearly in error in reversing the finding of the appellate Court, the last court of fact, particularly when it was arrived at on good grounds. The mere fact that the land was not recorded in the name of plaintiff No. 1 could not give rise to the making of the release and that is why the story of benami auction purchase was introduced.

5. The term 'transfer' is defined in following clause (e) of section 2 of that Act:

(e) "transfer" means transfer by private sale, settlement, lease, sub-letting, gift, mortgage or any contract or agreement but does not include a complete usufructuary mortgage or a mortgage to a Land Mortgage Bank registered or deemed to be registered under the Bengal Co-operative Societies Act, 1940, or registered under the Co-operative Societies Act, 1912[.]

The objects of the Act were:

"It was brought to the notice of Government that in some areas the land-holders were selling out or otherwise transferring all kinds of lands including waste lands in their khas possession on a large scale with a view to get a greater benefit out of the provisions of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Bill 1948, when enacted and put into operation. It was apprehended that if such transfers were allowed to go on unrestricted, the land-holders would dispose of their excess khas lands leaving little land to be acquired by Government under the proposed State Purchase Scheme, for distribution among agriculturists having no land or possessing uneconomic holdings. It was, therefore, considered necessary that immediate steps should be taken to restrict such transfers of khas lands on a large scale."

For achieving those objectives the term 'transfer' has been defined very widely and penal measure for forfeiture of the transferred property and imposition of fine on the transferor have been provided in section 6 of the Act. It is true that a penal provision in a statute is to be construed strictly, but it is also an established principle of construction that if the intent of a provision in a statute is clear then it must be given effect to and cannot be whittled down on the ground of hardship.

<u>6. The case of Mt. Goday Koowur Vs. Mt. Ladoo, 13 Moor Ind App 585 (PC), is the earliest authority of note for the proposition that a bare admission in a document, made without any consideration, that the executant has no interest in a property, cannot pass his subsequently acquired title to the property. In that case it was held that a petition admitting that the petitioner has no claim to a certain estate did not operate as a conveyance of the subsequently acquired title, the petition having been filed in a pending suit by a petitioner having no present interest in the estate with a view to avoid an objection as to want of parties, and without receiving any consideration for the transfer of her future title.</u>

<u>7. In Jadu Nath Poddar Vs. Rup Lal Poddar, ILR 33 Cal. 967 (983-984), Dharam Chand Vs. Mauji Saha, 16 CU 436, Naraklal Vs. Thagoo Lal, AIR 1915 Cal. 819, Mathura Mohan Saba Vs. Ramkumar Saha, AIR 1916 Cal. 136 (141), Mookerjee, J held that a deed of release or relinquishment could not operate as a conveyance and could at most be taken as an admission that the executant had no interest in the property.</u>

<u>8. After considering aforementioned cases in Thayil Manno and another Vs. Kottiath Ramunni and others, AIR 1966 (SC) 337 the Indian Supreme Court held that those cases do not lay down a proposition of universal application that a deed styled as a deed of release cannot operate as a conveyance. It further noted Hemendra Nath Mukerji Vs. Kumar Nath Roy, 12 CWN 478. In that case it was held that by a registered deed of disclaimer the executants relinquished all their right, title and interest and claim in the properties in favour of the releasee upon the condition that the releasee would discharge certain debts and the executants would be under no liberty to pay those debts. Maclean, CJ held that the deed of release, on its true construction, was a transfer though it was stamped only as a release and not with ad valorem stamp.</u>

9. The Indian Supreme Court then concluded : "We think that a registered instrument styled a release deed releasing the right, title and interest of the executant in any property in favour of the releasee for valuable consideration may operate as a conveyance, if the document clearly discloses an intention to effect a transfer."

<u>10. This principle was extended in Kuppuswami Chettiar Vs. ASPA Arumugam Chettiar and another AIR 1967 (SC) 1395, to a registered instrument of release executed without any consideration. After considering that under section 123 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a gift may be effected by a registered instrument signed by or on behalf of the donor and attested by at least two witnesses, it was held that a registered instrument releasing the right, title and interest of the releasor without consideration may operate as a transfer by way of a gift, if the document clearly shows an intention to effect the transfer and is signed" by or on behalf of the releasor and attested by at least two witnesses.</u>

<u>11. I am in respectful agreement with the above two decisions of the Indian Supreme Court. These decisions have been followed in a number of decisions of different High Courts of India, namely, Lakshman Naik and another Vs. Smt. Sushila Swain, AIR 1968 Pat. 274 and Satyesh Chandra Banerjee Vs. Sm. Rani Banerjee and others, AIR 1977 Cal. 509. In Sanjukta Chatterjee Vs. Mrinmoy Chatterjee and others, 84 CWN (1979-80) 688 a deed of release, executed by the husband in favour of his wife and attested by their two sons, was construed as a gift.</u>

12. In the instant case the release is executed by plaintiff No. 2 on demand of plaintiff No. 1. It is a registered document valued at Tk. 2000.00.Plaintiff No. 2, the promisor agreed to compensate plaintiff No. 1, the promisee, in case the latter suffers any loss, and held out that on the basis of the document plaintiff No. 2 shall have the right to get his name recorded and enjoy all other rights of property.

<u>13. In view of the unassailable finding of the last court of fact that the father of plaintiff No. 2 was the real owner and not a name-lender, as alleged in the plaint, it is clear that plaintiff No. 2 had right in the property and was competent to pass on that right to plaintiff No. 2. For all practical purposes the document is a document of transfer. Even if it is not construed as a document of conveyance under section 6 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, its nature as an agreement cannot be ignored. The document is a kind of contrivance that comes within the broad spectrum of definition of 'transfer' in clause (e) of section 2 of the Act.</u>

14. In view of the above, I allow the appeal, but without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment of the High Court Division is set aside and that of the Appellate Court is restored.

ATM Afzal J : I have gone through the judgments prepared by my learned brothers MH Rahman and Latifur Rahman, JJ;  I agree with that of MH Rahman, J.

Mustafa Kamal J : I have had advantage of going through the judgments proposed to be delivered by my learned brothers MH Rahman and Latifur Rahman, JJ; I concur with the decision of MH Rahman, J.

Latifur Rahman J : In this appeal, the primary question for consideration being, whether Ext. 7, a registered deed of release is a document of transfer, I find it extremely difficult to agree with the view of my learned brother MH Rahman, J : Hence I am writing this separate judgment.

18. The plaintiff-respondents filed the suit for declaration that the order dated 17.12.73 passed by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Bakerganj in Case No. 1/62-63 under the provisions of Act XXXIII of 1951, hereinafter, briefly, called the Act, is illegal, without jurisdiction and not binding upon them in respect of the disputed property. The case of the plaintiffs is that, plaintiff No. 1 had auction purchased the property in Rent Execution Case No. 533 of 1931 in the benami of Krishna Lal Kundu, father of plaintiff No. 2 Thereafter on 2.5.39 plaintiff No. 1 leased out some portion of that holding to Afsar Ali Akon and others on receipt of the kabuliyat from them. Plaintiff No. 1 thereafter brought rent Suit No. 952 of 1948 in the 4th Court of Munsif, Patuakhali for realisation of arrear rent against Afsar Ali Akon and others and in that suit plaintiff No. 2 was impleaded as a proforma defendant as his father Krishna Lal Kundu was dead. As the disputed land was recorded in the name of benamder, plaintiff No. 1 obtained a deed of release from plaintiff No. 3, the only heir of Krishna Lal Kundu. The Additional Deputy Commissioner, Barisal treated the said deed of release as a deed of transfer and forfeited the disputed land and also imposed a fine of Tk. 100.00 on plaintiff No. 2 under the provisions of the Act for transferring land in excess of 10 standard bigas as provided in that Act.

19. The defendant-Government contested the suit contending, inter alia, that Krishna Lal Kundu was not a benamder but the real auction purchaser of the suit property and that the so-called deed of release was in fact a deed of transfer and as such the order for forfeiture is valid and legal.

20. The trial Court decreed the suit upon holding that the deed of release, exhibit 7, executed by plaintiff No. 2 in favour of plaintiff No. 1 was not a deed of transfer.

21. On appeal the judgment of the trial Court was reversed by the first appellate Court on the finding that the deed of release was in fact a deed of sale and the appellate Court further held that plaintiff No.2 was not in the benamder of plaintiff No.1. In second appeal the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division took up only one question as to whether Ext. 7, the Nadabi patra could be treated as a deed of transfer under the Act. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division from the recitals of the deed of release did not find it to be a document of transfer.

Consequently, he set aside the judgment of the first appellate Court and affirmed the judgment of the trial Court.

22. Mr. Salehuzzaman, learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the Government mainly argued that, though the nomenclature of this document appears to be a deed of release releasing the right, title and interest of the releasor in favour of the releasee, but in reality it operated as a gift as contemplated under section 2(e) of the Act and as such the document in question comes within the mischief of the Act. Mr. Salehuzzamen in support of his argument has cited the case of Kuppuswami Chettiar Vs. ASPA Arumugam Chettiar and another reported in AIR 1967 (SC) 1395. The learned Deputy Attorney-General next faintly argued that the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division ought to have given a finding on benami transaction.

23. In the trial Court on the pleadings of the parties some issues were framed and the primary issues were issue Nos. 5 and 6 which are as follows:

"(5) Is the impugned order illegal, void, ineffective and not binding on the plaintiffs?

(6) Is the plaintiff entitled to any declaration as prayed for?

The plaintiffs suit was for a declaration that the order purported to have been passed by the ADC (Revenue) in Case No. 1/62-63 under the provisions of Act forfeiting his land is illegal, without jurisdiction and not binding against the plaintiffs.

24. The trial Court found from the recitals of Ext. 7 (deed of release) that it was not a document of transfer under the Act and consequently declared the impugned order of forfeiture of land of the plaintiffs as illegal, void, without jurisdiction and not binding against the plaintiffs.

25. The material finding of the learned Munsif in his judgment is quoted below:

"It is abundantly clear that no transfer could have been effected by the deed of release in the Muktipatra (Ext. 7). The learned lawyer for the defendant argues that the recitals in Ext. 7 would show that the plaintiff No. 2 was the benamder while the case in the plaint is that his father Krishna Lal was the benamder. Next he pointed out that Ext. A would show that Phatick Molla, the father of the plaintiff No. 1, was the auction purchaser. He thus argues that Krishna Lal was neither the real purchaser nor the ostensible purchaser."

16. Thus, from the above observation it patently appears that on behalf of the defendant no evidence was adduced challenging the benami transaction in between plaintiff No. 1 and the father of plaintiff No. 2, Krishna Lal Kundu. As a matter of fact the present suit was not deciding any benami issue between the parties. It was indeed difficult for the Government 0 adduce any evidence on the question of Benami as the transaction took place between plaintiff No.1 and plaintiff No. 2's father as far back as in 1931. As a matter of fact no evidence was adduced by either of the parties on the question of benami as no issue was raised on that behalf.

27. From the above observation of the trial Court it is clear that the lawyer of the defendant only argued the question of Benami. The question of Benami incidentally came up in the suit as because plaintiff No. 1 averred in the plaint that in the rent. sale he auction purchased in Rent Execution Case No. 355 of 1931 AD in the benami of plaintiff No. 2's father and he having died his son executed the deed of release Ext. 7. The whole argument of the defendant was really based on the release deed, Ext. 7 itself and from its construction the defendant argued that it was a transfer under the Act and hence the land stood forfeited. On the pleadings of the parties no issue was also framed by the trial Court as to whether plaintiff No. 2 was the benamder of plaintiff No. 1 as that was not the material proposition within the frame of the suit. The trial Court further made a positive finding that.

"The learned Additional Deputy Commissioner in his order (Ext. C) did not make any finding that the deed of release Ext. 7 was actually a deed of transfer although he made a finding that CP Satyendra made transfer of agricultural land by way of deed of release".

From the order-sheet (Ext. 5) of the Misc. Case No. 1 of 1962-63 of the Act, it appears that one Mr. Rafiqul Islam alleged that Satyendra Nath Kundu transferred agricultural land more than the quantity permitted by law. From the order sheet it further appears that after hearing arguments of the parties and on perusal of the document the land was forfeited without holding that the Nadabi-patra was a deed of transfer.

From the judgment of the lower appellate Court it appears that an issue was framed at the Appellate stage on the following effects:

"Was the plaintiff a real purchaser in Rent Execution No. 533 of 1931 ?"

It may be pointed out here that no such issue of benami was framed by the trial Court as there was no material proposition with regard to the question of benami before the trial Court. It appears that the lower appellate Court suo motu raised this issue of fact as to benami for the first time in the appellate Court when as a matter of fact this issue was not specifically raised in the trial Court nor any evidence was adduced by the parties in respect of benami. The land of plaintiff No. 1 having been forfeited by the Government, the plaintiffs asserted in the plaint that by virtue of the deed of release the defendant-Government cannot forfeit the land as this document was not a document of transfer. The Government's main contention in the written statement was that this deed of release was a document of transfer and the land stood forfeited to the Government. In view of the pleadings, it is really unfortunate that when no issue of benami was specifically mooted before the trial Court, the appellate Court went beyond its jurisdiction to frame an issue of fact at the appellate stage which was not at all taken up at the trial stage. Further, I may point out here that both the real owner and the ostensible owner filed the suit together for a declaration that the forfeiture of the land is not valid and legal in view of the deed of release Ext. 7. Thus, it is difficult to appreciate how the question of benami was relevant and a material proposition within the frame of the suit. The lower appellate Court without applying its mind to the real question of fact in issue as settled by the trial Court illegally decided the issue of benami in the present case when as a matter of fact no evidence was adduced by either side on the question of benami in the suit. I may point out that an issue of fact must be confined to the real question in controversy. Here the real question is, whether the defendant can forfeit the land of plaintiff No. 1 on the basis of transfer by Ext. 7. The mere reference of benami in the plaint and the denial of the same by the defendant in the written statement does not make the question of Benami a material question for the purpose of framing an issue at the appellate stage. Consequently, the lower appellate Court's judgment on this point is erroneous and not sustainable in law.

28. I may mention that in the four-corners of the judgment of the lower appellate Court there is not a word with regard to the recitals of the deed of release which was very vital for the lower appellate Court to consider for understanding the nature of the document. The lower appellate Court without at all applying its mind to the recitals on pure surmise and other extraneous and irrelevant considerations observed as follows:

"I am of the view that apparently the deed of release looks innocent but it is to all intent and purpose a deed of sale."

This finding of the lower appellate Court could have been sustained, if there would have been any independent consideration of the recitals of the document as such. But from the judgment it appears that without considering the recitals of the document itself the lower appellate Court held that the deed of release is a document of sale.

It may be pointed out that the lower appellate Court did not decide the vital question in the suit as to whether Ext. 7 is a document of transfer and this being the foundation of the defendant's forfeiture of the plaintiffs land, the judgment of the lower appellate Court cannot be maintained at all as the document has been totally misconstrued by the lower appellate Court. The vital issue having been left out, the issue on fact not raised and decided at the trial Court was illegally disposed of without any evidence on record.

29. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division rightly took up only one material question for consideration, whether Ext. 7, Nadabi patra was in reality a deed of release or a deed of transfer. I must mention here that the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division correctly and appropriately did not consider the issue of benami as that was wholly irrelevant within the frame of the suit and did not speak a word with regard to benami in his judgment. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division was perfectly correct in his approach in deciding the nature of the document from the recitals of the document itself and thereby construing the deed of release not as a document of transfer. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division correctly construed the document in its proper perspective within the frame of the suit and held as follows:

"This fact amply proved that long before the East Bengal Transfer of Agricultural Land Act 1951 came into being, plaintiff No.1 asserting his right as an auction purchaser possessed the disputed land. This being the position plaintiff No. 1 was not required to make any purchase from plaintiff No. 2. I, therefore, hold that the deed of release Ext. 7 was not a deed of transfer, it was a simple deed acknowledging the claim of plaintiff No. 1. In view of the facts, I hold that the impugned order passed under the Provisions of the East Bangal Transfer of Agricultural Land Act, 1951 (Act XXXIII of 1951) was illegal, void and not binding upon the plaintiffs".

30. It will be profitable to consider section 2 (e) of the Act which defines "transfer" as follows:

"transfer" means transfer by private sale, settlement, lease, sub-letting, gift, mortgage or any complete usufructuary mortgage or a mortgage to a Land Mortgage Bank registered or deemed to be registered under the Bengal Co-operative Societies Act, 1940, or registered under the Co-operative Societies Act, 1912."

31. It is to be stated that deed of release is not a primary document of transfer. Consequently, I am called upon to consider this document as a whole, particularly from the operative portion of the document as to whether the same can be construed as a transfer as defined in the said Act though this registered instrument is styled as a deed of release.

<u>32. It appears from the recitals of the deed of release (Ext. 7) that the property belongs to the plaintiff-recipient and the same was purchased with the fund of the recipient and he was in possession and enjoyment of the property. The recitals clearly show that the executant had never any right, title and possession in the schedule land of the document. The operative portion of the document shows, inter alia, that the schedule land of the deed of release was auction purchased with the money of the recipient in the name of the executant; that the recipient is the actual owner and possessor of the land; that the land has been recorded by the recipient in the name of the executant; that the same is being relinquished by this deed' of rei case so that the recipient may record his own name in the records of right and could pay rent as before in. his own name and that no valuable consideration passed between them by the execution of the deed of release other than fixing a valuation of the deed for the purpose of registration only. Thus, it is palpably clear that this document was executed accepting tile recipient as the rightful owner and possessor of the schedule land and the same was executed' only for the purpose of correction of the record of right as the property though purchased in the name of tile plaintiff-recipient with his own money stood-in the name of the executant who was only ostensible owner of the property. In that view of the matter, I find it legally difficult to construe the document as one intended to be one of transfer of ownership. If the document would have clearly disclosed an intention to effect a transfer, then, I would nave unhesitatingly held the same to be a document of transfer, even if it was styled as a release deed. But in the present case, Ext. 7 does not at all disclose an intention to transfer existing or future rights of the executant. Further, from the recitals of the document as indicated above it is wholly difficult to hold that any right, title and interest was being transferred from the executant to the recipient, when the executant himself admitted in the document that he had no right, title and interest in the property itself.</u>

33. I may mention here, that I have no dispute with the proposition of law enunciated in the case cited QY the learned Deputy Attorney-General.

In that reported decision, the same question was mooted as to whether a deed of release operated as a conveyance in favour of the recipient. In that case, the Supreme Court of India held on the construction of that document that a release deed releasing right, title and interest of the releasor without consideration may operate as transfer by way of gift when the document clearly shows the intention to effect a transfer. In that cited decision the recital was that the owner of the property died leaving the appellant as the only lawful heir and he released all his rights, title and interest that devolved upon him to the recipient of the documents. The further recital was that the entire immovable property belonging to the owner was released in favour of the recipient without any consideration. So, in the fact of that case, the learned Judges of the Supreme Court of India held that whatsoever may be the form of the document, in substance it was a transfer of ownership and the same was construed as a document of transfer as the document used words of sufficient amplitude to transfer title to one who had no title before transfer. I am afraid, the case cited by the learned Deputy Attorney-General has no manner of application in the fact of the present case. I may further point out here, that the learned Judges in AIR 1967 Supreme Court case, took note of the case of K Hatchibowder Vs. Bheana Gowden reported in AIR 1960-Madras-33 wherein it was observed that a release deed would not be effective to transfer title. A release deed can only feed title but cannot transfer right.

34. In the case of Thayil Manno Vs. Kottiath Ramunni reported in AIR 1966 SC 337, it has been held that a deed of release with valuable consideration may operate as a conveyance, if it clearly discloses an intention to effect a transfer and in that reported decision Ext. B-2 was held to be a document of transfer on its true construction.

35. Subsequently, the view of the Supreme Court of India was followed in the cases reported in AIR 1968 Patna-271 and AIR 1977 Calculta-509. In the case reported in AIR 1954 Bombay-95 Chagla CJ observed that the court is not to confine itself merely to the form of a transaction but it is open to the court to know the form and to ascertain the real nature of the transaction and in doing so the court is not allowed to ignore the true and legal position that arises out of the document in which the parties have chosen to embody the transaction and must determine what is the true nature of the transaction. In the case of Abdul Gafur Sardar Vs. Wazed Ali Talukder reported in 19 DLR 33 it was held that a Mukti-patra cannot confer title on any party in regard to land unless it is supported by a registered deed of transfer.

36. Thus on a careful consideration of the law and fact applicable in the case, I am of the view, that the deed of release Ext. 7 in the present case is not a document of transfer as defined in section 2(e) of the Act. I may also point out that transfer has also been defined in section 5 of the Transfer of Property Act as follows:

"5. "Transfer of property" defined.-In the following sections "transfer of property" means an act by which a living person conveys property, in present or in future, to one or more other living persons, or to himself, or to himself and one or more other living persons; and "to transfer property" is to perform such act."

According to Transfer of Property Act, the transfer means voluntary acts of transfer by which real rights in the property passes from one person to another. Section 5 of Transfer of Property Act has not spelt out transfer in broad details as has been done in section 2(e) of Act XXXIII of 1951. Section 2(e) of the Act having widely defined 'Transfer' the land of the plaintiff could be forfeited if it comes under any of the categories mentioned therein and not otherwise.

Consequently, I find it very difficult to lawfully construe the deed of release either as a private sale, gift or agreement in the present case. Hence, the appeal is dismissed without any order as to cost. The order of the forfeiture of the land by defendant-Government is illegal, without jurisdiction and not binding upon the plaintiffs.

Order of the Court

By a majority decision the appeal is allowed without cost.

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party to show cause as to why the judgment and order dated 27-4-98 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge. Daudkandi, Comilla in allowing Miscellaneous Case No.7 of 1998 under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure which was preferred against the ex parte decree dated 10-6-97 passed in Title Suit No. 4 of 1995 should not be set aside.

2. The petitioner as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No.4 of 1994 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge Sadar. Comilla for declaration of title and recovery of Khas possession alleging, inter alia, that the opposite party who is a tenant under him has no title and possession. It was alleged that the opposite party has been serving in the police department and taking this advantage the opposite party in spite of ex parte decree obtained by him in Title Suit No. 4 of 1995 stood in the way of recovery of Khas possession for which he preferred Civil Revision No. 916 of 1997 before this Court against the order of the learned Assistant Judge, rejecting the prayer for striking out the name of the defendant Nos. 2 and 3 i.e., the Deputy Commissioner and Superintendent of Police, Comilla, It was further alleged that the civil revision was allowed and the name of the defendant Nos. 2 and 3 i.e. the Deputy Commissioner and Superintendent of Police. Comilla were struck off and, subsequently a date was fixed for ex parte disposal and accordingly, it was decreed ex parte on 10-6-97. The opposite party thereafter filed Miscellaneous Case No. 7 of 1998 under Order 9 rule 13 for setting aside the ex parte decree dated 10-6-97 and for restoration of the original suit to its file and number and the learned Assistant Judge allowed the Miscellaneous Case setting aside the ex parte decree and restoring the original suit to its file and number.

3. Mr. Mokhlesur Rahman, learned Advocate for the petitioner, submits that the opposite party has no title and interest in the suit land and as such, Miscellaneous Case No. 7 of 1998 under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure should have been dismissed by the learned Assistant Judge as not being maintainable. He submits that the learned Assistant Judge committed an illegality in allowing the Miscellaneous Case under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure setting aside the exparte decree dated 10-6-97 and restoring the original suit being No. 4 of 1995 to its file and number and, as such, the impugned judgment and order of the learned Assistant Judge should be set aside.

4. Syed Mahmud Hossain, learned Advocate for the opposite party, submits that the learned, Assistant Judge allowed the Miscellaneous Case after due consideration of the evidences as adduced by the parties after giving compensatory cost of Taka 2000.00 to the petitioner and, as such, this revision should be dismissed. He further submits that the petitioner withdrew the cost awarded by the learned Assistant Judge in Miscellaneous Case No. 7 of 1998 and, as such, he cannot assail the court's order setting aside the ex parte decree and, as such, this revision should be dismissed.

<u>5. Heard the learned Advocates of both the sides and perused the revisional application along with affidavit-in-opposition filed by the opposite party and counter affidavit with its Annexures. It appears that the petitioner as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No.4 of 1995 before the Court of Assistant Judge, Comilla wherein he filed an application for striking out the name of defendant Nos. 2 and 3 i.e., the Deputy Commissioner and Superintendent of Police, Comilla from the plaint which was rejected by the learned Assistant Judge. It further appears that against this order of the learned Assistant Judge, the petitioner filed Civil Revision No. 916 of 1997 which was allowed striking out the name of defendant Nos. 2 and 3 from the plaint leaving only the petitioner as defendant. It also appears that after the order of the. High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 916 of 1997, the Title Suit No. 4 of 1995 was fixed for ex parte hearing on 10-6-97 on which date it was decreed ex parte. The learned Advocate for the opposite party contends that he has been in possession of the suit premises as a tenant under the Government as the same was declared vested and non-resident property. He further contends that he did not get any opportunity in filling written statement in Title Suit No. 4 of 1995 after the name of defendant Nos. 2 and 3 i.e. Deputy Commissioner and Superintendent of Police, Comilla was struck off and that the suit was decreed ex parte to his prejudice for which the opposite party filed Miscellaneous Case No. 7 of 1995 under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the ex parte order and for restoration of the original suit to its file and number and the learned Assistant Judge after due consideration allowed the miscellaneous case and restored the original title suit to its file and number subject to payment of compensatory cost of Taka 2000.00 and, as such, learned Assistant Judge did not commit any illegality in allowing the Miscellaneous Case. He also submits that the learned Assistant Judge by the impugned order dated 27-4-98 allowed the Miscellaneous Case with compensatory cost of Taka 2000.00 which was made condition precedent and that on being deposited the same by the petitioner, the opposite party withdrew the same and thereafter the learned Assistant Judge restored the original suit to its file and number and, as such, the petitioner cannot assail the order of the learned Assistant Judge after receipt of the compensatory cost. The petitioner as it appears, himself withdrew the compensatory cost of Taka 2000.00 by granting a receipt and that after such payment the learned Assistant Judge restored the suit to its file and number after setting aside the ex parte decree dated 10-7-97. The learned Advocate for the opposite party in support of his contention has cited the case of Purvada Satyanarayan Amurthy vs Gadepalli Sundara Rao, reported in AIR 1938 (Madras) 603 wherein it was held that the decree holder after accepting cost without protest cannot subsequently attack the court's order setting aside the ex parte decree. In the instant case the petitioner has accepted the compensatory cost of Taka 2000.00 awarded-by the learned Assistant Judge who after payment of compensatory cost set aside the ex parte decree and restored the original suit to its original file and number. In view of this admitted fact and the principle as enunciated in the above ruling, I am also constrained to hold the view that since the decree holder petitioner accepted the cost so he cannot attack the court's order for setting aside the ex parte decree as the petitioner cannot approbate and reprobate at the same time. It further appears that the learned Assistant Judge set aside the impugned order for ends of justice and also to give the opposite party an opportunity to contest the original suit after the names of the defendant Nos. 2-3 i.e., the Deputy Commissioner and Superintendent of Police, Comilla were struck off from the plaint. In this view of the fact and circumstances of the case, I do not find that the learned Assistant Judge committed any illegality in allowing the Miscellaneous Case under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The petitioner is, therefore, not entitled to the relief as prayed for. So, this revision must fail.</u>

6. In the result, the Rule is discharged on contest without any order as to costs. The learned Assistant Judge is directed to dispose the case as early as possible preferably within 3 months from the date of receipt of this order.

Let a copy of this order be sent to the, court below at once.

End.

full_judgment:
Syed Mahmud Hossain J: This appeal, by leave, is directed against the judgment and order dated 7-8-2008 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.9268 of 2007 making the Rule absolute.

2. The facts; leading to the filing of this appeal, are precised below:

Respondent .No. 1 brought the writ petition on the averment, inter alia, that three full brothers; namely, Noor Hossain, Mosharraf Hossain and Tozammal Hossain and one Saghir Ahmed initially formed a partnership firm under the name and style of Messrs East Pakistan, Rubber Industries in terms of an  agreement of a partnership dated 7-5-1957 (that' another brother Iqbal Hussain was admitted to the said partnership as a minor). The Government of erstwhile East Pakistan allotted a piece of land measuring 1 (one) acre appertaining to an industrial Plot No. 278 at Tejgaon Industrial Area, Dhaka in the name of the said partnership firm on 26-8-1960. the partner, Noor Hussain died on 23-7-1968 leaving behind his two sons, namely, Anwar Husain and Iftekhar Husain, four daughters, Jinnat Husain (Zinat Husain), Jesmin Husain (minor), Israt Husain (minor)! Sharmin Husain (mitior), a widow Rowshan Ara Hussain and mother Zohra Khatun. They became partners of the said firm as Noor Hossain's legal heirs. Meanwhile, minor Iqbal Husain having attained majority became a full-fledged partner along with others under a reconstituted deed of partnership dated 24-7-1968. A standard lease deed for a period of 99 years in respect of the said industrial plot was executed on 20-1-1970 and registered on 17-2-1971 between the Government of erstwhile East Pakistan and the said partnership firm. On 31-8-1970, another partner Mosharaf Husain resigned from the partnership business in term of a compromise decree passed in Title Suit No. 65 of 1970 in the third Court of the then learned Subordinate Judge, Dhaka. After liberation war, the name of the firm was changed as 'Bangladesh Rubber Industries by a deed of rectification. In consequence thereof the change was, recorded with the Registrar of Firms. Thereafter, a deed of agreement for dissolution of the firm was executed on 31-12-1975 by the remaining partners, namely, Mrs. Rawshan Ara Hossain, Mr Iftekhar Hussain, Mr Anwar Hossain and Miss Zeenat Hossain (heirs of late Noor Hossain) on the one hand and Mr Tofazammel Hossain, Mr Iqbal Hossain, Mrs. Zohra Khatun and Mr Sagir Ahmed, on the other hand, vide Annexure-D under the terms and conditions stated therein. After dissolution of the aforesaid partnership, late Noor Hossain's heirs, namely, Anwar Hussain and Iftekhar Husain, four daughters, Zinat Hussain, Jesmin Hussain (minor), Ishrat Hussain (minor) and Sharmin Hussain (minor) and widow Rowshan Ara Hussain, executed a fresh partnership deed dated 1-1-1976 (admitting the minors to, the benefit of partnership) to run and continue a partnership business vide Annexure-E and they got it registered with the Registrar of Joint Stock Companies and Firms under the Partnership Act being Registration No.PF/22285 (wrongly written PR 33385) dated 9-11-1976. Thereafter, the heirs of late Tozammel Hussain (i.e. the present appellants) filed an application in the office of respondent No.1 for getting their names mutated in place of Bangladesh Rubber Industries as per their share (i.e. two big has of land in term of the deed of dissolution, vide Annexure-D). The Senior Assistant Secretary (respondent No.3 in writ petition) on the basis of the aforesaid application served notices upon the parties concerned on 6-2-2005 and 20-2-2007 to appear before the Joint Secretary (respondent No.2 in writ petition) with their respective documents. On hearing both the sides, he rejected the prayer for mutation, vide his letter dated 12-6-2007 (Annexure-I) expressing that the Ministry had no scope to interfere with the matter of mutation since a civil suit was pending in this regard but nevertheless directed the parties concerned to inform the Government of the fate of the pending suit or the result of the compromise, if made in the meantime. The further case of the writ-petitioner is that after issuance of letter dated 12-6-2007, the present appellants (respondent Nos.7-9.in writ petition) did not follow the directive of the said notice and beyond the knowledge of present respondent No.1 (petitioner in writ petition) and in collusion with the officials of the Government got the impugned order dated 13-9-2007 (Annexure-J) allowing mutation of their names in respect of two big has of land without serving any notice whatsoever to them and simultaneously communicated the said order to the Assistant Commissioner Land, Tejgaon Circle, Dhaka and other concerned officials for compliance.

3. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the letter dated 13-9-2007 issued by writ-respondent No.1, the writ-petitioners filed a writ petition before the High Court Division and obtained Rule Nisi in Writ Petition No. 9268 of 2007.

4. Writ-respondent Nos. 7-9 contested Rule by filing affidavit-in-opposition controverting the material statements made in the writ petition. Their case, in short, is that they accepted the material facts as reproduced in paragraph-z about the formation of partnership firm on 7th May, 1957 under the name of East Pakistan Rubber Industries, subsequent reconstitution of the said firm and ultimate dissolution on 31st December 1975 under the terms of the deed of dissolution (vide Annexure-D). The said deed of dissolution narrates (in recitation portion) about the formation of the partnership firm on 14-5-1957 and its subsequent reconstitution and ultimate dissolution of the said partnership firm on 1st December 1975 on apportions of the shares among the existing partners in the form of land; cash money and good-will of the said firm.

5. The learned Judges of the High Court Division, upon hearing the parties by the judgment and order dated 7-8-2008 made the Rule absolute.

6. Feeling aggrieved by and dissatisfied with judgment and order passed by the High Court Division, the writ- respondents as the leave- petitioners moved this Division by filing Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal Nos. 2237 of 2008, on which, leave was granted on 6-1-2009; resulting in Civil Appeal No.1 of 2010

7. Mr. MI Farooqui, learned Senior Advocate, appearing on behalf of the appellants, submits that the High Court Division committed error of law in construing the deed of dissolution of partnership dated 1-12-1975 (Annexure-D) as a deed of agreement although pursuant to the dissolution of the partnership firm of 1957 the existing partners were entitled to apportion of their respective shares in the form of land, cash money, and the 'good will' of the dissolved firm. After that, some of the partners formed another partnership firm on 9-11-1976 using the name of the firm by virtue of their right in terms of deed of dissolution and would reap the benefit’s of its 'good-will' and got it registered with the Registrar of Firm (Annexure-E). He further submits that by the deed of dissolution (Annexure-D), the partnership registered on 25-5-1957 was dissolved on 31-12- 1975 and the share of the appellants' ancestor, Mr Tozammel Hossain in two bighas of land as per clause-4 of the deed of dissolution of the partner- ship would be moveable property as a result of dissolution under the Partnership Act. Such dissolution would not be required compulsory registration and the Government committed no illegality in mutating the names of the heirs of late Tozammel Hussain in respect of 2 bighas of land. He also submits that the High Court Division committed error of law by giving legal entity to a registered partnership firm because a partnership firm (registered or unregistered) does not come within the meaning of legal person and that in a partnership business, partners carry on business both as principals and as agents for each other within the scope of partnership firm and as such-the impugned judgment should be set aside.

8. Mr AM Aminuddin, learned Senior Advocate,appearing on behalf of respondent Nos.1-6, on the other hand, submits that Bangladesh Rubber Industries is a registered Partnership Firm constituted under the provision of Partnership Act, 1932;· As such, it is capable of holding immovable property in its Own name and the immoveable property measuring' 01 acre of land. comprising Industrial' Plot No. 278 of Tejgaon Industrial Area, Dhaka, having been allotted and transferred to the said partnership firm through registered perpetual lease deed, it has become the owner of the said immovable property. As such, to divest the title of the said immoveable property from the partnership firm, a registered deed of transfer, is required and the findings of the High Court Division in this regard is the correct exposition of law and, as such, no interference is called for. He further submits that the deed of dissolution of partnership (Annexure- D) cannot be termed as a deed of dissolution and that if the said deed is construed as a whole .it appears that it is merely an agreement between the parties, Therefore, the High Court Division-rightIy held that the deed of dissolution was, in fact; a deed of agreement among the partners. He also submits that writ-respondent No. 1 with a malafide intention and beyond the knowledge of the respondent-firm issued the letter mutating 2 bighas of land belonging to the respondent firm in the name, of the appellants and, as such, the High Court Division was perfectly justified in declaring the said letter to have been issued without lawful authority.

9. We have considered the submissions of the learned Senior Advocates of both the sides, perused the impugned judgment and the materials on record.

10. Before entering into the merit of the appeal, it would be pertinent to go through the grounds; for which, leave was granted. The grounds are quoted below:

"The High Court Division committed error of law in construing the deed of dissolution of partnership dated 1-12-1975 (Annexure-D) as a deed of agreement although pursuant to the dissolution of the partnership firm of 1957 the existing partners were entitled to apportion the respective shares in the form 'of land, cash money, and the 'good-will' of the dissolved firm and that thereafter, some of the partners formed another partnership firm on 9-11-1976 using the name of the firm by virtue of their right in terms of deed of dissolution to reap the benefits of its 'good-will' and got it registered with " the Registrar of Firm (Annexure-E). ,

By the deed of dissolution (Annexure-D), the partnership registered on 25-5-1957 was dissolved on 1-12-1975 and the share of the 'appellants" ancestor, 'Mr Tozammel Hossain in two big has of land as per clause-4 of the deed of dissolution of the partnership would be moveable property as a result of dissolution under the Partnership Act and such dissolution would not' be required compulsory registration and the Government committed no illegality in mutating the names of the heirs of late Tozammel Hussain in respect of 2 bighas of land The High Court Division committed, error of law by giving legal entity to a registered partnership firm because a partnership firm (registered or unregistered) does not come within the meaning of 'legal person' and in a partnership business, partners carry on business both as principals and as agents for each other within this scope of partnership business, that the firm's name is a. mere expression, not a legal entity although for convenience it may be used for the sake of suing or being sued, a partnership under the Partnership Act is not a legal person, it is not an entity and it is merely a collective name for the individuals who are the members of the partnership."

11. Admittedly, the Government allotted one acre of 'land in the name of the then partnership firm, East Pakistan Rubber Industries by a registered deed of lease executed on 20-11-1970 and registered on 12-2-1971. By a deed of dissolution dated 31-12-1975, the partnership firm formed on 7-5-1957 was dissolved with divisions of assets, good-will etc. among the partners. Soon after dissolution of the earlier firm a new partnership firm in the name of Bangladesh Rubber Industries was formed among the heirs of Noor Hossain as is evident from (Annexure-E), the letter dated 9-11-1976 according registration to the newly created firm.

12. Having gone through Annexure-D, the deed of dissolution of partnership, the High Court Division came to a finding that although the heading of Annexure-D and some of its statements manifest that the parties named this deed as the deed of dissolution of partnership, but practically the partnership had not been dissolved and that the same had continued after 'retiring 'of some partners as evident from vital condition No.2 of the said deed. The High Court Division held that Annexure-D, in fact, is an agreement between the existing partners of M/s Bangladesh Rubber Industries in' respect of retirement of particular partners from the partnership firm. The High Court Division came to a finding that clause-4 of Annexure-D stipulated the terms as to the benefit of outgoing partners which manifested that Mr Tozammel Hossain would get two bighas of land from Industrial Plot No. 278 of Tejgaon Industrial Area, Dhaka, owned by the partnership firm while Mr Iqbal Hossain, Mr Sagir Ahmed and Mrs. Zohura Khatoon would be paid in terms of cash for their shares in the properties of the firm and that they would not get any share in the landed property. The High Court Division held that Annexure-B, the deed of lease was registered under the' provision of section 17 of the Registration Act, 1908 since title to the immovable property was to be transferred from the Government of the then East Pakistan to the predecessor of MIs Bangladesh. Rubber Industries by way of perpetual lease. Therefore, the High Court Division held that to divest the said title from the registered partnership firm M/s. Bangladesh Rubber Industries by way of transfer to anybody, a registered instrument was required in accordance with the provision of section 17 of the Registration Act, 1908. The High Court Division observed that when the partnership firm is registered under the provision of section 59 of the Partnership Act, 1932, the acquisition of immovable property in the name of registered partnership firm could not be treated as acquisition by the partners of the firm and that the said immovable property always remained as the property of the registered partnership firm under the provision of section i4 of the Partnership Act,1932.

13. We have gone through the deed of dissolution of partnership dated 31-12-1975 (Annexure-D) which starts with heading "Deed of Dissolution of Partnership". Page-4 of Annexure- D states, amongst others, as follows:

AND WHEREAS the partners mutually and amicably decided amongst themselves to dissolve the' Partnership Firm M/s Bangladesh Rubber Industries on arid from 31st December, 1975.

NOW THIS DEED OF DISSOLUTION OF PARTNESHIP witnesseth that the part- hers as mentioned above do HEREBY mutually and amicably dissolve the partnership, firm M/s Bangladesh Rubber Industries on and from 31st December, 1975 on the terms and condition as-

That this deed of dissolution of partnership shall come into effect on and' from 31st

December,1975.

Clauses-4 and 5 of the Annexure-D run as follows:

4. That the landed property measuring one acre at plot No.278, Plan No. TP 21/48 dated 25-11-1948 in Tejgaon Industrial Area fully described in schedule which stands in the name of the firm "M/s East Pakistan Rubber Industries" at present "M/s Bangladesh Rubber Industries" shall be shared and owned exclusively by the partners as under;

(i) Mr Tozammel Hussain two bighas, (ii) Mrs Rowshan Ara Hussain along with her children-one bigha.

That the other partners shall execute and register a deed for transferring the landed property in the names of the persons mentioned in para 4 of this deed and also do such other acts and things as will be necessary for this purpose.

14. Soon after execution of the deed of dissolution of partnership dated 31-12-1975 (Annexure-D), respondent No. 1 applied for registration of Mis Bangladesh Rubber Industries by submitting a deed of partnership dated 1-1-1976 to which registration was accorded by the Registrar, Bangladesh Firms on 9-11-1976. Therefore, it appears that respondent No.1, M/s. Bangladesh Rubber Industries started as a newly registered firm on and from 9-11-1976 as is evident from Annexure-E. pursuant to partnership deed bearing No. PR/22285 dated 9-11-1976.

15. Having gone through Annexure-D, the deed of dissolution of partnership, in general, and Annexure-E, the letter dated 9-11-1976, in particular, according registration to M/s Bangladesh Rubber Industries, we are of the view that in fact, M/s Bangladesh Rubber Industries registered on 25-5-1957 is no longer in existence and that a newly registered M/s Bangladesh Rubber Industries has come into being on 9-11-1976.

16. Now the question is to be resolved whether title of one acre of land was transferred to Mr Tozammel Hossain and Mrs Rousan Ara Hossain along with her children pursuant to the deed of dissolution (Annexure-D) without any registered instrument of transfer as contemplated under section 17 of the Registration Act.

<u>17. Whether a partner's share in a partnership property is treated as moveable property or not, it is necessary to examine the nature of a partnership property. What is important to mention here is that section  a of the (Bangladesh) Partnership Act, 1932, when read along with relevant sections, shows that it is a property which has been originally brought in by the partners when the partnership is formed and also the property which is acquired in the course of business of the firm: There is no gainsaying the fact that as the property belongs exclusively to the firm, no partner can claim any part of the property as his own and what a partner is entitled to is his share of profits only, so long the partnership continues. Upon dissolution of the partnership, his share is his proportion of money representing the firm's asset including immovable property after liquidation of the partnership debts and liabilities. The Partnership Act has been mainly based on English Partnership Act of 1890 and section 22 of that Act referred to 'partnership property' in the following words: ,</u>

<u>"Where land or any heritable interest therein has' become partnership property, it shall, unless the contrary intention appears be treated as between the partners (including the representatives of a deceased partner), and also as between the heirs of a deceased partner and his executors or administrators, as personal or moveable and not real or heritable estate."</u>

18. Commenting thereon Lindley in his partnership stated as follows: "From the principle that a share of a partner is nothing more than his proportion of the partnership assets after they have been turned into money and applied in liquidation of the partnership debts, it necessarily follows that, in equity, a share in a partnership, whether its property consists of land or not, must, as between the real and personal representatives of a deceased partner, be deemed to be personal and not real estate:'

<u>19. On dissolution of firm each of the partners is entitled to receive his share of assets of the firm to which he was entitled. Section 32 of the Partnership Act provides for retirement of a partner from the partnership but it makes no provision of separation of share of the retired partner but this matter has been left to be determined by agreement between the partners. In the case of Ajudhia Pershad Ram Pershad vs Sham Sunder, AIR 1947 Lahore 13 Cornelius J elaborately discussed this provision of the law and held as under:</u>

<u>"There would thus appear to be no doubt that the share of a partner in an existing partnership is essentially movable property, notwithstanding that a part of the partnership property may be immovable."</u>

20. In the case of Addanki Narayanappa vs Bhaskara Krishnappa, AIR 1966 SC 1300, members of two joint Hindu Families Addanki family and Bhasakara family-entered into a partnership business of rice-hulling. Subsequently, Addanki family retired by an agreement and relinquished their share in the partnership assets including immovable properties in favour of the Bhaskara family and the terms of the settlement were recorded in a document styled "Karat". It was not a registered document. Subsequently the Addanki family filed a suit against the Bhashkara family for dissolution of the partnership and for accounts contending that the partnership assets included immovable properties and the Karar which recorded the relinquishment of their interest in those was compulsorily registerable under section 17(1)(3) of the Registration Act, but as it was not registered the document was inadmissible in evidence to prove to dissolution of the partnership and settlement of accounts. This contention was rejected; the suit was dismissed and it was held that "the interest of the partners of Addanki family in the partnership assets was movable property and the document evidencing the relinquishment of that interest was not compulsorily register able under section 17(1) of the Registration Act."

21. In this case reliance may be placed on the case of Lui Ying Ping vs. Leon Fang AI (1984) 36 DLR (AD) 273. In the aforesaid case, leave was granted to consider the question namely upon the dissolution of the partnership whether the immovable property can be considered as the property of the individual partner and whether such property can be partitioned and further whether a separate registered deed was necessary to convey the share of the parties in the immovable property notwithstanding the agreement of settlement.

The Appellate Division held as under:

In the instant case, the respondent by the agreement Ext. 2(a), with her partner retired from the partnership and relinquished all her interests including her share in the land and building at Motijheel on consideration of cash payment of Taka 20,000. This document was not required to be registered under the Registration Act. Consequently, her interest .in the land and building stood transferred to the appellant who thereupon converted all his assets into a proprietorship and mutated his name accordingly in all relevant public documents."

22. In the case of N Khandervali Saheb (dead) by LRS vs N Gudu Sahib (dead) (2003) 3 see 229, the question arose whether an award by which residue assets of a partnership firm are distributed amongst the partners on dissolution of the partnership firm requires registration under section 17 of the Registration Act,1908. On dissolution 'of the partnership firm, accounts are settled amongst the partners and the assets of the partner- ship are distributed amongst the partners as per their respective shares in the partnership: firm. Thus, on dissolution of a partnership firm, the allotment of assets to individual partners is not a case of transfer of any assets of the firm The assets which hereinbefore belonged to each partner will after dissolution of the firm stand allotted to the partners individually. There is no transfer or assignment of ownership in any of the assets. This is the legal consequence of distribution of assets on dissolution of partnership firm. The distribution of assets may be done either by way of an arbitration award or by mutual settlement between the partners themselves. The document which records the settlement in this case is an award which does not require registration under section 17 of the Registration Act since the document does not transfer or assign interest in any asset.

23. In the case of SV Chandra Pandian vs SV Sivalinga Nadar (1993) 1 SCC 589, it has been held as under:

"This Court noticed that the award read as a whole made it clear that the arbitrators had confined themselves to the property belonging to the partnership firm and had scrupulously avoided other properties. While distributing the residue assets, the arbitrators allocated the properties to the partners. Section 48 of the Partnership Act was applied and the properties were allocated to the partners as per their share on the distribution of the residue. The award sought to distribute the assets of the partnership firm after settlement of accounts on dissolution. This Court took the view that the property falling to the share of the partner on distribution of the residue would naturally belong to him exclusively but since in the eye of law it is money and not immovable property there is no question of registration under section 17 of the Registration Act."

It was further observed (at SCC page 607, para 18) even if one looks at he award as allocating certain immovable property since there is no transfer, no partition or extinguishment of any right therein, there is no question of application of section 17(1) of the Registration Act. '"

24. 'In the case of Commissioner of Income 'Tax, West Bengal, Calcutta vs Juggilal Kamala pat AIR 1967 (SC), 401, the question arose whether non-registration' of the' relinquishment deed invalidates the transfer of the business assets to the new partnership.

The Supreme Court of India in the above case held as under:

The Deed of Relinquishment, in this case, was in respect of the individual interest " of the three Singhania Brothers in the assets of the partnership firm in favour of the Kamla Town Trust, and consequently, did not require  registration, even though the assets of the partnership firm included immovable property, and was valid without registration. As a result of this deed, all the assets of the partnership vested in the new partners of the firm."

<u>25; Having considered the, cases cited above, We find that a deed of dissolution of partnership is not required to be registered under section 17 of the Registration Act because the share of a partner in a partnership is essentially moveable property notwithstanding that a part of the partnership property may be immovable.</u>

26. In addition to the above, the provisions of rule 49 of XXI of the Code of Civil Procedure are closely modeled on section 23 of the English Partnership Act, 1890. Sub-rules (1), (2) and (3) of rule 49 of Order XXI of the Code of Civil Procedure correspond to section, 23 (1), (2) and (3) of the English Partnership Act, 1890. An interest of a partner in partnership business is intended to be treated as moveable property under this rule. The reason is that the share of a partner is nothing more than his proportion of the partnership assets after they have been turned into money and applied in liquidation of the partnership debts, notwithstanding that when it is charged or sold, the assets include immovable property.

27. Therefore, the deed of dissolution (Annexure-D) was not required to be registered under the, 'Registration Act. Consequently the interest in two big has of land was transferred to the appellants by the deed, of dissolution and mutation was rightly accorded in respect of two big has of land as per clause-4 of the deed of dissolution of partnership.

28. For the sake of argument, event if Annexure-D. the deed of dissolution of partner ship is construed as an agreement, the heirs of late Noor Hossain are under obligation 'to execute and register a deed of transfer in favour of the appellants as per terms of Annexure- 'D'. But with a view to frustrating implementation, of Annexure- D the heirs of late Noor Hossain filed the writ petition before the High Court Division. Such an attitude of the heirs of late Noor Hossain is a bizarre hoax and, as such, the writ petition itself was not maintainable.'

29. The High Court Division erroneously came to a finding that a partnership, firm has an

independent legal entity.

30. Under the Partnership Act, a partnership has riot been given any 'legal status. It is not a juristic person and the independent status given to the partnership firm under the Act has to be 'limited only for the purposes of that Act, Such a legal position becomes cleat from the land marked judgment of the Supreme court of India in CIT vs  RM Chidambaram pillai (1977) 106. In this case, the Supreme Court of India exclusively dealt with the concept of a partnership firm and quoted, with approval a paragraph,from Lindlay on partnership as under:

"The firm is not recognized by English Lawyers as distinct from the members composing it. In taking partnership accounts and in administering partnership assets, courts have to some extent adopted the mercantile view, and actions may now, speaking generally, be brought by or against partners in the name of their firm; but, speaking generally, the firm as such has no ldeal recognition.The law, ignoring the firm, looks to the partners composing it; any change amongst them destroys the identity of the firm;, what is called the property of the firm it their property, and what are called the debts and their liabilities of the firm are 'their debts and liabilities. In point of law, a partner may be the debtor or the creditor of his co-partners, but he cannot be either debtor or creditor of the firm of which he is himself a member, nor can he, be employed by his firm, for a man cannot be his own employer."

<u>31. English as well as Indian jurisdiction has, for some specific purposes, relaxed its rigid notions and extended a 'limited personality to a firm. Nevertheless the general concept a partnership, firmly established in both system of law, still is that a firm is not an entity or 'person' in law but is merely an association of individuals and a firm name is only a collective name of those individuals who constitute the firm. In other, words, a firm name is merely an expression, only a compendious mode of designing the persons who have agreed to carry on business, in partnership.</u>

<u>In the light of the findings, we 'find 'substance in this appeal. Accordingly, this appeal is allowed without any order as to costs and the impugned judgment delivered by the High Court Division is set aside.</u>

End.

caseno: Appeal from Appellate Decree No. 105 of 1987.
lawyer:
MI Farooque with Saleemullah ----- For the Appellant.
Zia-Ur-Rahman Khan ----- For the Respondent.

Motiul Hoque ----- Appellant
