case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 21.8.2011 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 4608 of 2009 and Writ Petition No. 6766 of 2011).
full_judgment:
AHM Shamsuddin Choudhury, J: These two Civil Petitions for Leave to Appeal have been preferred by one Md. Ayub Hossain Khan, acting in a fiduciary capacity for a trust, named Imam Gazzali Trust, impugning a judgment and order a Division Bench of the High Court Division passed in two writ petitions, registered as Writ Petition Number 4608 of 2009 and 6677 of 2011 respectively. 2. Issues and subject matters in both the petitions being identical, the Division Bench concerned took up both the petitions together for adjudication and disposed both of them by a single judgment, dated 21st August, 2011. 3. The Rule engendered by the Writ Petition No. 4608 of 2009 has been discharged on merit while the Rule issued in respect to the Writ Petition No. 6766 of 2011 has been discharged as the same had become redundant. The petition that has been discharged on merit i.e. the Writ Petition No. 4608 of 2008 was filed by the instant leave to appeal petitioner, whereas the Writ Petition number 6766 of 20 11, discharged on ground of infructuity, was filed as a PIL by a non-governmental organisation, named Human Rights and Peace for Bangladesh. 4. Incidentally both the "leave to appeal" petitions have been filed by the petitioner of Writ Petition No. 4608 of2009. By Leave Petition No. 1901 of 20 11, he impugned the judgment and the order dated 21-8-2011, whereby the eviction order issued by the authorities had been affirmed while by Leave Petition No. 1902 of 2011 he challenged another aspect of the same judgment and order whereby the High Court Division directed the government to implement their decision to establish "Suchitra Sen Sangrahashala" immediately. 5. Not surprisingly, the PIL petitioners (the petitioners in Writ Petition No. 6766 of 2011) found no reason to apply for leave to appeal, apparently because their aspiration has been squarely met at the order the High Court Division passed on the government to set up Shuchitra Sangrahashala. 6. The Writ Petition No. 4608 of 2009 was structured on the following assertions; By an order dated 23rd March 1987, the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Pabna, demised the subject property in favour of the petitioner on an year to year lease, the commencing date being the 1st day of Poush, 1393 of the Bengali era. It was stipulated in the lease deed that an application, if any, is to be made for the renewal of the lease at the beginning of the year following the expiry of the lease, failing which the lease shall stand cancelled. Having procured registration from the education authority, the petitioner, as the Principal of an Institution named Imam Gazzali Institute, commenced imparting primary education to the Children of Pabna. 7. By a memo dated 6th August 1991, the Ministry of Land intimated the petitioner that as there existed no provision for permanent settlement of vested properties, the leasehold tenure on the schedule land, a vested property, would be renewed every year until such time the government takes a final decision on the settlement of vested properties. 8. Since no decision has been taken on the settlement of vested properties, the petitioner is entitled to have the tenure renewed, as per the promise, yet, instead, the respondents have served the impugned notice dated 22nd June, 2009 asking the petitioner to surrender possession of the subject property and had, thereby, acted without lawful authority. 9. The respondent No. 4 in the aforementioned Writ Petition, in his endeavour to rebut the petitioner's assertion and claim, had it to state that the property in question with a single story building on it originally belonged to Korunamoiya Das Gupta, who sailed to India for good before 1960 and hence the government requisitioned his property in 1960 and subsequently designated the same as a vested property after the vested property scheme came into being. On 23rd March 1987, the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) Pabna, demised the property on a temporary yearly lease to the petitioner conditionally for the year 1383 of the Bengali Calendar. Thereafter, the petitioner's afore named institute obtained some 1.29 acres of land in a nearby location from the Public Works Department (PWD) on permanent settlement with a nominal consideration, and erected thereon a four storied building. 10. The opposing respondent went on expressing that the Legendary Diva of the Bengali film industry, who occupies a cozy, irreversible place in the minds of the Bengali speaking people, was indeed the only daughter of Korunamoiya Das Gupta, the original owner of the dwelling and that the government in consonance with the popular demand and with a view to attract tourist who would visit the coveted venue to pay respect to the memory of their Sublime Idol, want to establish Shuchitra Sen Memorial Complex at her natal home. 11. The petitioner failed to pay rent from 1398 BS to 1401 BS. 12. Averments figured in Writ Petition No. 6766 of 2011, which has been filed as a public interest litigation, are, in succinct form, as follows; 13. A report published in a national daily, named "Sokaler Khobor" on 13th July 2011, on the paternal abode of Shuchitra Sen came to their notice. The report divulges that the said threshold was being grabbed by some local people with the support of the law enforcers and the government has taken no initiative to recover the Mega Star's toddling house. The report, quoting the local inhabitants, reveals that Shuchitra Sen along with her family left for Kolkata. Their house has been listed as a vested property. In 1987 this house and its adjacent land was taken on lease by a political party, which set up an education centre by flexing muscle. Jamate Islam is maintaining an education centre in the house although the district administration asked them to vacate the premises. Journalists and artists have asked the authorities to recover it and establish a cultural centre therein to immortalise Shuchitra Sen's memory. Although a huge chunk of land has been bought by the aforesaid education centre from the government for Taka 3 (Taka three) only and a three storied building has already been erected thereon for Imam Gazzali Institute, they have not yet parted with the possession of Suchitra Sen's house. 14. The respondent No.7 in the Writ Petition No. 6766 of 2011, who is indeed the leave to appeal petitioner before us, and was the petitioner in Writ Petition No. 4608 of 2009, filed an affidavit to oppose the averments scripted in Writ Petition No. 6766 of 2011, stating, inter alia that after demising the property on a year to year lease in his favour, the district administration, Pabna, has consistently renewed the tenure on the lessee's application who has been paying rents in advance. The swearing respondent invested substantial sums of money for repairing and refurbishing the roof of the building pursuant to approval granted by the Ministry of Land to permit such repair work, of which the authorities were aware. The swearing respondent applied for renewal of the lease for 1416-1417 BS and sought to deposit advance rent therefor, but the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) Pabna, refused to accept the rent and then asked him to quit stating that a museum is to be floated on the land. He claimed to have a legitimate expectation to have the tenure renewed, because of unambiguous practice of the authorities for the last 22 years. He also invoked the doctrine audi alteram partem asserting that no notice was served upon him before the notice to quit was issued. The property was never listed as a national heritage by the Ministry of Culture and there is no record with the said Ministry or the Ministry of Land to prove that the property is that of Shuchitra Sen's patriarch and that inquiry with the office of the Assistant Commissioner (Land) Pabna, revealed otherwise. It cannot be a public interest litigation as no public interest is involved. 15. As we took up the leave to appeal application for consideration, Mr AJ Mohammad Ali, the learned Senior Advocate for the petitioner, proffered before us that the High Court Division misdirected themselves by failing to recognise that (1) failure to adhere to the principles of natural justice steered the authorities move to a nullity (2) the doctrine of estoppel stood as an invincible a hurdle against the authorities' decision to evict the petitioner (3) the petitioner is also fortified with legitimate expectation. 16. In his attempt to ward off Mr Mohammad Ali's contention, Mr Mahbubey Alam, the learned Attorney General articulated that the High Court Division had come up with an exquisite judgment which cannot be dislodged. In his view none of the principles advanced by Mr Ali can be engaged in the backdrop of factual as well as legal elements that orbit round the case in hand. He expressed that nothing could, in the instant case, impair the government's decision against renewing the lease concerned, particularly when they have resolved to proceed with a noble scheme of preserving the legacy of the Prima Donna of the Bengali filmdom, Shuchitra Sen, which is destined to survive in history till eternity. 17. Salient features of the High Court Division Judgment, as much as they are pertinent for the disposal of this petition, are figured below: 18. Since both the parties admit that the subject property is a vested and non-resident one, submission as to the compliance with the provisions as outlined in the Government and Local Authority Land and Buildings (Recovery and Possession) Ordinance 1970 is otiose. 19. The petitioner of the Writ Petition No. 4608 of 2009 expressed nothing regarding the ownership of the subject property when he filed that petition and a lessee is not, in any event, legally entitled to raise any dispute on the title of the leasehold property. 20. Since the authority concerned did not renew the lease, the petitioner of the Writ Petition No. 4608 of 2009 is not entitled to hold the premises and must vacate the same. The petitioner, a habitual defaulter, acquired no vested right in the property. 21. As steps for setting up "Shuchitra Sen Smrity Sangahashala" has already been taken by the authority there is no need to interfere with Writ Petition No. 6766 of 20 11. 22. The High Court Division projected with vivid details the evolution of the vested property legislations which commenced its maiden voyage with the passage of East Pakistan Enemy Property (Land and Buildings) Administration and Disposal Order 1966 and then reproduced some parts of the decision in the case of Dulich and Omraolal vs Bangladesh, reported in 33 DLR (AD) 30, in which their Lordships of the Appellate Division depicted the transformation of the Enemy Property Legislations after the Liberation of Bangladesh through the Enemy Property (Continuance of Emergency Provisions) (Repeal) Ordinance 197 4 (the Ordinance IV of 1974) which repealed Ordinance 1 of 1969, the Vested and Non-Resident Property (Administration) Ordinance 1974, (Ordinance V of 1974), Enemy Property (Continuance of Emergency Provision) (Repeal) Act, 1974, (Act XLV of 1974), the Vested and Non-Resident Property (Administration) Act 1974, (Act XLVI of 1974), the Vested and Non-Resident Property (Administration) (Repeal) Ordinance 1976, (Ordinance XLII of 1976), which repealed Act XLVI of 1974, followed by the Enemy Property (Continuance of Emergency Provision) (Repeal) (Administration) Ordinance 1976, (Ordinance XLIII of 1976) which amended section 3 of Act XLV of 1974 by providing that properties which had vested in the government the right of administration, control, management and disposal of by transfer or other- wise be conferred on the government or such officer or authority as the government may direct, to depict a comprehensive and consolidated picture on the custody, administration, control and demising of properties that vested in the government. The High Court Division also cited Appellate Division's Decision in Mofazzal Hossain vs Bangladesh, 43 DLR (AD) 137, which referred to a circular dated 23rd May, 1977, that emanated from the Ministry of Land Administration, containing instruction for the administration management and disposal of vested properties, and reproduced the text in clauses 4(1),5,6 and 7 of the circular. 23. By embarking on a hair-split analyses on the said legislations, decisions and the circular, the High Court Division held that as both the parties admit that the subject property is a vested one, its status gives rise to no dilemma and then cited two aforementioned decisions to re-instate that (I) the right of administration, control, management and disposal by transfer or otherwise, which stand vested in the government, pursuant to Ordinance XLIII of 1976 remains conferred on the government or such office or authority as the government may direct (II) as per the circular dated 23rd May 1977, issued by the Ministry of Land Administration, which though is not a piece of legislation, yet binding, the Additional Deputy Commissioner may, with the previous approval of the government, transfer or otherwise dispose of any vested property, in whose jurisdiction it is situate, provided that no such approval shall be necessary for granting lease or letting any such property for a period not exceeding one year at a time (III) no lessee or tenant of a vested property shall acquire any right of occupancy and shall not be entitled to hold on after the expiry of the lease period (IV) the lessee or the tenant, as the case may be, shall be liable to be evicted on the expiry of the lease period (V) Clause 7 of the circular, which speaks of 7 days notice before eviction move, read together with clauses 5 and 6 thereof, reveals that it is applicable for those in unlawful possession, not for lessees who turned unauthorised occupant after the expiry of the tenure of the lease (VI) the word "shall" has been inserted in both clauses 5 and 6 meaningfully to indicate that it is the duty of the lessee to vacate the property at the end of the stipulated tenure, it is his obligation and, even if it is accepted that the phrase "unlawful possession" as used in clause 7 of the circular, is referable to former tenants, such a former lessee is not entitled to hold on the property (VII) as per section 14 of the অর্পিত সম্পত্তি প্রত্যার্পন আইন ২০০১, until returned, vested properties shall remain under control of the Deputy Commissioners who shall demise the same on lease in accordance with the prevailing laws of the land, (VIII) in the backdrop of the circumstances taken up for scanning, it is to be held that the petitioner's possession in the subject property cannot be protected in any manner and he is not entitled to continue with the possession of the property, (IX) the petitioner was allowed 15 days time to quit: so it is not a case of compelling the petitioner to vacate the premises without notice, notice meaning making something known to a person who was, or might have been, unaware of that scenario. 24. The High Court Division then directed the government to implement the decision to establish "Shuchitra Sen Smrity Sangrahashala" immediately. 25. We must accentuate that the level of ingenuity the High Court Division exhibited in dissecting, scanning and analysing the applicable legislations and decisions, are simply impeccable and beyond reproach. We trace no misdirection or error whatsoever either in the mode they applied to arrive at their conclusion or in the conclusion itself. 26. In discarding the submission audi alteram partem, the High Court Division has commendably taken the pain of exploring several Indian and English decisions to lend support to the enunciation that rules of natural justice are not always rules of thumb; they are flexible and their applications depend on the setting and the back ground of the postulated statutory provisions, nature of the right and the consequences which may entail its application, and reminisced Lord Denning's observation that if a man sees as a privilege to which he has no particular claim, he can be turned away without a word. 27. Right to be heard is, beyond qualm, an indispensable safety valve to protect rights of the postulants: it is an integral part of the principle of fairness. 28. By developing the principles of natural justice the courts have devised a kind of code of fair administrative procedure. 29. Natural Justice plays much the same part in British Law as does "due process of law" in the U.S. Constitution. However wide the powers of the state and however extensive the discretion they confer, it is always possible to require them to be exercised procedurally fairly. 30. Sir William Wade and Sir Christopher Forsyth expressed in their book "Administrative Law, (9th edition page 439);"As governmental powers continually grew more drastic, it is only by procedural fairness that they are rendered tolerable". 31. Eternity and Divinity of the principle was projected by the Court of Kings Bench in the classic Bentleys case, (R vs University of Cambridge 1723 1st 557) by stating that the petitioner should have received a notice "as required by the laws of God and man". 32. Byles J, whose observation is frequently quoted, expressed in Cooper vs Wards worth Board of Works (1863 14 CB NS 180), "Long course of decisions beginning with Dr. Bentleys case, and ending with some recent cases, establish that, although there are no positive words in statute, requiring that the party shall be heard, yet the justice of Common Law will supply the omission of the legislature". 33. Lord Russel emphatically stated, "It is to be implied, unless the contrary appears, that Parliament does not authorise by the Act the exercise of power in breach of the principles of natural justice ..... (Fairmount Investments Ltd. vs SOS for the Environment (1976 1 WLR 1255) 34. Seetley, J. stated that Procedural justice has by now secured an invincible bridgehead in the territory of administration. 35. In O'Reilly vs Mackman (J 983 2 AC 237), Lord Diplock said that the right of a man to be given a fair opportunity of hearing what is alleged against him is so fundamental to any civilised legal system that it is to be presumed that Parliament intended that a failure to observe it should render null and void any decision reached in breach of this requirement. 36. Jackson J of the United States Supreme Court stated, "Procedural fairness and regularity are of the indispensable essence of liberty. Severe substantive laws can be endured if they are fairly and impartially applied." (Shareghnessa vs US 345 US 2061953). 37. According to Frankfurter J, " The history of Liberty has largely been the history of the observance of procedural safeguards" (M Nabb vs United States, 318 US 332 1943). 38. All these said however, bridles that obscurate the application of this precious tenet, when fairness permits departure, must not be over looked. 39. In reply to the self generated question, "How far is it right for the courts of law to try to impart their own standards of justice to the administration?" 40. Prof. Sir Wade and Sir Forsyth (Supra) observed, "Since the decisions to which the rules apply are very various, they have to be flexible and their precise content depends on the circumstances". (Page 442) 41. Lord Denning expressed, ."The rules of natural justice or fairness are not cut and dried. They vary infinitely (R vs Home Secretary exparte Santillo 1981 QB 778). He also said, " it is not possible to lay down rigid rules as to when the principle of natural justice are to apply: nor as to their scope and extent. Everything depends. on the subject matter" (R vs Gaming Board for Great Britain ex P Benaim and Khaida 1970 20B 417). It has been emphasised in George vs SOS for Environment (1979 77 LGR) that there must have been some real prejudice to the complainant: there is no such thing as a merely technical infringement of natural justice. 42. It has been held in Commission of Business Franchises vs Borenstein (1984 VR 375). that it is always possible for hearing to be excluded by the scheme of the legislation. 43. It is Lord Bridge's following observation on flexibility of the application of the doctrine that has attracted widest attention: "My Lords the rules of natural justice are not engraved on tablets of stone. To use the phrase which better expresses the under lying concept, what the requirement of fairness demand when any body, domestic, administrative, or judicial, has to make a decision which will affect the rights of individuals, depends on the character of the decision making body, the kind of decision it has to make and the statutory or other framework in which it operates." ( Lloyd vs Me Maheri 1987 AC 625). 44. Lord Denning MR, who, according to Lord Devlin, nurtured the conception that justice is above the Law (Lord Devlin's Foreword for the book "Lord Denning: The Judge and the Law Edited by JL Jowell & JPWB Me Anslan) figured the most robust expression against the abusive and illusory application of the doctrine, in following terms in Reg vs Home Secretary, Ex-P Mughal (1974 QB 313): "The rules of natural justice must not be stretched too far. Only too often the people who have done wrong seek to invoke the rules of natural justice so as to avoid the consequences". 45. Lord Denning's above quoted observation is squarely applicable in the instant case as the petitioner invoked audi alteram partem after he indulged upon wrong doing by failing to vacate the premises after he was asked to do so following the admitted cessation of the year to year lease period, to avoid the consequences. 46. Even in the epochal English decision in in Commission of the case of Ridge vs Baldwin (1964 AC 40) which has literally resuscitated the doctrine from dormancy, the House of Lords made flexibility principle quite explicit by stating, "It is common sense that normally the principle audi alteram partem should apply, but in each case the obligation depends on the words of the particular statute". 47. To draw the line between the kind of cases where right to be heard are imperative and the cases where such rights are not available, Lord Reid in the aforementioned case expressed; "Sometimes the functions of a Minister or department may also be of that character, and then the rules of natural justice can apply in much the same way. But more often their functions are of a very different character. If a Minister is considering whether to make a scheme for, say, an important new road, his primary concern will not be with the damage which its construction will do to the rights of individual owners of land. He will have to consider all manner of questions of public interest and, it may be, a number of alternative schemes. He cannot be prevented from attaching more importance to the fulfillment of his policy than to the fate of individual objectors, and it would be quite wrong for the courts to say that the Minister should or could act in the same kind of way as a board of works deciding whether a house should be pulled down." 48. Lord Evershed in the same case stated, "It has been said many times that the exact requirements in any case of the so-called principles of natural justice cannot be precisely defined; that they depend in each case upon the circumstances of that case. According to Sir Frederick Pollock, the meaning of the phrase "natural justice" is the ultimate principle of fitness with regard to the nature of man as a rational and social being; and he went on to point out that the origin of the principle could be traced to Aristotle and Roman Jurists. (Jurisprudence and Legal Essays 1961, Page 124). Your Lordships were, therefore, not unnaturally referred to a great many cases, but, as I believe that your Lordships agree, it is by no means easy to treat these decisions as entirely uniform and still less easy to be able to extract from them the means of propounding a precise statement of the circumstances or of the cases in which the principles can be invoked before the courts". 49. Lord Devlin on the question of applicability of natural justice, stated in the same case; "whether or not they are to be applied to any statutory procedure depends upon an implication to be drawn from the statute, itself ". 50. The House of Lord's Judgment in this Star Ship case (i.e. Ridge vs Baldwin, Supra), transmit undistorted message to the effect that, audi alteram partem shall apply when a decision taker relies on a given ground, which is prima facie contentious in the sense that it is open to the affected person to put forward his version on the alleged fact in question. In other word, right to be heard cannot be claimed where visibly and on the face of it no contentious ground exists. As Lord Evershed stated in Ridge vs Baldwin, Supra; "My Lords, if the only question which was here involved was whether the appellant should have ceased in March, 1958, to be chief Constable and whether, therefore, the watch committee was entitled without more to decide, I would for my part, say that there was, in the circumstances, no call for the watch committee to observe the so called rule, audi alteram partem". 51. What are amply clear from the amalgam of all the decisions scanned above are that the plea of mere technical infringement of natural Justice must be dis-budded, that to be permitted to hoist a plea, there has to be a prima facie contentious issue capable of fortifying the person aggrieved with some apparently recognisable argument in his favour, that there cannot be any inflexible rule as to its application; as the same would vary from case to case, that it cannot be allowed to be used as a vexatious device to waste Courts' time in visibly open and shut, barren cases. 52. In the case in hand, admittedly the subject premises was demised on a year to year lease and the tenure had come to an end and, admittedly again, the circular concerned, upon which even the learned Senior Advocate for the petitioner in Writ Petition No. 4608 of 2009 relied, unambiguously required the lessees to give up possession on the extinction of the lease period without further ado. It is, hence, a thoroughly fallacious and spurious exercise to claim audi alteram partem in this case. 53. When it is not disputed, and unbroken chain of authorities proclaim that a year to year lessee acquires no vested right, (Mallikpur Fishermen Co-operative Society Ltd. vs The Secretary, Ministry of Land (15 BLD AD 241), purported claim to audi alteram partem is like arguing that before a civil servant proceeds to retire having attained super annuation, he is entitled to be given an opportunity to be heard. The government demises on lease on different terms many Jal Mahals, Hats, Bazars etc. Can it be argued that these lessees cannot be evicted without a hearing when their tenure end? Such a contention would not only be bizarre, but shall also put things topsy turvy. 54. It is true that this Division in the decisive case of Sharping Matsajibi Samabay Samity vs Bangladesh, (39 DLR AD 85) illustrated the necessity of show cause notice. But that was under a diametrically divergent factual scenario. Unlike the instant one, that was a case of cancellation of lease in the midway, involving no question of fresh renewal at the expiry of the original term, and most importantly, the ground that was assigned, as under the term of the lease in that case such a ground was indispensable to cancel a lease, was fiercely contentious ones even to the extent that two different relevant government functionaries supplied two mutually destructive report on the prime question as to whether the writ petitioner had undertaken required development work in the Jalmahal. Obviously this conspicuously disputed question, on which the authorities' power to cancel the lease entirely depended, could not be resolved without hearing the party that claims it undertook development work. 55. Verbatim observation of BH Chowdhury J, reproduced below, will make the difference quite discerable. "The learned Attorney-General could not specifically inform the court whether there had been an inquiry previous to the filing of the bad conduct certificate issued by the ADC on 7-4-1985. It is clear there is nothing on the record to substantiate that there had been any inquiry before filing such adverse report nor any show cause notice was ever issued as contended by Mr Ishtiaq Ahmed. In this position there is no hesitation in saying that it is another case of non-application of mind which operated adversely in so far as the appellant is concerned". 56. Shahabuddin J's observation, which runs as follows, is also pertinent; "As to the execution of the development work the lease deed shows that the lessee was to execute development work once in every 3 years according to the direction of officers of the Fishery Directorate. The lessee appellant contended that he did execute the development work as per approved plan and produced a certificate to this effect from the District Fishery Officer. But the Additional Deputy commissioner obtained a report from the Thana Revenue Officer showing that no development work was done. The Government, while cancelling the lease on the Additional Deputy Commissioners report,did not refer to the certificate of the Fishery Officer. It clearly shows malafide intention on the part of the Additional Deputy Commissioner and non-application of mind and arbitrary action on the part of the government in cancelling the lease without giving the appellant any opportunity whatsoever to show cause against the proposed action." 57. It goes without saying that when a decision is based on an allegation, more so when that allegation is a fervently contentious one, the principle of natural justice warrants that the claimant cannot be condemned unheard. 58. So, in no way can the instant case be equated with that of SMS Samity vs Bangladesh, Supra. Here there is no question of cancellation of a lease on reliance upon a stipulated ground before expiry of the term, and the authorities have assigned no reason, as they are not required to, in exercising their unfettered discretion against renewal of the lease after its tenure came to an end. It also does not invite the question as to whether the authorities acted in breach of the lease covenant. 59. Mr AJ Mohammad Ali also attempted to engage the doctrine of promissory estoppel and relied on a memo dated 6th August, 1991 his client received from a Senior Assistant Secretary at the Ministry of Land, text of which is reproduced below for ease of exploration. ANNEXURE-E. গণপ্রজাতন্ত্র বাংলাদেশ সরকার ভূমি মন্ত্রনালয় শাখা-৬। স্মারক নং ভূঃমঃ/শা-৬/স্থায়ী বন্দোবস্ত/১০৪/৯১-২৩৩ তারিখঃ ৬-৮-৯১ইং ২২-৪-৯৮ বাং প্রেরক ঃ চেয়ারম্যান ইমাম গাজ্জালী ইনষ্টিটিউট পাবনা। বিষয়ঃ ভি,পি কেস নং-৩ (পাব)/৮৬-৮৭ ভূক্ত অর্পিত ও অনাগরিক সম্পত্তি পাবনা ইমাম গাজ্জালী ইনষ্টিটিউটের জন্য স্থায়ী ইজারা বন্দোবস্ত প্রসংগে। সূত্রঃ তাহার স্মারক নং ১৭১৩-ভি,পি তাং ১৬-৭-৯১ইং/৩১-৩-৯৮ বাং। উপরোক্ত বিষয় ও পত্র সূত্রে নির্দেশক্রমে জানানো যাইতেছে যে, বর্তমানে অর্পিত সম্পত্তি স্থায়ী বন্দোবস্ত বিধান নাই ফলে যতদিন পর্যন্ত অর্পিত সম্পত্তি সম্পর্কে চুড়ান্ত সিদ্ধান্ত গৃহিত না হয় ততদিন পর্যন্ত উল্লেখিত অর্পিত সম্পত্তি প্রতিষ্ঠানটির অনুকুলে একসানা বন্দোবস্ত থাকিবে। স্বঃ (সৈয়দ আখতার হোসেন) সিনিয়র সহকারী সচিব স্মারক নং ভূঃমঃ/শা-৬/স্থায়ী বন্দোবস্ত/১০৪/৯১-২৩৩ তারিখঃ ৬-৮-৯১ইং ২২-৪-৯৮ বাং অনুলিপি অবগতির জন্যঃ (সৈয়দ আখতার হোসেন) ১। জেলা প্রশাসক, পাবনা। সিনিয়র সহকারী সচিব স্বঃ অপাঠ্য 60. Before construing the legal position on this dogma, it is necessary first to scrutinise the factuality of the claimed promise, the petitioner is bent upon, to see if it can be compartmentalized as an estoppel generating promise at all in concord with the High Trees principle and the subsequent development that followed. By the message transmitted through the docket dated 6-8-1991 the Assistant Secretary concerned stated that as there existed no provision for permanent settlement of vested properties, the yearly lease would be extended untill such time a final decision is arrived at on vested properties. So, since a final decision has in fact been taken in respect to the subject vested property, it is factually not open to the petitioner to say that the promisors have resiled from their promise. The so-called promise was not ad-infinitum, but was an event bound one, which event, i.e. a permanent decision had in fact been taken on the vested property concerned. 61. Most importantly, the given facts cannot in any event constitute promissory estoppel because under the High Trees principle, which is the progenitor of this doctrine, which had survived the passage of time, to constitute a claim for promissory estoppel, factum of detriment by the promisee must be established, detriment being unamputable spark to ignite promissory estoppel. In the instant case, the petitioner was quite conspicuously and, without any equivocation, intimated vide a letter dated 25-5-92 that it was for him to decide whether to spend any money in the premises, but that such spending will not create any right or claim in his favour. So, when the petitioner was explicitly warned that no expenditure would arm him with any right or claim, it is not open to him to claim that he suffered detriment by reciprocating the promise. 62. The petitioner's submission on the invocation of the doctrine of promissory estoppel begets a bit of comprehensive legal analyses. 63. Promissory estoppel, also known as equitable estoppel as it was innovated to grant relief outside the inflexible rules of Common Law, though it is neither in the realm of contract nor in the realm of equity, (India vs Godfrey Philips AIR 1986 SC 806). was first brought into being by none other than that great English innovating Judge, Denning J. (as he was at the relevant time i.e. in 1947). In the pivotal case concerned ( i.e. Central London Properties Trust Ltd. vs High Trees House Ltd. 1947 KB 130: the adventurous decision that hiked Denning-J on the platform of prominence- (Lord Devlin felt that by this bold decision Denning J, a very recent puisne, preferred to cut a channel from the mainstream. Lord Devlin's foreward, supra) the plaintiff, who sued the defendants for full rents for the last quarter of the year 1945 and for future, leased a block of flats to the defendants. In view of the War time lull in the rental market, the plaintiff in January 1940, agreed in black and white to reduce the rent, without specifying the time span for such concessionary rate. The defendants paid at the reduced rent during 1940-45 period but as the tenants' scarcity waned with the cessation of hostility in 1945, the plaintiff demanded rent at the originally fixed sum, retrospectively as well as for the future and then initiated the said civil action for originally fixed rent for the last two quarters of 1945, as the defendant declined to give in to that demand. 64. As the agreement for reduced rent fell short of a contract because of the absence of consideration, the defendant could not foster the plea of breach of contract, but instead, he raised a surrogated defence with the claim that the plaintiff could not resile from its promise on the basis of which the defendant spent some money to repair the flat to its detriment. 65. Denning J expressed that the agreement of January, 1940 was intended as a temporary expedient only and has ceased to operate early in 1945 and hence rent originally fixed by the contract was payable as from 1945 and the plaintiffs were entitled to judgment for the period from 1945 onward, stating however that, had the plain- tiffs sued for arrears for 1940-45 period, the agreement made in 1940 would have operated to defeat their claim. 66. Denning J. agreed that there was no consideration for the plaintiff's promise to reduce the rent. If, therefore, the defendants had themselves sued upon that promise, they must have failed. They could not claim on contract as one of the essential elements, i.e. consideration, was missing. But, Denning J. raised a question as to why, when such a promise is used merely as a defence, presence or absence of consideration be relevant? He expressed that the defendants were not seeking to enforce a contract and need not prove one. In quest of a rule under the English Law, whereby the plaintiffs could be prevented from ignoring their promise, he felt at the first sight that the doctrine of general estoppel would supply the answer. But Denning J's supposition on the applicability of the doctrine of (Legal) estoppel faced a stumbling block from the 1854 House of Lord's decision in Jordan vs Money (1854 5 HL Case 158) in which the House of Lords held that estoppel would operate only on a representation of existing fact and hence it could be applicable in High Trees type situation where the defendant sought to rely on a promise of future intention. To overcome this quandary, Denning J sought to tap a slender stream of authority which had flowed in equity rather than in Common Law. He extended the equitable doctrine of forbearance, as propounded by the House of Lords in Hughes vs Metropolitan Railway (1877 2 App. Case 439), stating that the plaintiffs would have been precluded by the equitable doctrine of Hughes vs Metropolitan Railway, supra, from suing for the full rent for the period which was covered by the 1940 agreement adding; " The logical consequence no doubt is that a promise to accept a smaller sum, if acted upon, is binding notwithstanding the absence of consideration" and thus the fullest effect of "equitable" or "promissory" estoppel surfaced as a quasi-equitable remedy, about which Lord Pearson stated, " Promissory estoppel was far removed from familiar estoppel by representation of fact and seems to be more like waiver of contractual rights" (Wood house AC Israel Cocoa Ltd. vs Nigerian Produce Marketing Co. Ltd. 19-72 AC 741). 67. Gist of promissory estoppel is that (1) there is to be an unequivocal, clear promise meant to be relied on by the promisee (2) acted upon the promise by the promisee to his detriment, (3) it could only be used as a "shield" not as a sword (Combe vs Combe 1951 2 KB 215). (The Indian Supreme Court deprecated the 3rd element). 68. Although the doctrine was born as a private Law concept through a civil suit between two private parties, its effect soon pervaded to public law domain in the UK and India and then to our jurisdiction. In the past it was accepted that an estoppel could sometimes be raised against a public body in order to prevent it from resiling from an officials undertaking (Robertson vs Minister of Pensions 1949 1 KB 227, Wells vs Minister of Housing and Local Government 1967 1 WLR 1000, Lever Finance vs West minister LBC 1971 1 QB 222), though doubt was expressed by the House of Lords in Howell vs Falmouth Boat Construction (1951 AC 837) on its application in public law domain. 69. The Court of Appeal in Western Fish Products vs Penrith DC (1981 2 All ER 204), stated that estoppel can only be raised against a public body in some narrow circumstances, such as where the representor had ostensible authority and the decision was intra vires and the power could have been delegated to the representor. 70. However, following the House of Lords' decision in R. [Reprotech (Pebsham) Ltd. vs East Sussex CC (2003 1 WLR] estoppel by representation no longer applies in the UK in public law cases, as Lord Hoffman expressed obitar, that it was unhelpful to introduce private law concept of estoppel into planning law because estoppel is not suited to the public law context, because estoppel binds individuals on the ground that it would be unconscionable for them to deny what they have represented or agreed, but the doctrine of estoppel is a blunt tool in the Public Law context because public authorities also have to take into account the interest of the general public which the authority exists to promote. 71. In Lord Hoffman's view the solution lay in jettisoning estoppel from public law entirely in favour of the principle of legitimate expectation. He expressed, obitar. " It is true that in early cases such as the Wells case and Lever Finance Ltd. vs Westminister (City) London Borough Council (1971) 1 QB 222, (1970) 3 All ER 496 Lord Denning used the language of estoppel in relation to planning law. At that time the public law concepts of abuse of power and legitimate expectation were very undeveloped and no doubt the analogy of estoppel seemed useful. In the Western Fish the Court of Appeal tried to reconcile these invocations of estoppel with the general principle that a public authority cannot be estopped from exercising a statutory discretion or performing a public duty. But the results did not give universal satisfaction: see the comments of Dyson J. in the Powergen Case (2000) JPL 629, 638. It seems to me this area, public law has already absorbed whatever is useful from the moral values which underlie the private law concept of estoppel and the time has come for it to stand upon its own two feet." 72. The Indian Supreme Court in MP Sugar Mills Ltd. vs UP (AIR 1979 SC 621) held that the government was barred by the promise if it had been made by an agent having authority to make such promise and if such promise was not contrary to law even though it might relate to its sovereign function. In the later case of Jit Ram vs Hariyana (AIR 1980 SC 1285) however, the same court deviated from the MP Sugar Mills decision, only to revert back to the same through the 1986 case of India vs Godfrey Philips (AIR 1986 SC 806). This is to be mentioned that the Indian Supreme Court examined scores of English authorities beginning with the decision in the ice breaking High Tries case to arrive at the MP Sugar principle. Latest English Development that came into vogue through the House of Lords decision in R (Reprotech) (Pebsham) Ltd. Vs East Sussex CC, supra, was yet to be known. It is to be seen whether the Indian Apex Court in future follows this decision to say that promisory estoppel has no application in public law, as the doctrine of legitimate expectation has, of late, achieved sufficient progression and sophistication to render promissory estoppel redundant in public law domain. 73. Even if promissory estoppel is to be applicable in public law cases, restrictive factors fencing its bounds, must not be obliterated. The Indian Supreme Court in MP Sugar Mills, supa, also, observed that promissory estoppel is an equitable doctrine and it must yield when equity so demands, stating; "If it can be shown by the Government that having regard to the facts as they have subsequently transpired, it would be inequitable to hold the Government to the promise made by it the court would not raise an equity in favour of the promise against the Government.. ... ". 74. The Apex Court in India in Kasinka Trading vs Union of India (1995 (1) SCC 274) held that the government being satisfied about public interest in withdrawing something granted earlier, is bound by no unequivocal promise as representation extending by merely specifying the period of operation of the grant in the notification, so as to attract the doctrine of promissory estoppel, in the absence of manifest injustice, malafide or fraud, expressing further that when something is granted in exercise of a statutory power, it is implicit that the same can also be rescinded or modified at any time in exercise of the same power. The Court also observed, "The doctrine of promissory estoppel cannot be invoked in the abstract and the courts are bound to consider all aspects including the result sought to be achieved and the public good at large, because while considering the applicability of the doctrine, the courts have to do equity and the fundamental principles of equity must forever be present in the mind of the court while considering the applicability of the doctrine. The doctrine must yield when the equity so demands if it can be shown, having regards to the facts and circumstances of the case, that it would be inequitable to hold the government or the public authority to its promise, assurance or representation." 75. So far as our own jurisdiction is concerned although the Appellate Division in a couple of cases gave relief on the basis of promissory estoppel (Collector of Customs vs Abdul Hannan 42 DLR (AD) 167, Secretary, Industries vs Saleh Ahmed, 1981 BLD (AD) 91), on the basis of the facts peculiar thereto, nevertheless remained unequivocal to express in Khandker Delwar Hussain vs Bangladesh Italian Marble Works (62 DLR (AD) 298) that estoppel cannot be pleaded against or in respect of statute, much less against the Constitution. 76. In Chairman .RAJUK vs Abdur Rouf Chowdhury, 61 DLR (AD) 28, this Division enunciated the prevailing view that promissory estoppel cannot be invoked to enforce a promise contrary to law. 77. This Division in Chairman Bangladesh Textile Mills vs Nasir Ahmed Chowdhury (22 BLD (AD) 199 = 7 BLC (AD) 144) stated in the context of both promissory estoppel and legitimate expectation, that "In this conflict of doctrine the demands of fairness are proving the stronger. But these demands cannot be pressed to the point where they obstruct change of policy which a government should be at liberty to make within its discretionary power or legitimate practice". 78. The legal position after analyising the above authorities can be summed up by succinctly stating that while the government may be prevented from backing out of a promise its functionaries made and the promisee acted upon it to his detriment, estoppel cannot have any threshold to prevent a state functionary from performing a duty the law or the Constitution thrust upon him. He can obviously not turn intra vires an ultra vires action (Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries vs Hulkin, unreported, has been quoted in Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries vs Mathews 1949 2 All ER 724,) nor can it be taken in aid when equity deserves the converse and that the doctrine being based on equity, resiling would be permissible if equity so warrants. 79. In the case in hand the property concerned bears great historic and cultural significance being the tenement where the most illustrious star in the galaxy of Bengali film, Suchitra Sen was born in. She is our Pride (but not Prejudice) and shall live as our invaluable heritage till the twilight of civilisation. It is no exaggeration to say that the Government is saddled with a constitutional duty to adopt measures required for its protection under Articles 23 and 24 of the Constitution. Furthermore, it would be inequitable to try to hold the authorities to their purported promise not only because of their constitutional obligation to protect and preserve it but also because plunging the government to the claimed promise would mean depriving the nation of a prodigious relic. 80. Authorities of spectacular preponderance ordain that the doctrine of promissory estoppel cannot be animated against the Government if that impedes the Government's constitutional responsibility. 81. The Indian Supreme Court in Sankaranarayan vs State of Kerala (AIR 1971 SC 1997) held that the powers conferred by an Article of the Constitution cannot be curtailed by any agreement. 82. The said Court emphasised in MP Sugar Mills case, supra, that it would be deemed inequitable if the Government can demonstrate that overriding and overwhelming public interest required the Government to be absolved of its past promise. 83. Shuchitra Sen, generally venerated as a Sage, was the most revered Regina of Bengali Silver screens, which we take judicial notice of, and hence, in addition to what have been stated by the writ respondents, it goes without saying that duty to preserve her memory by setting up an archive, far transcends any other interest and hence public interest to protect and preserve it, is beyond any qualm, overriding and over whelming. 84. We do also note that the petitioner cannot claim equity based relief as he has not come with clean hands, firstly because, as the High Court Division concluded, he had been a defaulter and, also because after obtaining a big chunk of land for a throwaway price from the government in the same town, ( a fact that is not refuted) it was neither ethical nor scrupulously on his part to hold on to another government property and it would also be in-equitable on the part of the authorities to allow the same Imam Gazzali Institute to retain two sets of government lands simultaneously. 85. The petitioners' learned Senior Counsel also included the doctrine of legitimate expectation in his index of submissions. 86. This concept, the latest entrant into the domain of public law, again evolved by none else than Lord Denning, is distinct from equitable estoppel notwithstanding its visible resemblance with the latter. A promise, a representation, whether oral or written or a continuous conduct or practice may ignite an expectation based right if relied on by the promisee, representee. The expectation can be procedural or substantive. 87. The most important difference between a promissory estoppel and legitimate expectation is that while detriment suffered by the promisee is a sine qua non for a promissory estoppel, no such detriment is necessary to erect a claim on legitimate expectation (R vs Department of Education and Employment, Ex P Begbie (2000 1 WLR 1115, R (on the application of Bibi) vs Newham LBC (No.1) 2002 1 WLR 237, R vs Falmouth and Turno Port Health Authority Ex P South West Water Ltd. 2001 QB 445, R (Wagstaff) vs Secretary of State for Health 2001, 1 WLR 292, AG of Hong Kong vs Ng Yuen Shiu1983 2 AC 629). The strongest authority to say that the promisee need not incur any expenditure or otherwise to act to his detriment, is, R vs SOS for the Home Department Ex P Ruddock ( 1989 1 WLR 1982). Legitimate expectation is also different in that while promissory estoppel is a product of equity, legitimate expectation is an extension of the principle of fairness as propounded by the Common Law Judges in the realm of Administrative Law. As such, while relief under promissory estoppel is granted if the court concludes denial would be inequitable, a promise under the doctrine of legitimate expectation may be enforced if resiling from the promise by a public authority is deemed to be an unfair abuse of power. (R vs North and East Dewan Health Authority ex-P Coughlan 2001 QB 213). In R vs SOS Home Department ex-P Hargreaves (1997 1 WLR 906), on substantive expectation, as opposed to procedural ones, it was held that provided that the public body acted rationally in the Wednesbury sense, it is free to determine where the, balance lay between the policy factors pointing towards frustration of the expectation and the unfairness which would thereby be occasioned to the representee. Lord Brown Wilkinson in R vs SOS for Home Department Ex-P Variables, expressed, "When Parliament confers a discretionary power exercisable from time to time, such power must be exercised on each occasion in the light of the circumstances at that time. In consequence, the person on whom the power is conferred cannot fetter the future exercise of his discretion by committing himself now as to the way in which he will exercise his power in the future. He cannot exercise the power nunc pro tunc." (1998 AC 407). 88. High profile authorities affirm that Courts are far slower to enforce substantive expectation, as opposed to procedural expectation 89. Prof. Richard Moules of Cambridge in his book, "Actions Against Public Officials: Legitimate Expectation, Misstatements and Misconduct, by analysing various decisions, states. "While it is uncontroversial that a procedural legitimate expectation should normally be protected by ordering the expected procedure to be followed, the position in respect to substantive legitimate expectation is more complex. This is because substantive legitimate expectation impinges on the public body's discretion to a much greater extent: it constrains the decision which the body is entitled to make, rather than merely the procedure which must be followed". (Page 93). 90. It is thus, within the comprehensible range of vision that whereas promissory estoppel is conditioned and circumscribed by all the equitable maxims, a legitimate expectation is an extended form of fairness, designed to prevent abuse of power and the same is liable to fall through if, amongst other factors, interest of the society so warrants. 91. In quest of an answer to the question whether the doctrine of legitimate expectation is available to the instant petitioner, it is incumbent upon us to examine the circumstances in which this principle was gestated and what stumbles its application. 92. This latest permeated doctrine in the realm of public law made its maiden appearance with the deliberation of the judgment in the case Schmidt vs Secretary of State for Home Affairs (1969 All ER Vol. 1904). 93. Lord Denning MR, arguably one of the greatest English catalyst in juristic excellence, who evolved this doctrine from nihility by expanding the notion of fairness, while dismissing an American citizen's claim to have his stay visa in the UK extended after the same expired, to enable him to follow the course of study for which he was allowed to enter the UK., stated obitar, "If his permit is revoked before the time limit expires, he ought, I think, to be given an opportunity of making representations; for he would have a legitimate expectation of being allowed to stay for the permitted time. Except in such a case, a foreign alien has no right and I would add, no legitimate expectation of being allowed to stay. Once his time has expired he has to go." 94. With this observation, this hitherto unveiled concept came to the vogue. During the intervening period, this concept passed through manifold developments, not only in its natal home in the UK but also beyond. 95. Precisely, a legitimate expectation can arise when the public authority concerned, by a promise or a representation, whether verbal or written, or by conduct or continuous practice, ignites an expectation in the mind of the promisee or the representee that the promise, representation or the practice would be followed. 96. Unlike in promissory estoppel, the promisee is not required to show any detriment on his part, for the principle is an extension of the doctrine on fairness, not of equity. It is reckoned that fair play requires a public authority to honour its promise. 97. As the wings of the doctrine spread all around, so did the wing clipping factors. 98. It is, by now, a deeply trenched rule that neither form of legitimate expectation is absolute and an individual's entitlement may be denied in furtherance of an overriding public interest, particularly in substantive expectation cases. According to Laws LJ in R (Niazi) vs SOS for Home Department ( 2008 EWCA CIV 755) there are two situations in which it would be lawful for a public authority to resile from a legitimate expectation, namely (1) where there are countervailing considerations which justify not giving effect to the legitimate expectation in the public interest and (2) where it would be unlawful for the public authority to give effect to the legitimate expectation. 99. In the Hallmark case of R vs North and East Devon Health Authority, Ex-P Coughlan (2001 QB 213), it has been articulated that (1) in the first place the court is restricted to rationality or Wednesbury review, (2) concerning procedural expectations the court will decide whether the decision is procedurally fair, (3) the court must itself decide whether frustration of an individual's expectation was so unfair as to amount to an abuse of power. 100. The Court of Appeal thus emphasised that once the legitimacy of the expectation is established, the court will have the task of weighing the competing requirements of fairness against any overriding interest relied upon for the departure from the promise. 101. It has been stated by the Court of Appeal in R vs SOS for Education, Ex P Begbie( Per Laws LJ) (2000 1 WLR 1115), "In some cases a change of track by a public authority, though unfair from the applicant's stance, may involve question of general policy affecting the public at a large or a significant section of it." 102. In R (Niazi) vs SOS Home Department, supra, the court of Appeal (Per Laws LJ), held that the public authorities could resile from legitimate expectation where countervailing public interest so justifies. 103. The most glaring example of a public authority being permitted to resile from a legitimate expectation originating utterance or practice has been provided by the decision in the celebrated case of Council of Civil Service Unions vs Minister for Civil Service, (the GCHQ case) 1985 AC 374), in which case the House of Lords held that considerations of national security were sufficient to justify departure. 104. It has also been emphasised by the English authorities that a public body will be absolved from giving effect to a legitimate expectation if it is required to act contrary to the expectation of the statute. (R (X) vs Head Teacher and Governors of Y School 2008 1 All ER 249. 105. It has been held in R vs Ministry of Agriculture Fisheries and Food, Ex P Hamble Fisheries Ltd. ( 1995 2 All ER 714), that to bind public bodies to an unlawful representation would have the duel effect of extending statutory power and destroying ultra vires doctrine by permitting public bodies to arbitrarily extend their power. 106. Lord Denning MR in R vs Liverpool Corporation, Ex-P Liverpool Taxi Fleet Operators Association (1972 2 QB 299) relied on Lord Binkenhead's dictum in Birkendale District Electricity Supply Company Ltd. vs South port Corporation (1926 AC 355) to the effect that a public body cannot contract out of its statutory duties. Lord Denning expressed that a public body could not act incompatibly with the exercise of its powers or the discharge of its duties. 107. This British originated doctrine did not take much time to reach our sub-continent and quite naturally we followed the English decisions and the English guidelines as much as the interdictory devices the English Courts devolved, the English Courts being the innovating fora. 108. So far as the Indian Jurisdiction is concurred, the ratio in MP Oil Extraction vs MP (AIR 1998 SC 145) provides with a significant and comprehensive analyses, in which the Indian Supreme Court by placing under the scanner the English authorities, held that this doctrine has been judicially recognised in India. 109. Indian Apex Court followed the same exclusionary provisions as the English courts had and held in Dr Chancha lGoyal vs Roysthan (AIR 2003 SC 1713) that clear words in the statute or policy statement defeat legitimate expectation. It held in India vs Hindusthan Development Corporation (AIR 1994 SC 988) that the protection of legitimate expectation does not require the fulfillment of the expectation where an overriding public interest surfaces with greater accentuation. 110. In Food Corp of India vs Kamdhenu Cattle Feed Industries (1993 SC 160) the same court, though recognised the existence of legitimate expectation, refused to grant relief because overriding public interest outweighed the individual's expectation. 111. By anatomising the English decision in R vs Home Secretary ex P Hargreaves (1997 1 WLR), the Indian Supreme Court came up with the irrefutable conclusion that a change in Policy can defeat a substantive legitimate expectation provided it can be justified on Wednesbury reasonableness. 112. Courts in our own jurisdiction had dis- played no outwardly approach either. On the constraining application of the doctrine, the Appellate Division in Chairman BTMC vs Nasiruddin Chowdhury, supra, while holding that the given facts are incapable of igniting such an expectation, nevertheless, expressed obitar, that though a substantive legitimate expectation cannot normally be defeated, overriding public interest clearly requires negation. 113. The above stated authorities can be summed up as follows: (1) While a representation, promise, verbal or scripted, a continuous practice that has been followed, if relied on, can procreate a legitimate expectation in the mind of the recipient as to their followance, his claim to the expectation may be liable to be defeated for numerous reasons, such as, if honoring the expectation; (a) would founder overriding public interest, (b) would be repugnant to any constitutional, or statutory mandate or even constitutional or statutory expectation: if honoring the expectation would be ultra vires any constitutional or statutory provision. (c) would be inconsistent with a changed policy provided the change is not unreasonable in the Wednesbury sense. 114. The primordial question before us is where does the petitioner stand in the backdrop of the factors dissected above so far as his claimed legitimate expectation is concerned? 115. We reckon it irresistible in the first place to explore the question as to whether the text in the documed annexed as Annexure-E to the Writ Petition No. 4608 of 2009 can be treated as a promise capable of generating a legitimate expectation, and if it does, to what extent? It is plenteously clear from the text that the authorities concerned stated that the yearly lease would be extended every year until a permanent decision is taken on the vested properties. So, the expectation, if any, died a natural death when the authorities resolved to convert the subject property into an archive to preserve Shuchitra Sen's memory, i.e. when a permanent decision had been taken on this vested property. 116. Expectation, if any, (and indeed reliance on promissory estoppel) must have been a stale one even from the inception from the legal perspective as well, because; (i) it cannot be honoured without clogging the hands of the authorities from implementing what Article 23 and 24 of our Constitution ordains. Although provision of these Articles are not judicially enforceable, they do nevertheless, impose upon the State inalienable obligation, which cannot be compromised by any promise or practice. To do so would be tantamount to defeating constitutional sermon and expectations, (ii) it is beyond the expectation of the statutes, which stand in force to regulate vested properties, that the authorities should be allowed to clog their discretion by making any promise of infinite duration and thereby deprive themselves of chalking further schemes of benevolent nature in future. (iii) it is beyond qualm that late Shuchitra Sen is an Acclaimed Maestro who reigned over our film world for over three decades unrivelled. She is preciously adored by our people, whose vibrant desire for the protection and preservation of the earlier's memory and works in her natal home mounts to a level high enough to be ignored, and it is this inviolable aspiration that undoubtedly animates an overriding public interest of utmost importance, which cannot be flouted or crucified, which interest must prevail over the petitioner's claim. (iv) if the claim advanced by the petitioner is accepted, that would effectively mean emasculating the authorities to the extent that they would be debarred from performing their statutory obligations as per the mandates that emanates from the Antiquities Act 1968 section 2(e), read with section 2(c)(ii), when the cite shall attain the statues of a centenarian, an event which is quite foreseeable without any haze as it is not far away, because Shuchitra died aged 83, of which we take judicial notice. (v) it would amount to fettering the authorities' discretion to adopt a different policy which is not unreasonable in the Wednesbury sense, or irrational in the GCHQ sense. 117. For the reasons assigned above, our irrestible conclusion is that the High Court Division's judgment and order are irreprehensible, above board and rigidly infallible. We cannot detect even a microscopic particle of error or misdirection in the merit oriented judgment in Writ Petition No. 4608 of 2009. Arguments purportedly structured on natural justice, promisory estoppel and legitimate expectation are obfuscating and destined to end in futitity and fiasco. 118. So far as the fate of Writ Petition No. 6766 of 2011 is concerned, the High Court Division quite cogently noted that as the authorities have resolved to do what the petitioner ofthat petition aspired, this petition has become infructuous. 119. We find both the leave to appeal application totally devoid of merit, founded upon total delusive introspection and hence both of them, namely, Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1901 of 2011 and 1902 of 2011 are bound to falter, wherefore they are hereby dismissed. 120. The High Court Division's direction upon the Government to implement the decision to establish "Shuchitra Sen Smrity Sanghrohashala" without delay to protect and preserve her birth place for her indubitable contribution to our cultural arena, is hereby reiterated, requiring the authorities to begin the process forthwith without any delay whatsoever by evicting the petitioner and his institute, if that has not already been done by now. 121. Before parting we must also note with disquiet that Mr Imran Siddique, the learned Advocate for the petitioner in Writ Petition No. 4608 of 2009 as early as in August, 2011, prayed for an stay of the operation of the High Court Division's order for two months so that the school could be shifted and the said prayer was granted. Yet, instead of shifting the school, for which stay was successfully applied for, the petitioner filed these Civil Petitions for Leave to Appeal, and thereby kept the property under their possession for three more years, by doing which, in our view, the learned Advocate and his client resorted to clear fraud upon the court for which they deserve to be reprimanded. End.  

Appellate Division

(Civil)

Surendra Kumar Sinha CJ

Order

This petition is for expunging some remarks made by this court in the operating part of the judgment.

2. We have heard the learned Counsel and perused the judgment of this court. The learned Counsel for the petitioner submits that the petitioner has not been afforded any opportunity before making adverse remarks and that he was not involved in filing the leave petition. On perusal of the judgment we find merit in the submission of the learned Counsel.

3. The following remarks made in the operative part of the judgment "Before parting we must also note with disquiet that Mr Imran Siddique, the learned Advocate for the petitioner in Writ Petition No. 4608 of 2009 as early as in August, 2011, prayed for an stay of the operation of the High Court Division's order for two months so that the school could be shifted and the said prayer was granted. Yet, instead of shifting the school, for which stay was successfully applied for, the petitioner filed these Civil Petitions for Leave to Appeal, and thereby kept the property under their possession for three more years, by doing which, in our view, the learned Advocate and his client resorted to clear fraud upon the court for which they deserve to be reprimanded" be expunged.

4. This petition is accordingly disposed of with the above expunction.

End.
