case_source: (From the judgment and order dated the 8th day of July, 2003 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition Nos. 433 of 1998, 998 of 2002, 3770 of 2000, 2518 of 2001, 3769 of 2000, 2311 of 2001, 2822 of 2001, 4068 of 2000, 2776 of 2001, 2465 of 2001, 3237 of 2000 and 1515 of 2001).
full_judgment:
Md. Muzammel Hossain CJ: I have gone through the separate judgments prepared by my learned brother, Surendra Kumar Sinha, I and my learned brother, Md. Abdul Wahhab Miah, J. I agree with the judgment of Md. Abdul Wahhab Miah, J.

SK Sinha J: Leave granted.

2. The writ petitioners sought for directions in the form of mandamus for issuance of licence and registration of their, fishing trawlers for fishing in deep sea. Facts relevant for the disposal of these matters are as under.

3. Some writ-petitioners who are respondents purchased the fishing trawlers in question in auction from different organizations of the Government, while some others purchased their trawlers from the auction purchasers and some of them imported from abroad. Except a few, all these trawlers was Thai-fishing trawlers and when they were illegally fishing within the Bangladesh territorial waters, they were seized by the Government of Bangladesh. As the trawlers were used for fishing, the writ-respondents would allow them for fishing and accordingly they carried out necessary repair works. Later on the writ-petitioners filed applications to the appropriate authorities including the Prime Minister and the Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock for granting them licence for catching fish in the deep-sea water. Even after the recommendation, the writ-respondents did not grant inspection certificates, registration and license.

4. The High Court Division heard all the writ petitions analogously and disposed of them by a single judgment making the rules absolute. The High Court Division reproduced the submissions of the learned counsel at the Bar and without assigning reasons for the decision made the rules absolute observing "In these cases the Government having forfeited the Thai deep-sea fishing trawlers for illegal poaching in the Bangladesh territorial waters sold them to the petitioners. The sale of the trawlers under consideration to the petitioners by the Government knowing that those trawlers could only be used for deep-sea fishing should be construed as promise by the Government to Issue necessary registration and license to these trawlers if applied for and were found fit for deep-sea fishing. Moreover, since after the aforesaid expert report dated 20-5-1997 there has been no other report till date issued by any competent authority discouraging or prohibiting granting licence to any other trawlers for deep-sea fishing, we are inclined to hold that the refusal of the respondent No. 1 to grant registration and licence to the trawlers in question is illegal and without jurisdiction being hit by the principle of promissory estoppel".

5. Learned Attorney-General appearing for the appellants raises two points, first, the principles of promissory estoppel and legitimate expectation would in no way apply in the facts of the given cases and the High Court Division on a superficial consideration of the facts applied the doctrine of 'promissory estoppel' and secondly, in the absence of pleadings on the doctrine of 'Promissory estoppel' or 'legitimate expectation', the direction given by the High Court Division is not justified by the judicial principles.

6. Admittedly none of the Writ Petitioners made any statement to the effect that as per assurances of the writ-respondents for giving them licence for fishing in deep sea they or their vendors purchased the trawlers and renovated them with huge money. It can be concluded that there is no pleading at all in support of the relief(s) claimed on the doctrine. In Course of hearing this Division wanted to know from Mr M Amirul Islam, learned counsel appearing for the writ petitioners as to the basis for claiming relief (s) by the writ petitioners. Learned counsel submitted that even in the absence of pleadings, as per constitutional mandate, the promissory estoppel merges into an area of substantive right of rule of law, equality and justice in pursuing one's lawful trade and business. Mr. M Amirul Islam argued that the doctrine of legitimate expectation could be applied in appropriate cases against the Government as well. In this connection the learned counsel quoted from Blacks Law Dictionary the meaning of the expression 'promissory estoppel'.

7. On perusal of the petitions it can safely be concluded that under any jurisprudential point of view the High Court Division is not justified in giving the direction to the writ respondents to issue deep-water fishing licence to the writ petitioners. There must be positive and sufficient pleadings if someone is claiming for a right on the doctrine of promissory estoppel. The pleadings on behalf of the writ petitioners are almost same except in two cases. It must be remembered that a person is not estopped from asserting a right, which he had said that he would not assert. Estoppel deals with no rights. To appreciate the points raised by the learned counsel for the writ-petitioners and the reasons assigned by the High Court Division, it would be profitable if I narrate the facts stated by each of the writ petitioners.

8. In Civil Appeal No. 127 of 2005 which arose out of Writ Petition No. 433 of 1998, the trawler, 'FV SATELLITE-1' was sold by Chalna Customs House to one M/s Farhana Trading on 14th January, 1989, The purchaser by executing a higher purchase agreement with the Islami Bank Limited, Mogholtuly Branch, took loan and ultimately it failed to repay the money. Accordingly Islami Bank Limited, Mogholtuly Branch advertised for sale of the trawler. The writ-petitioner Satellite Fishing Limited purchased it on auction from the Islami Bank Limited. Thereafter it prayed to the Prime Minister on 28th December, 1992 for allowing the trawler for fishing stating that the writ petitioner converted it fit for fishing from dilapidated condition. The writ-petitioner renewed its prayer in May, 1994 and then to the concerned Ministry. The Directorate of Fisheries initially accorded permission on 18th November, 1995 for three trial trips subject to obtaining no objection certificate from the Mercantile Marine Department. Thereafter the Directorate accorded two more trial trips. Ultimately the concerned Ministry expressed its inability to give licence by order dated 8th October, 1997 until the Cabinet Division decides on the matter as per recommendation of Dr Mahamudul Karim's report. The writ-petitioner thereupon moved the writ petition and secured an interim order from the High Court Division, which directed the writ-respondents to allow the writ-petitioner's trawler to fish in the Bay of Bengal.

9. In Civil Appeal No. 128 of 2005 which arose out of Writ Petition No. 998 of 2002, the trawler 'FV RUKCHAI MONDKOL' renamed 'FV FLEMINGO' was sold in auction by the Mercantile Marine Department to Kazi Gulam Tabasasum sometimes in January, 2001. There after the auction purchaser entered into an agreement for sale with M/s Continental Marine Fisheries Limited, the writ-petitioner on 10th January, 2002. The writ-petitioner then prayed to the Minister of the concerned Ministry for trial trip in February, 2002. The Ministry intimated to the writ-petitioner that as per terms of the tender, the trawler could not be allowed to catch fish in the Bay and rejected the prayer. The writ-petitioner challenged the said order in the High Court Division.

10. In Civil Appeal No. 129 of 2001 which arose out of Writ Petition No. 3770 of 2000, the trawler 'FV PARKNUM RUNANG-003' renamed 'FV FISH HUNTER' was sold in auction by the Mercantile Marine Department in March, 1999. The writ-petitioner took delivery of the vessel and thereafter, prayed to the Minister-in-charge of the Ministry of Fisheries and Lives Stock for granting licence. As per recommendation of the Minister, the Mercantile Marine Department asked the writ-petitioner to produce papers in support of the trawler on 1st December, 1999. The writ-petitioner without awaiting any decision from the Mercantile Marine Department issued a legal notice through its lawyer and moved the writ petition on 10th April, 2000. The High Court Division at the time of issuance of rule made an interim order directing the writ-respondents to give to the trawler trial trips subject to obtaining fitness certificate from the Mercantile Marine Department. In this petition the writ-petitioner did not impugn any order and seeks a direction upon the writ-respondents to issue licence to the writ-petitioner. Pursuant to the interim order, the Mercantile Marine Department on inspection of the vessel in its certificate, of inspection which was enclosed in the additional paper book at page 229 pointed out deficiencies and directed for rectification but it failed to rectify the technical faults despite taking time thrice.

11. Civil Appeal No. 130 of 2009 which arose out of Writ Petition No. 2518 of 2001, the trawler 'FV SUTIPONGCHAI' was sold in auction to one Mozaher Sawdager by the Mercantile Marine Department in the latter part of 1995. Thereafter he sold the trawler to the writ-petitioner, Some Fish Limited. After purchase the writ-petitioner prayed to the Minister for issuing fishing licence. The writ-petitioner also renewed its prayer to the Secretary of the concerned Ministry. The writ-petitioner without awaiting any decision of the authority moved the writ petition seeking a direction upon the writ-respondents to issue licence to the fishing trawler. Accordingly the High Court Division while issuing rule made an interim order. As per direction of the High Court Division, the Mercantile Marine Department in its inspection certificate (page 109 of the additional paper book), which was enclosed by the writ-petitioner, noticed deficiencies in the trawler.

12. In Civil Appeal No. 131 of 2005 which arose out of Writ Petition No. 3769 of 2000, 'MV CHOW SOHAMIT" renamed 'FV BISMILLA' was sold in auction some times in July, 1997. Writ-petitioner after depositing the money took delivery of possession of the trawler on 4th December, 1998 and thereafter it prayed to the concerned Ministry for giving temporary licence on 8th November, 1999. The Ministry referred the matter to the Mercantile Marine Department for examining the trawler on 21st November, 1999. The writ-petitioner without awaiting decision moved the writ petition and secured interim order from the High Court Division, which directed the writ-respondents to issue licence to the writ-petitioner's trawler.

13. In Civil Appeal No. 132 of 2005, which arose out of Writ Petition No. 2822 of 2001, the trawler 'FV PANDO', renamed 'FV MARINE HARVESTER-2' was sold in auction on 31st May, 2001. The writ-petitioner after taking delivery of possession .prayed to the Secretary of the concerned Ministry for trial trip. The prayer was refused on the ground that as per policy no licence was given to any fishing trawlers by the Ministry. The writ-petitioner filed the writ petition seeking declaration of the said order is illegal with a prayer to direct the writ-respondents to grant licence to the trawler.

14. In Civil Appeal No. 133 of 2005 which arose out Writ Petition No. 4068 of 2000, the vessel 'FV RANAG-1' renamed 'FV KARNAPHULI' was sold in auction and the writ-petitioner took delivery of possession of the fishing trawler on 5th August, 1997. Thereafter it prayed to the Minister for a trial trip on 3rd March, 1999. The writ-petitioner sought for a declaration that the withholding of licence to the writ-petitioner's trawler was illegal. The writ-petitioner did not await for the reply of his representation and he did not even challenge any order of the writ-respondents.

15. In Civil Appeal No. 134 of 2005 which arose out of Writ Petition No. 1282 of 2003. The writ-petitioner sought for a direction to restore licence dated 16 February, 1984 in respect of fishing trawler 'FV Unique 15. The writ-petitioner claimed that it had imported two trawlers with prior permission, one of which was 'POR EKODOMPORN-3; the trawler sailed till 31st December, 1984 and thereafter it was not traceable. Thereafter, it purchased one trawler TV ORSIRISAREECHAI' from M/s SEEGRAL Deep Sea Fishing on 23rd June, 2001. The writ-petitioner then prayed to the Secretary of the concerned Ministry for issuing a licence in replacement of the earlier licence granted to its trawler 'POR EKODONPORN'. Its prayer was rejected on the plea that it's trawler was not included in the Zaman committee report. The writ-petitioner challenged the said order and obtained an interim order from the High Court Division.

16. Civil Appeal No. 135 of 2005, which arose out of Writ Petition No. 2465 of 2001, the trawler TV NILPHI renamed FV FALCON', was sold in auction by the Mercantile Marine Department to Unique Traders, the writ-petitioner. After taking delivery of possession it prayed for licence for fishing in the deep sea. The prayer was refused on the plea that as per terms of tender the fishing trawler could not allowed to explore fish in deep sea. The writ-petitioner thereupon challenged the said order.

17. Civil Appeal No. 136 of 2005, which arose out of Writ Petition No. 3237 of 2007, the trawler 'FV CHOCKSISRUN-001 renamed FV SIX STAR-2', was sold in auction to one Md Yousuf Ali Sowdagar on 12th December, 1995. The writ-petitioner purchased it from the auction purchaser on 1st October, 1997. Thereafter it prayed to the Prime Minister for the registration of the trawler. The writ-petitioner without awaiting any decision filed the writ petition seeking a direction upon the writ-respondents to issue licence to the trawler for catching fish. The High Court Division issued an interim order.

18. In Civil Appeal No. 137 of 2005 which arose out of Writ Petition No. 1515 of 2001, the writ-petitioner claimed that it imported to second hand trawlers from Singapore, namely (1) 'YUNG TSING-6', (2) 'YUNG TSING-11' and thereupon prayed to the concerned Minister in charge to the Ministry for no objection certificate. Thereafter it prayed for renewing the licence to the Secretary of the concerned Ministry. The writ-petitioner challenged the order and sought for a direction to register the trawlers and to issue licence and permission of replacement/substitution of licence of 'FV Salam-2' against its earlier fishing trawler 'FP Paradise-12.

19. In Civil Appeal No.135 of 2005 which arose out of Writ Petition No. 2311 of 2001, the trawler 'FV BANNAN' renamed 'FV SADMAN' was sold in auction on 11th April, 2001. After taking delivery of possession of the trawler the writ-petitioner prayed to the Board of Investment to give trial trip licence. The prayer-was refused. The Writ-petitioner thereupon challenged.

20. It is evident from the facts averred in the petitions that in Writ Petition Nos. 3770, 3769, 3237 and 4068 of 2000, 2518 of 2001, the authority did not make any order pursuant to the writ-petitioners' prayer for issuing temporary trial trips. In Writ Petition Nos. 1282 of 2003 and 1515 of 2001, the writ-petitioners sought for replacement and/or substitution of licence on the ground that they had licence in respect of their old fishing trawlers, which were not traceable, and therefore, they are entitled to the replacement of the licence in respect of the new ones, which they had purchased.

21. The writ-petitioners have relied upon the conduct of the authority stating that since the writ respondents who are responsible for issuing licence sold the trawlers, which were used as fishing trawlers and they purchased the trawlers on the understanding that they would be given necessary licence for fishing and accordingly, they installed fishing gears and equipment's and obtained certificates of inspection and registrations, which according to them had accrued rights to get licence. These are mere assumptions and presumptions on hypothesis, which do not confer any right or interest under any established doctrine or principle. These presumptions, even if there be any, are not obligatory. A presumption is a rule that a particular inference shall be drawn from particular facts whoever proved them. The writ petitioners having not pleaded in support of the claim and in the absence of established precedents or rules from which it may be inferred, the writ petitioners are not authorised by law to get licence, to speak the least, under any theory of law.

22. It is argued by Mr. Islam that the concerned authority be estopped retracting from the promises and entitlement created by the conduct of sale being followed by promises provided under the law. I fail to understand which conduct of the writ respondents constitutes the promise to issue licence to the writ petitioners in the absence of statements constituting conduct. It is further contended that the State being the authority for both holding auction for fishing trawlers and granting licence, it is bound by the promises and conditions laid down under the law. This is the repetition of the earlier arguments without having any foundation on the point. Learned Counsel has referred to sections 7, 17, 18 and 19 of the Marine Fisheries Ordinance, 1983 and Articles 31 and 40 of the Constitution in support of his contention. Reliance was also given to the cases of Collector of Customs vs A Hannan, 42 DLR (AD) 167, Abdur Rahim vs Government of Bangladesh, 48 DLR (AD) 538, Union of India vs Anglo Afghan Agencies, AIR 1968 SC 718 and Silver vs Ocean Steamship Company Limited, (1930) 1KB 416.

<u>23. Before I deal with the points canvassed, I would like to point out that I am unable to be persuaded by the majority opinion on the question of legitimate expectation in the facts of the given cases. The opinion that 'where a public authority represents that it will act in a particular way, that representation may give rise to a legitimate expectation on the part of the represented that the public authority will so act, and the public authority may have to give effect to that expectation', in my humble view is against pleadings and even if, there be any, do not give rise to legitimate expectation. The mere reasonable or legitimate expectation of a person may not by itself be a distinct enforceable right. A legitimate expectation cannot be the same as anticipation. A desire or a hope cannot amount to a ground of a right. A legitimacy of an expectation can be inferred only if it is founded on the sanction of law or custom or an established procedure followed in regular sequence. It must also be shown that the decision of the authority affected the writ petitioners by depriving them of the benefits of the licence which in the past they had been permitted to enjoy either they were given reasons for its withdrawal or from the existence of a regular practice, which they could reasonably expect to continue, gave rise to an implied limitation on the authorities exercise of power. The other question which is required to be considered is that the public authority has represented and/or assured the writ petitioners or the vendors of some of the writ petitioners for issuing licence to the trawlers for fishing in the deep sea.</u>

24. Learned counsel M Amirul Islam in his written argument as well as in his submissions did not claim that there was any representation on the part of the public authority for issuing licence. In paragraph 9 of his written argument he stated 'it will be seen that the government with full knowledge and understanding that these fishing vessels would be used for fishing, conducted the auction and sold them to the petitioners with an undertaking that with the permission of the government those fishing vessels can be used for fishing. Moreover, section 17 and 18 of Marine Fisheries Ordinance, 1983 provides that the certificate of Inspection and Registration are necessary for having fishing licence. Under such circumstances the fishing vessels owners (writ petitioners) can legitimately expect that the government's policy is that upon fulfillment of S 17 and 18 of the Marine Fisheries Ordinance, 1983 they will be given licences'.

25. Though the learned counsel used the expression 'undertaking' at one stage, there is nothing on record either in the averments of the writ petitions or by filing documents in support of the claim. I fail to understand wherefrom my learned brother expressing the majority opinion came to the conclusion that 'when in the writ petitions, a positive case of 'legitimate expectation' was asserted and in support of the case, documents were annexed thereto, in the absence of any denial of the assertions of the writ petitioner's case as well as the annexure annexed to the petitions, their case cannot altogether be rejected or ignored'. Where the learned counsel himself admitted that even if there is no statement 'The doctrine of 'legitimate expectation' has been defined as a promise made in the shape of a statement of policy or a procedure adopted by the administrative authority which may give rise to legitimate expectation and it has been established as a corollary to the principle of 'promissory estoppel'. My learned brother made out a third case without mentioning the assertions made by the writ petitioners in support of their claim, not to speak of filing any documentary evidence and this will be evident from the submissions of the learned counsel as quoted above.

26. In Writ Petition No. 433 of 1998 it is averred in paragraph 10 that 'after successful completed of trial fishing the petitioner was expectation (sic) to regular licence for deep see fishing but all on a sudden it received the impugned letter issued by the Ministry of Fisheries and Lives Stock respondent No. 2 herein vide its Memo No. Matsha (Unit) 2/96-306 dated 8-10-1997 communicating to the petitioner the Government decision not to grant any new licence at this stage". Are these statements sufficient to give rise to legitimate expectation for getting a deep water fishing licence on the doctrine? If the answer were in the affirmative, there would be need for giving a new definition of the doctrine after reviewing the earlier opinions.

<u>27. The moot points are whether a fishing vessel sold by a governmental department is under obligation to issue a licence for fishing in the deep sea if the purchaser repaired it after purchase for fishing on the doctrine of 'promissory estoppel' or 'legitimate expectation' in the absence of foundation in support of the claim and secondly, these doctrines can be applied against the state to bind itself to fetter its executive action or its agencies. What the writ petitioners really prayed for in the petitions are various directions, which are purely the functions of the Director appointed under the Ordinance. If these prayers are allowed, it would not be legitimate exercise of judicial power. It should be remembered that the Courts cannot run the Government or any of department. It is not within the domain of the Court to issue a direction to issue fishing licence or to register trawler for fishing in the deep sea as it is a matter of policy on which decision has to be taken by the Director. This is wholly unconstitutional because no organ of the Government can usurp the functions assigned to another. Judicial review is a weapon to restrain unconstitutional exercise of power by the Legislature and Executive. The exercise of this power is subject to judicial restraint the self-imposed discipline of judicial restraint. Frankfuter, J in Trop vs Dulles, 2 L Ed 630 356 US 86 (1957) observed "It also must be on guard against encroaching beyond its proper bounds, and not the less so since the only restraint upon it is self-restraint..."</u>

28. The directives sought for in the petitions require the expertise of administrative and technical know-how officials. The Court should not give such directions because that would violate the principle of separation of powers under the Constitution. These are also highly technical matters to be left with the persons assigned by the Marine Fisheries Ordinance, 1983, shortly the Ordinance, who have experience and expertise in the matter. The modem trend points to judicial restraint in administrative actions. This view has been taken by the Supreme Court of India in Tata Cellular vs Union of India, AIR 1996 SC 11 and in a large number of cases including the United States Supreme Court. The Courts must not embarrass the administrative authorities and realise that administrative authorities have expertise in the field of administration. In this connection it would be appropriate to quote the words of Bernard Schwartz in Administrative Law, 2nd Edn. page 584 'It is not the function of a judge to act as a super board, or with the zeal of pedantic schoolmaster substituting its judgment for that of the administrator.' It should also be remembered that while exercising power of judicial review of the administrative action, the court is not an appellate authority.

29. According to Black's Law Dictionary, 'promissory estoppel' means:

"Which arises when there is a promise which promissory should reasonably expect to induce action or forbearance of a definite and substantial character on part of promise and which does induce such action or forbearance, and such promise is binding if injustice can be avoided only by enforcement of promise"

<u>30. The doctrine of promissory estoppel is an equitable doctrine. A plain meaning of the doctrine is that a representation made by one party for the purpose of influencing the conduct of the other party and to be acted upon by him will in general be sufficient to entitle to assistance of the Court of equity for the purpose of making good such representation. But where there is no such representation or the agreement to issue licence and registration, the claimant cannot plead for issuance of licence under the principle of promissory estoppel. Before a person claims entitlement of a licence on the doctrine, it must be proved that (a) there was a representation or promise in regard to something to be done in future; (b) the representation or promise was intended to effect the legal relations of the parties and intended to be acted on accordingly; and (c) it is one which the other side has acted to his prejudice.</u>

31. The elements of estoppel are generally claimed where there is a representation in any form, a declaration, act or omission, the representation must have been the existence of a fact; the representation must have been made under circumstances which amounted to an intentional causing or permitting belief in another. Some persons must have believed the representation to be true and that persons must have acted on the belief so induced and been thus led to change their former position thereby to their prejudice. The rule of estoppel depends for its application on certain question of fact. Generally there can be no estoppel against state or its organization where the act done is ultra vires the State or its Organization.

32. Denning, J in Robertson vs Minister of Pensions, (1949) 1KB 227 argued as to its applicability against crown as under:

"The Crown cannot escape by saying that estoppels do not bind the Crown for that doctrine has long been exploded. Nor can the Crown escape by praying in aid the doctrine of executive necessity, that is, the doctrine that the Crown cannot bind itself so as to fetter its future executive action. That doctrine was propounded by Rowlett, J in Rederiaktiebolaget Amphitrite vs The King (1921) 3KB 500) , but it was unnecessary for the decision because the statement there was not a promise which was intended to be binding but only an expression of intention. Rowlett, J, seems to have been influenced by the cases on the right of the Crown to dismiss its servants at pleasure, but those cases must now all be read in the light of the judgment of Lord Atkin in Reilly vs The King ((1934) AC 176, 179). In my opinion the defence of executive necessity is of limited scope. It only avails the Crown where there is an implied term to that effect or that is the true meaning of the contract."

33. The English Courts did not accept the views of Denning, J The House of Lords in Howell vs Falmouth Boat Construction Company Limited, 1951 AC 837 disagreed with the views of Lord Denning observing 'the observations of Denning , LJ in Robertson V Minister of Pensions on the doctrine of 'executive necessity' were, I think, directed to a case of that sort. Here we are dealing with an act done for a general executive purpose, and not done for the purpose of achieving a particular result under the contract in question'. In that case Devlin, J stated the principle as under:

"When the crown or any other person, is entrusted, whether by virtue of the prerogative or by statute, with discretionary powers to be exercised for the public good, it does not when making a private contract in general terms, undertake and it may be that it would not even with the use of those powers, and in the exercise of the discretion."

34. Similar views have been taken by the American jurisprudence on the doctrine of promissory estoppel. Ray, CJ in Ramanathan Pillai vs State of Kerala, AIR 1973 SC 2641 quoted with approval a passage from American Jurisprudence, Second Edition, Paragraph 123 at Page 783 as under:

"Generally, a State is not subject to an estoppel to the same extent as an individual or a private corporation. Otherwise, it might be rendered helpless to assert its powers in Government. Therefore, as a general rule the doctrine of estoppel will not be applied against the State in its Governmental, public or sovereign capacity. An exception however arises in the application of estoppel to the State where it is necessary to prevent fraud or manifest injustice."

35. The statement of law argued by the House of Lords has been accepted as correct by the Supreme Court of India in Excise Commissioner UP Allahabad vs Ram Kumar, AIR 1976 SC 2237, wherein it has been observed: "the Government cannot divest itself the right incidental to its office by conduct which, in the case of a private person would amount to estoppel and in characterizing the demand for sales tax made by the appellants as illegal."

36. We find from these authoritative pronouncements that this doctrine cannot be invoked to prevent the Government from acting in discharge of its duty under the law. In M/s Jit Ram Shiv Kumar vs State of Haryana, AIR 1980 SC 1285, the Supreme Court evaluated all its previous decisions and those of English and American jurisdictions on the principle and summed up as under:

(1) The plea of promissory estoppel is not available against the exercise of the legislative functions of the State.

(2) The doctrine cannot be invoked for preventing the Government from discharging its functions under the law.

(3) When the officer of the Government acts outside the scope of his authority, the plea of promissory estoppel is not available. The doctrine of ultra wires will come into operation and the Government cannot be held bound by the unauthorized acts of its officers.

(4) When the officer acts within the scope of his authority under a scheme and enters into an agreement and makes a representation and a person acting on that representation puts himself in a disadvantageous position, the Court is entitled to require the officer to act according to the scheme and the agreement or representation. The Officer cannot arbitrarily act on his mere whim and ignore his promise on some undefined and undisclosed grounds of necessity or change the conditions to the prejudice of the person who had acted upon such representation and put himself in a disadvantageous position.

(5)The officer would be justified in changing the terms of the agreement to the prejudice of the other party on special considerations such as difficult foreign exchange position or other maters which have a bearing on general interest of the state."

37. There can also be no promissory estoppel against the exercise of legislative power of the state. The Supreme Court of India noticed the opinion of professor SA De Smith in his Judicial Review on his Administrative Action, 3rd Edn, who summed up the position thus: 'contracts and covenants entered into by crown are not to be construed as being subject to implied terms that would exclude the exercise on general discretionary powers for the public good: on the contrary they are to be constructed as incorporating an implied term that such powers remain exercisable. This is broadly true of other public authorities also." Prof Wade in his Administrative Law, 4th Edn, pointed out that the doctrine of estoppel cannot be allowed to impede the proper exercise of public and statutory functions by the state or public authorities. In public law the most obvious limitation on the doctrine of estoppel is that it cannot be invoked so as to give an authority powers, which it does not in law, possess.

38. Thus there are unanimous opinions that Crown cannot be allowed to tie its hands completely by prior undertakings is as clear as the proposition that the Courts cannot allow crown to evade compliance with extensively binding obligations whenever it thinks fit. If a public authority lawfully repudiates or departs from the term of a binding contract in order to exercise its overriding discretionary powers, or if it is held never to have been bound in law by an extensively binding contract because the undertaking would improperly fetter its general discretionary powers, the other party to the agreement has no right whatsoever to damages or compensation under the general law, no matter how serious the damages that party may have suffered.

39. The unanimous views taken by the superior courts of United Kingdom, United States and India in this regard are that the doctrine cannot be invoked for preventing the Government from acting in discharge of its duty under the law. The Government would not be bound by the act of its officers as agents, who act beyond the scope of their authority and a person dealing with the agent, of the Government must have noticed of the limitations of the authority. The Court can enforce compliance by a public authority of the obligation laid on him if he arbitrarily or on his mere whim ignores the promises made by him on behalf of the Government. It would be open to the authority to plead and prove that there were special considerations, which necessitated it not being able to comply with its obligations in public interest. I find no reason to depart from those principles that the doctrine of promissory estoppel can be invoked for preventing, the Government from acting in discharge of its duty under the law.

40. The Supreme Court of India in Chhagnnlal vs Narandas, AIR 1982 SC 121, explains as to what constitutes estoppel within the meaning of section 115 of the Evidence Act that—"

(i) there must be a representation by a person or his authorized agent to another in any form-a declaration, act or omission;

(ii) the representation must have been of the existence of a fact and not of promises de futuro or intention, which might or might not be enforceable in contract;

(iii) the representation must have been meant to be relied upon;

(iv) thier must have been belief on the part of the other party in its truth;

(v) there must have been action on the faith of that declaration, act or omission, that is to say, the declaration, act or omission must have actually caused another to act on the faith of it, and to alter his former position to his prejudice or detriment;

(vi) the misrepresentation or conduct or omission must have been the proximate cause of leading the other party to act to his prejudice;

(vii) the person claiming the benefit of an estoppel must show that he was not aware of the true state of things. If he was aware of the real state of affairs or had means of knowledge, there can be no estoppel;

(viii) only the person to whom representation was made or for whom it was designed can avail himself of it. A person is entitled to plead estoppel in his Own individual character and not as a representative of his assignee."

41. This Division in Bangladesh Parjatan Corporation vs Mofizur Rahman, 46 DLR (AD) 44, with approval quoted the arguments of the Judicial Committee in Sarat Chunder Dy vs Gopal Chunder Laha, 191A 203 as under :

"The doctrine will apply, which is to be found, I believe, in the laws of all civilised nations , that if a man, either by words or by conduct has intimated that he consents to an act which has been done, and that he will offer no opposition to it although it could not have been lawfully done without his consent, and he thereby induces others to do that from which they otherwise might have abstained, be cannot question the legality of the act he had so sanctioned, to the prejudice of those who have so given faith to his words or to the fair inference to be drawn from his conduct I am of opinion that, generally speaking, if a party having an interest to prevent an act being done has full notice of its having been done, and acquiesces in it, so as to induce a reasonable belief that he consents to it, and the position of others is altered by their given credit to his sincerity, he has no more right to challenge the act to their prejudice than he would have had if it has been done by his previous license."

42. As regards the cases referred by Mr Islam, I failed to understand why he had referred to them. In respect of the cases of Supreme Court of India and Kings Bench Division, the Indian Supreme Court and House of Lords over ruled the views taken in those cases . An estoppel deals with question of facts and not of rights. A man is not estopped from asserting a right, which he had said that he would net, assert. It is also well known principle that there cannot be estoppel against the statute or the state or its agencies or any public authority or organisation.

43. Learned Attorney-General has drawn our attention to clause 8 of the tender documents, in respect of fishing trawler 'RUKCHAI MONDKOL' which has been accompanied with the additional paper book in CA No. 127'of 2003, which is reproduced below:

“নিলামকৃত RUKCHAI MONDKOL" ট্রলারটি বাংলাদেশ সরকারের অনুমতি ব্যতীত মতস্য ট্রলার হিসাবে রেজিষ্টেশন করা হইবে রা এবং ইহা দ্বারা কোন অবস্থাতেই বাংলাদেশ মতস্য শিকার করা যাইবে না। এই মর্মে দরপএ দাতাকে দরপত্রের সহিত ১৫০৯একশত পঞ্চাশ) টাকা মূল্যের নন-জুডিশিয়াল ষ্ট্যাম্পে অঙ্গীকারনামা প্রদান করিতে হইবে। তবে আটককৃত ট্রলার প্রতিস্থাপনে অনুমতি প্রাপ্ত কোন কোম্পানী নিলাম মাধ্যমে ক্রয় করিতে পারিলে স্ক্যাপের পরিবর্থে উহা প্রতিস্থাপিত ট্রলার হিসাবে ব্যবহার করিতে পারিবে।

44. In respect of other trawlers, the writ petitioners in their additional paper books have accompanied with the copies of tender notices and in clause 8 there are stipulations that the purchasers could not claim licence for fishing in deep sea and that they were required to give undertakings in that regard. The said clause reads thus:

“নিলামকৃত গবেষণা জাহাজটি মতস্য ট্র্রলার হিসাবে ব্যবহার করা যাইবে না এবং গ্রহীতা কর্তৃক ভবিষ্যতে কোন অবস্থাতেই মতস্য ট্রলার হিসাবে লাইসেন্স প্রদানের জন্য আবেদন করিতে পারিবেনা। এই মর্মে দরপএ দাতাকে দরপত্রের সহিত ৩০০(তিনশত) টাকা মূল্যের নন-জুডিসিয়াল ষ্টাম্পে অঙ্গীকারনামা প্রদান করিতে হইবে। (অঙ্গীকারনামার নমুনা সংযোজনী-গ)

45. In the majority opinion my learned brother observed 'It is not the case of writ respondents that the fishing trawlers sold in the auction could be used for any other purpose and definitely the writ petitioners did not purchase those for using them as fire wood or as scrap'. With due respect, my learned brother failed to notice that the dispute was not for issuing licence to the trawlers for fishing, the real dispute was whether the trawlers could be given licence for fishing in the deep sea. Section 13 of the Ordinance prescribes the limitation for using the licence wherein it is provided 'licence shall be valid only with respect to the species of fish and the type of fishing year or the method of fishing or the location specified in the licence'. This provision and section 16(2)(a), which provides 'the areas within which, and the period during which, fishing is authorized' are read conjointly there cannot be any doubt that the owner of a vessel or trawler cannot claim any licence as of right for fishing in deep sea only because he has purchased it from the authority. It is a discretionary power of the authority to issue such licence subject to fulfillment of certain conditions in specified location and area. What's more, after purchase of the trawlers, the writ petitioners undertook as per terms of the tender forms not to use the trawlers for fishing, a copy of such undertakings in respect of 'FV RUKCHAI MONDKOL' has been included in the additional paper book in CA No. 128 of 2008, which runs as follows:

“এই মর্মে অঙ্গীকার করিতেছি যে নিলামকৃত ট্রলার FV RUKCHAI MONDKOL ট্রলারটি প্রাপ্ত হইলে বাংলাদেশ সরকারের অনুমতি ব্রতিত মতস্য ট্রলার হিসাবে ব্যবহার করিব ন।।

46. This is an unconditional promise in writing by the purchaser to the vendor by giving undertaking that he would not use the trawler in question without prior approval of the Government. The expression 'undertake' means to agree; to promise; to accept an obligation to do or perform. He retains no right for claiming a licence and left the matter of granting or permitting licence for fishing with the discretion of the authority. An undertaking is a promise, pledge or engagement which, necessarily infers anything undertaken. Section 2(d) of the Contract Act states that when at the desire of the promisor, the promisee or any other person has done or abstained from doing, or does or abstains from doing, or promises to do or to abstain from doing something, such act or abstinence or promise is called consideration for the promise. According to Salmond's Law of Contracts, Second Edition, the presence of a promise as to something to be done in the future is an essential mark of a contract, but is no part of a conveyance, surrender or grant. Promise is here used in a broad sense to cover both an undertaking by the obligor to do or refrain from doing something; and an undertaking by him that a certain state of facts exists or that someone else will do something.

47. These tender documents clearly stipulated that the auction purchasers would in no way claim for issuing licence for fishing with the trawlers. The vendor on being satisfied with the promises sold and delivered possession of the trawlers. That being the admitted position, the writ-petitioners had waived their right of claiming registration trawlers and issuance of licence for fishing in the deep sea with these trawlers. It is observed by Lord Russell of Killowen in Dawson's Bank Limited vs Nippon Menkwa Kabushiki Kaisa, 62 IA 100, "waiver is contractual, and may constitute a cause of action; it is an agreement to release or not to assert a right". A right created by a contract may be waived either expressly or impliedly. True, a plea of waiver has to be pleaded and proved. But the learned counsel in his written argument having admitted that the writ petitioners gave undertakings that 'the trawlers could be used in fishing with the permission of the Government', it being an admitted fact need not be proved. Waiver means abandonment of a right and it may either be express or implied from conduct but its basic requirement is that it must be 'an intentional act with knowledge'. It signifies nothing more than an intention not to insist upon the right. It cannot be said that the writ petitioners or their vendors did not give the undertakings voluntarily. By these undertakings, they left the matter of granting licence at the discretion of the authority. A right on the basis of a contract can be claimed only, where it is agreed between the parties that the right created by contract shall be given up and the other side, as a result thereof, alters his position.

48. These undertakings may also operate as admissions, that is to say, a statement, which suggests any inference as to any fact in issue or relevant fact, and may be evidence, though not conclusive, against the party who has made it. Therefore, apart from the statements of law discussed above, if the principle of promissory estoppel is taken into consideration, it is the writ-petitioners who are estopped from claiming licence or registration of the fishing trawlers on this principle. What's more, this doctrine is in no way applicable against the Government or any of the writ-respondents in its governmental, public or sovereign capacity to the same extent as an individual or a private corporation as argued by Mr M Amirul Islam.

<u>49. To sum up, the doctrine of promissory estoppel cannot be invoked for presenting the government or its agency or any statutory authority for preventing them from discharging its function under the law. If any agency acts outside the scope of its authority the plea is not available. It can only be applied against the state or statute where it is necessary to prevent fraud. But there must be sufficient pleading and foundation for the plea. The rule is that the government cannot divest itself the right incidental to its office by conduct. If a public authority repudiates or departs from terms of a contract in order to exercise its overriding discretionary power, the undertaking would improperly fetter its general discretionary power. The doctrine cannot be allowed to impede the power of public function by public authority.</u>

<u>50. Now turning to the point of legitimate expectation, a doctrine which is akin to that of a promissory estoppel. Under this doctrine if a person can show that he has been left with taking certain action on the basis of or on the legitimate expectation that the Government would abide by such policy or guideline. The concept of legitimate expectation can be traced back to European Community Law. According to the doctrine, where a person is the victim of an unfavourable decision taken by a public authority, this may amount to an infringement of that person's legitimate expectation where, for example, the decision contradicts an earlier promise or course of conduct on the part of the public authority concerned.</u>

51. The High Court Division did not direct the writ respondent No. 1 to grant registration and issue licence in respect of the trawlers on the doctrine of legitimate expectation. It is at the appellate stage before this Division Mr M Amirul Islam has raised this point vigorously. It is contended that legitimate expectation is a corollary to the principle of promissory estoppel and may be used as a composite concept. The doctrine of legitimate expectation is a promise made in the shape of a statement of policy or a procedure adopted by the administrative authority which may give rise to legitimate expectation, the learned counsel argued. According to the learned counsel, the writ-petitioners can legitimately expect that upon fulfillment of sections 17 and 18 of the Ordinance, they will be given licence but the Government delayed the process in violation of the doctrine of legitimate expectation. Legitimate expectation gives the person seeking judicial review sufficient locus-standi but the doctrine does not give scope to claim relief straightway from the administrative authorities as no crystallize as such is involved. Such expectation does not require the fulfillment of the expectation where an overriding public interest requires otherwise. Even if substantive protection of such expectation is contemplated that does not grant an absolute right to a particular person. It simply ensures the circumstances in which that expectation may be denied or restricted.

The executive function is harder to define, but includes actions taken for the maintenance of order, is the implementation of law, for the defence of the state, in the conduct of external affairs and in the administration of internal policies. 78. The oracle who is always consulted and cited on this subject is the celebrate Montesquieu. If he be not the author of this invaluable precept In the science of politics, he has the merit at least of displaying and recommending it most effectually to the attention of mankind. The doctrine of separation of powers was first formulated in England. After 1650, it was part of the general currency of political thought, but it was only one of a number of stands which had to be interwoven into the texture of the changing Constitution. It is there that the doctrine of separation of powers is propounded, although Montesquieu himself does not use that term he begins with the classification of the functions of Government. "In every Government there are three sorts of power; the legislative, the executive in respect of the matters involved in the law of nations, and the executive in respect of domestic law". The third stage of Montesquieu's argument may be expressed as being that "the agencies should perform their respective functions of Government separately". That is certainly the essence of the doctrine. It is tolerably clear that he advocates, at the minimum, that one agency of Government should not be performing the function appropriate to another. Montesquieu gave support to the notion of there being 'checks and balances' by which the branches of Government might legitimately influence or even impose certain limits on each others.

79. "There can be no liberty where the legislative and executive powers are united in the same person, or body of magistrates," Or, "if the power of judging be not separated from the legislative and executive powers," Montesquieu said. He did not mean that these departments sought to have no partial agency in, or no control over, the acts of each other. His meaning, as his own words import, and still more conclusively as illustrated by the example in his eyes, can amount to no more than this, that where the whole power of one department is exercised by the same hands which possess the whole power of another department, the fundamental principles of a free constitution are subverted. This would have been the case in the Constitution examined by him if the king, who is sole executive magistrate, had possessed also the complete legislative power, or the supreme administration of justice; or if the entire legislative body had possessed the supreme judiciary, or the supreme executive authority.

The doctrine of separation of power was put for work as a prescription ought to be done for the promotion of certain value and the question of its validity is a question of political theory.

In the Federalist Papers in Chapter 'THE PARTICULAR STRUCTURE OF NEW GOVERNMENT AND THE DISTRIBUTION OF POWER AMONG ITS DIFFERENT PARTS' Madison stated "No political truth is certainly of greater intrinsic value, or is stamped with the authority of more enlightened patrons of liberty than that on which the objection is founded. The accumulation of all powers, legislative, executive, and judiciary, in the same hands, whether of one, a few, or many, and whether hereditary, self appointed, or elective, may justly be pronounced the very definition of tyranny. Were the federal Constitution, therefore, really chargeable with this accumulation of power, or with a mixture of powers, having a dangerous tendency to such an accumulation, no further arguments would be necessary to inspire a universal reprobation of the system. I persuade myself, however, that it will be made apparent to everyone that the charge cannot be supported, and that the maxim on which it relies has been totally misconceived and misapplied. In order to form correct ideas on this important subject it will be proper to investigate the sense in which the preservation of liberty requires that the three great departments of power should be separate and distinct".

"This, however, is not among the vices of that Constitution. The Magistrate in whom the whole executive power resides cannot of himself make a law, though he can put a negative on every law; nor administer justice in person, though he has the appointment of those who do administer it. The judges can exercise no executive prerogative, though they are shoots from the executive stock; nor any legislative function, though they may be advised by the legislative councils. The entire legislature can perform no judiciary act, though by the joint act of two of its branches the judges may be removed from their offices, and though one of its branches is possessed of the judicial power in the last resort. The entire legislature, again, can exercise no executive prerogative, though one of its branches constitutes the supreme executive magistracy, and another, on the impeachment of a third, can try and condemn all the subordinate officers in the executive department".

82. In an article 'Judicial Activism versus Judicial Restraint' published in SPAN Magazine, May Edition, 1997, written by AG Noorani, it is observed 'Zeal leads Judges to enter areas with whose terrain they are not familiar; to order minutiae of administration Without reckoning with the consequences of their orders. Judges have made orders not only how to run prisons but also hospitals, mental homes and schools to a degree which stuns the professional. In their judgments they draw on material which is untested and controversial and which they are ill equipped to value. A constitutional Bench constituting seven members in P Ramchandra Ro vs State of Karnataka, (2002) 4 SCC 578 approved the opinion of Prof SP Sathe in his work in 2002 'Judicial Activism in India-Transgressing Borders and Enforcing Limits, touches the topic 'Directions: A New Form of Judicial Legislation'. While speaking on judicial activism, Prof Sathe cautioned against Court 'legislating' exactly in the way a legislature legislates. The Court has taken over the legislative function not in the traditional interstitial sense but in an overt manner and has justified it as being an essential component of its role as a constitutional Court the author observed. "In a strict sense these are instances of judicial excessivism that fly in the face of the doctrine of separation of powers These were not legitimate exercise of judicial power".

83. In common cause (2008 ) 5 SCC 511, on the point of judicial excessivism Markandey Katju, J argued 'while expansion of the meanings of statutory or constitutional provisions by judicial interpretation is a legitimate judicial function, the making of a new law which the Courts in this country have sometimes done, is not a legitimate judicial function. The Courts of the country have sometimes clearly crossed the limits of the judicial function and have taken over functions which really belong either to the legislature or to the executive. This is unconstitutional. If there is a law, Judges can certainly enforce it. But Judges cannot create a law by judicial verdict and seek to enforce it".

84. While speaking on judicial excessive, the Supreme Court of India in Divisional Manager, Golf Club vs Chander Hass (2008) 1 SCC 683 observed "recently, the courts have apparently, if not clearly, strayed into the executive domain or in matters of policy. For instance, the orders passed by the High Court of Delhi in recent times dealt with subjects ranging from age and other criteria for nursery admissions, unauthorised schools, criteria for free seats in schools, supply of drinking water in schools, number of free beds in hospitals on public land, use and misuse of ambulances, requirements for establishing a world class burns ward in the hospital, the kind of air Delhiites breathe, begging in public, the use of subways, the nature of buses we board, the legality of constructions in Delhi, identifying the buildings to be demolished, the size of speed-breakers on Delhi roads, auto rickshaw overcharging, growing frequency of road accidents and enhancing of road fines, etc. In our opinion these were matters pertaining exclusively to the executive or legislative domain. If there is a law, judges can certainly enforce it, but judges cannot create a law and seek to enforce it".

85. In Dennis vs United States, 341 US 494-592, Frankfurter, J observed:

"Courts are not representative bodies. They are not designed to be a good reflex of a democratic society. Their judgment is best informed, and therefore, most dependable, within narrow limits. Their essential quality is detachment, founded on independence. History teaches that the independence of judiciary is jeopardized when Courts become embroiled in the passions of the day and assume primary responsibility in choosing between competing political, economic and social pressure".

86. In common cause (2008) 5 SCC 511, Markandey Katju, J. argued "Moreover, if once the courts take upon themselves the task of issuing ukases as to how administrative agencies should function, what is there to prevent them from issuing directions as to how the State Government or the Central Government should administer the State and run the country? In our opinion such an approach would not only disturb the delicate balance of powers between the three wings of the State, it would also strike at the very basis of our democratic polity which postulates that the governance of the country should be carried on by the executive enjoying the confidence of the legislature which is answerable and accountable to the people at the time of elections. Such an approach would in our opinion result in judicial oligarchy dethroning democratic supremacy".

87. The doctrine of separation of power has been well defined in the American Constitution, such as, in Article I, Section I, it is provided 'all legislative powers shall be vested in a congress'. Article II, Section I says 'The executive powers shall be vested in a president and in Article III, Section 1, it is said the judicial powers shall be vested in the Supreme Court and in such inferior Courts as congress may from time to time ordain and establish'. Though in our constitution there is no such defined and express provision of the doctrine, nonetheless, a fine and delicate balance is envisaged under our Constitution among the three organs of the State, the Legislature the Executive and the judiciary. The conferment of judicial power has been under Articles 101, 102, 103, 104, 108, 110 and 111.

88. The Marine Fisheries Ordinance, 1983 and the rules framed there under deal with the grant of licence and registration of fishing trawlers which is a contained Code and in respect of the rights and liabilities created by the said Ordinance and the manner of enforcement must be sought within the Ordinance itself. This is a comprehensive enactment on the subject. Under the law the authorities have been assigned to perform their functions. They are equipped with the skills, expertise and resources to discharge the functions. The Courts are not equipped with the expertise to discharge the functions that belong to the other organ of the government. Courts institutional equipment is wholly inadequate for undertaking administrative or execution functions. The High Court Division should not substitute its own view for the view taken or discretion exercised by the specified authority under the Ordinance. However extensive the jurisdiction of the High Court Division may be it seems to me that the jurisdiction is not so wide or large as to enable it to convert itself into a Court of appeal by examining for itself the correctness of the decisions of the writ-respondents under the Ordinance.

89. Part-III of the Marine Fisheries Ordinance, 1983 contains "General Provisions Governing Licence". Section 8 empowers the Director appointed under section 4 of the Ordinance for issuing licence in respect of all Marine fishing in Bangladesh Fisheries Water. Section 12 provides that where any local fishing vessel ceases at any time to be a local fishing vessel, any licence issued to such fishing vessel shall cease to be valid forth with. This being the provision of law, Writ Petition Nos. 1282 of 2003 and 1515 of 2001 are apparently not maintainable in view of the admitted fact that the writ-petitioners are seeking a direction for the replacement/ substitution of the licence issued in favour of their old trawlers on the grounds that the whereabouts of those fishing vessels were not traceable. They could not claim for replacement of their missing fishing trawlers' licence to the new vessels they have purchased later on.

90. Section 16 provide that each licence shall be issued on attaching condition, such as; (a) the areas within which at the period during which fishing will be authorized; (b) the species, size, sex, age and quantities of fish that may be caught; (c) the method by which fish may be caught; (d) the types, size and amount of fishing there that may be used by the fishing vessel act Section 17 imposes restriction for issuing a licence in respect of a local fishing vessel unless it is registered. Section 18 provides, a local fishing vessel is not entitled to a licence unless it holds a valid certificate of inspection and that the certificate must be issued in respect of that vessel. Section 19 empowers the Director to refuse a licence in respect of a local fishing vessel if he is satisfied that for proper management, conservation and development of any particular fishery in accordance with any fisheries management conservation and development or in the interest of Marine Fisheries Industry to do so or the person applying for or holding the licence is unfit to hold a licence. These provisions confer a discretion upon the Director to restrict marine fishing operations which in their face might seem to be absolute. This conferment of power cannot be said to be arbitrary. This power has been given for conservation and development of fisheries. The discretion has been given to promote the purpose of the Ordinance. The High Court Division cannot arrogate to it the powers given to the Director of Marine Fisheries or to control the powers of the Director given in Parts III and IV of the Ordinance. The High Court Division also cannot trespass into the Field of the Director of Marine Fisheries.

91. In Vcerappa vs Raman and Raman Limited, AIR 1952 SC 192, Chandrasekhara Aiyar,J speaking for the Supreme Court as under:

"The Motor Vehicles Act is a statute which creates new rights and liabilities and prescribes an elaborate procedure for their regulation. No one is entitled to a permit as of right even if he satisfies all the prescribed conditions. The grant of a permit is entirely within the discretion of the transport authorities and naturally depends on several circumstances which have to be taken into account. The Regional Transport Authority and the Provincial Transport Authority are entrusted under section 42 with this power. They may be described as administrative bodies exercising quasi-judicial functions in the matter of the grant of permits. Under Rule 3 of the Madras Motor Vehicles Rules, the Regional Transport Authority is called the Road Traffic Board and the Provincial Transport Authority is called the Central Road Traffic Board. These bodies or authorities are constituted by the provincial Government."

92. All the fishing trawlers are very old which is evident from the representation made by the Managing Director of the writ-petition No.433 of 1998 to the Prime Minister dated 28th December, 1992, Annexure-B, wherein he stated, “প্রস্তাবিত FV Satellite-1 নামে একটি অচল এবং ধ্বংস থাই ট্রলার ক্রয় করে বিহত ৪/৫ মাসের অক্লান্ত পরিশ্রমে এটাকে মতস্য শিকার উপযোগী করে তুলেছি। Similar statements have been made in other applications for registration and issuing licence to the authority. In Dr Mahmudul Karim's report dated 28th May, 1997 it was recommended in paragraph 3.5 as

under:

“৬.৪/২.১৫ বছরের বেশী পুরানো এবং অদক্ষ ট্রলার বাতিলকরণঃ-মূল পুতিবেদন (ক) অত্যাধিক জ্বালাণী খরচ ও সমুদ্রে নিরাপত্তার কথা বিব্চেনা করে ১৫ বছরের বেশি পুরানো  ট্রলারগুলি আগামী ২ বছরের মধ্যে ক্রমান্বয়ে নতুন ট্রলার দিয়ে বদল করে ফেলার সুপারিশ জানান হয়েছিল। বাংলাদেশ মেরিন ফিশারিজ এসোসিয়েশনের অনুরোধ এ সুপারিশ বদল করে নিম্নরুপ দেওয়া হয়”

কোন ফিশিং ভেসেলৈর লাইফটাইম বা সমুদ্র গমনোপ যোগিতা বর্তমানে প্রচলিত বিধান মোতাবেক সমুদ্র পরিবহন অধিদপ্তরই(মেরিন মার্কেন্টাইল ডিপার্টমেন্ট) স্থির করবে।

অদক্ষ ট্রলার বাতিল করণের উপর মূল পুতিবেদনের ৬.৪.২(খ) নং সুপারিশ অপরিবর্তিত থাকেবে।”

93. The High Court Division over looked sections 12, 16, 17, 18 and 19 of the Ordinance and on a superficial consideration of Dr Mahmudul Karim's report, directed the writ-respondents to issue necessary registration and licence to the fishing trawlers without considering the consequences of such direction. In the impugned order, in Writ Petition No. 433 of 1998, it has been stated that for ascertaining the exploitation of Marine fishery and its development a committee headed by Dr Mahmudul Karim has been working and pending final assessment by the said committee, the Cabinet Division has decided not to grant any new licence to any fishing trawler until the Cabinet Division decides the number of trawlers to be allowed to explore in the deep-sea fishing. This statement proved that the decision was taken at the highest level of the Government.

<u>94. In judicial review of administrative actions, the Court has to start with the presumption of regularity of the official act and the burden of proof is on the person who alleges the contrary. Whenever a power is given by statute to an authority, whatever may be fairly regarded as incidental to or consequential upon things authorized by legislature should not be declared ultra vires (AG vs Great Eastern Rly Co (1880) 5 APP case 473). The Courts should not compel a public authority by issuing a writ of mandamus to perform an act which are within its domain. In Islamic Republic of Pakistan vs Muhammad Sneed, 13 DLR (SC) 94, Hamoodur Rahman, J argued after considering English and American decisions on the principle of the powers of the High Court to issue direction or order for any purpose to any person or authority including any Government in respect of writ of mandamus as under:</u>

<u>"So far as the writ of mandamus (which was the writ purported, to be issued in the present case) is concerned, the Courts in England or America never sought to compel by mandamus the performance of duties which were not involving the exercise of any discretion of judgment. They have never arrogated to themselves the authority to control legislative departments, in the exercise of their legislative powers, by mandamus. "The legislative", it is said, "cannot be compelled to pass an Act, even though the Constitution expressly commands it, nor be restrained from passing an act, even though the Constitution expressly prohibits it" (vide Ferris on The Law of Extraordinary Legal Remedies page 362). In this country too, the functions of Government are divided into the distinct branches-legislative, executive and judicial-each independent of the other whilst acting within its own sphere. For the harmonious working of such a system it is incumbent on each to know the limits of its own jurisdiction and not seek to trespass into the field of the other. The writ of mandamus cannot, therefore, issue for enforcing the performance of any and every kind of duty by Government or its officials. They might be so compelled only when they are under a legal obligation towards a subject to carry out specific Ministerial duties, in relation to that subject, clearly imposed upon them by law. The duty to make rules in exercise of statutory powers can hardly be conceived to fall within the ambit of such Ministerial duties as might be commanded to be performed by mandamus."</u>

95. The scope of judicial review of Government policy is now well defined. The Courts do not and cannot act as appellate authority examining the correctness, suitability and appropriateness of a policy. Nor are the Courts advise to the executive on matters of policy which the executive is entitled to formulate. The scope of judicial review when examining a policy of Government is to check whether it violates the fundamental rights of the citizens or is opposed to the provisions of the Constitution or opposed to any statutory provisions or is manifestly arbitrary. Courts cannot interfere with the policy either on the ground that it is erroneous or on the ground that a better, fairer or wiser alternative is available. Legality of policy, and not the wisdom or soundness of policy is the subject of judicial review. Reference in this connection is the case of Directorate of Film Festivals vs Gaurav Ashwin Jain, (2007) 4 SCC 737.

96. In considering several factors which give rise to such legitimate expectation must be present. The decision taken by the authority must be found to be arbitrary, unreasonable and not taken in public interest. If it is a question of policy, even by way of change of old policy, the courts cannot interfere with a decision. In a given case whether there are such facts and circumstances giving rise to a legitimate expectation, it would primarily be a question of fact. If these tests are satisfied and if the Court is satisfied that a case of legitimate expectation is made out then the next question would be whether failure to give an opportunity of hearing before the decision affecting such legitimate expectation is taken, has resulted in failure of justice and whether on that ground the decision should be quashed. If that be so then what should be the relief is again a matter which depends on several factors?

<u>97. An aggrieved person claiming denial of legitimate expectation on the plea of arbitrary or discriminatory or unfair or biased on gross abuse of power or violation of principles of natural justice, the same may be questioned on the well-known grounds attracting Article 27 of the Constitution. The question whether the expectation and the claim is reasonable or legitimate is a question of fact. It must be raised in the petition and unless a foundation is laid, it cannot be claimed or enforced as a substantive right. Legitimate expectation depends very much on the facts and recognized general principle of the administrative law applicable to such facts. Therefore, the concept of legitimate expectation is not the key which unlocks the treasury of natural justice and it ought not to unlock gates which the Court outweigh review on the merit. As regards the argument of Mr. Islam that as the writ petitioners are entitled to get licence under the provision of the Ordinance, they are denied equal protection of law under Article 27 of the Constitution, it is to be remembered, the tools in the hands of judiciary must be used with great circumspection and in exceptional cases. Article 27 should not be misused by the Courts to justify every kind of directive or to grant every kind of claim of a citizen.</u>

98. In the cases in hand, there is no representation either by words or by conduct intimating the writ petitioners that the Government or its officials consented to issue licence to them if they had repaired the trawlers after purchase for making them suitable for fishing in deep sea. Therefore, there is no scope for a Court of law to give a direction in the manner the High Court Division has directed to the writ respondents to follow.

<u>99. In some petitions the authority did not give any decision on the prayers of the writ-petitioners. The writ-respondents did not give any assurance to the writ-petitioners that they would be given licence, rather the writ-petitioners gave written undertakings to the effect that they would not claim any licence if the trawlers are sold to them. Therefore, there is no foundation at all in the writ petitions to claim registration and licence on the doctrine of promissory estoppel or legitimate expectation. There must be a promise or representation that may be made by the authority against whom such right is claimed. Where the legitimate expectation is not raised and no foundation was laid for such a plea being advanced, it could not be considered by a Court. They could not claim as of right the registration and the issuance of licence in respect of the fishing trawlers. Therefore, they have no locus-standi to maintain the writ petitions. The facts do not give rise to such legitimate expectation in these cases since they have no right to claim licence or registration of the fishing trawlers. It cannot be said that the authority did not give licence arbitrarily or unreasonably. Rather Dr Mahmudul Karim's report sufficiently suggested that some applications were rejected in the public interest for safety and security of the crews of the fishing trawlers.</u>

<u>100. Legitimate expectation could in a given case be Claimed where the Court is satisfied that the claimant has made out a case of legitimate expectation and the courts jurisdiction to interfere against the decision of the policy maker is very limited. Therefore, I find no substance in the contention of Mr M Amirul Islam. The writ-petitioners are not legally entitled to registration and licence in respect of the disputed fishing vessels on the doctrine of promissory estoppel or legitimate expectation. The direction of the High Court Division to issue necessary registration and licence to the trawlers, in the premises, is nothing more than sheer abuse of judicial process. I find merit in these appeals.</u>

101. These appeals are, therefore, allowed without any order as to costs.

The case of the writ petitioner-respondent in Civil Appeal No. 133 of 2005 arising out of Writ Petition No.4068 of 2000 is that he purchased his fishing trawler in the auction held by the Government, while case of the others is that they purchased their fishing trawlers from the auction purchasers in the auction held by the Government. 108. A Division Bench of the High Court Division hearing the writ petitions analogously by a common judgment and order dated 8-7-2003 made the Rules absolute in all writ petitions directing the "concerned authorities" to issue necessary registrations and licences to the trawlers in question belonging to the petitioners in accordance with law.

Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and order passed by the High Court Division, the writ-respondents, appellants herein filed leave petition Nos.1275- 1285 of 2003 and 1420 of 2003; leave was granted by this Division on 23-4-2005 to consider the submissions made by the learned Additional Attorney-General as follows:

110. Mr Mahbubey Alam, learned Attorney-General, appearing for the appellants, by referring to clause 8 of the Nilam Dar Patra Dalil, in respect of the trawler, RUKCHAI MONDKOI, incorporated in the additional paper book, filed in Civil Appeal No. 128 of 2005, submitted that in all Darpatras for holding auction of the seized Thai trawlers, similar clause was incorporated wherein it was clearly stated that without the permission of the Government of Bangladesh, the respective trawler sold in the auction, would not be registered as fishing trawler and in no circumstances, fishing could be done in Bangladesh by such trawlers without permission of the Government and the respective auction purchaser had filed an Angikarnama in Taka 150 non-judicial stamp to the above effect. In this regard, he referred to the Angikarnama in respect of the said fishing trawler like others which reads as follows:

“এই মর্মে অঙ্গিকার করিতেছি যে নিলামকৃত ট্রলার FV RUKCHAI MONDKOI ট্যলারটি প্রাপ্ত হইলে বাংলাদেশ সরকারের অনুমতি ব্যতীত মতস্য ট্রলার হিসাবে ব্যবহার করিব ন।”

And since the respective auction purchaser participated in the tender for purchasing the fishing trawlers in question accepting the said condition of auction, the writ-petitioners could not claim to have licences for fishing in the deep sea as a matter of right.

111. The learned Attorney-General by referring to sections 18 and 19 of the Marine Fisheries Ordinance, 1983(the Ordinance, 1983) further submitted that the Director of Marine Fisheries was not bound to issue licence in respect of a local fishing vessel, so no illegality was committed by the writ-respondents in refusing to give licences to the fishing trawlers of the writ-petitioners, but the learned Judges of the High Court Division failed to consider the said provisions of law while making the Rules absolute. The learned Attorney-General further submitted that the High Court Division fell into an error in making the Rules absolute on the principle of legitimate expectation and promissory estoppel inasmuch as the writ-respondents neither by their conduct nor by any correspondence made any promises to the writ-petitioners to give licences for fishing in the deep sea to their trawlers purchased in auction. He further submitted that the Government or the legislature has power to evolve new policy in public interest which includes its power to withdraw the old policy and the Court cannot bind the Government and the legislature to stick to its old/previous policy by invoking the doctrine of 'legitimate expectation' as has been done in the instant case unless the change in policy is vitiated by illegality, irrationality, procedural impropriety, malafide and abuse of power, which must be pleaded and proved to the satisfaction of the Court and in the instant cases, the petitioners failed to plead and prove any such case.
