118. In the context, let us see whether the High Court Division was correct in giving direction upon the writ-respondents, appellants herein, to issue necessary registration and licence to the respective trawler of the respective writ-petitioner.

119. From the judgment of the High Court Division, it appears that the learned Judges made the Rules absolute on two grounds; (i) on legitimate expectation and (ii) on the principle of promissory estoppel. Although, in the concluding portion of the judgment, the learned Judges gave stress on "the principle of promissory estoppel", before that they observed that: "After careful scrutiny and examination of the statements made in the writ petitions and documents annexed thereto, we find that the submissions made by the learned Advocate for the petitioners have a good deal of force,"

120. Mr. Khandaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed who appeared for the writ-petitioners before the High Court Division made categorical submission that:

"Since the petitioners were allowed to purchase their trawlers from the Government in auction sale with full knowledge that these were purchased by the petitioners for using them in deep sea fishing and since the petitioners by completing necessary repairing works have kept the trawlers fit for deep sea fishing and have maintaining (sic) them at a huge expenses they have legitimate expectation that the required registration and license will be issued to them in due course. But the respondents have failed to leave up to the said expectation in failing to grant registration and license and have thus acted illegally and without jurisdiction. Hence, the respondents are under legal obligation to issue registration and license and other allied certificate for the purpose of enabling the petitioners to use their respective trawlers in deep sea fishing without any further delay."

The High Court Division further observed that:

"In these cases, the Government having forfeited the Thai deep-sea fishing trawlers for illegal poaching in the Bangladesh territorial waters sold them to the petitioners. The sale of the trawlers under consideration to the petitioners by the Government knowing that those trawlers could only be used for deep sea fishing should be construed as promise by the Government to issue necessary registration and license to these trawlers if applied for and were fit for deep sea fishing."

The High Court Division also relied upon the expert report dated 20-5-1997 (the correct date is 9-12-1997) wherein it was clearly recommended that the Government could increase the number of deep sea fishing trawlers by about 20 in number to the existing 55 trawlers already in the field.

121. The phrase 'legitimate expectation' originated from English Law and it was first coined by Lord Denning in the case of Schmidt vs Secretary of State for Home Affairs (1969) 2Ch 149. In the said case, the moot question for decision was whether the Home Secretary ought to have given a hearing to the foreign alien students before refusing their prayer for extension of their stay in the United Kingdom. Lord Denning by referring to the decision of the House of Lord in the case of Ridge vs Baldwin (1964) AC 40 held:  an administrative body may, in a proper case, be bound to give a person who is affected by their decision an opportunity of making representations. It all depends on whether he has some right or interest, or I would add, some legitimate expectation, of which it would not be fair to deprive him without hearing what he has to say."

122. At that time 'legitimate expectation' was limited to a legal right which was contravened. Lord Denning himself explained the legal position prevalent at that time by referring to foreign alien students in the following language:

"He has no right to enter this country except by leave; and, if he is given leave to come for a limited period, he has no right to stay for a day longer than the permitted time. If his permit is revoked before the time limit expires, he ought, I think, to be given an opportunity of making representations: for he should have a legitimate expectation of being allowed to stay for the permitted time. Except in such a case, a foreign alien has no right-and, I would add, no legitimate expectation-of being allowed to stay. He can be refused without reasons given and without a hearing."

<u>123. The ratio decidendi of this case, as explained by Lord Denning was that 'legitimate expectation' of a person can only be enforced if he has got a legal right, otherwise not. By the passage of time, there has been a sea of change in the concept and now, it has assumed the character of a recognized legal principle known as the 'doctrine of legitimate expectation.' We do not consider it necessary to give the gradual history of the 'doctrine of legitimate expectation' as it stands today in the legal arena, as that would make this judgment a voluminous one. As, by now, the 'doctrine of legitimate expectation' has been accepted as a part of substantive law in our jurisdiction as well as in the jurisdiction of other countries, it has the genesis in the field of Administrative law, a branch of public law and it remains in vogue where unreasonable decisions of the executive and their actions are challenged in a Court of law, particularly invoking the power of a judicial review. In a proceeding for judicial review, it applies the principle of fairness and reasonableness to the situation where a person has an expectation or interest in a public body. 'Legitimate expectation' is a new category of fairness. It is based on right, it is grounded in the rule of law, as requiring regularity, predictability and certainty in the Government's and statutory authority's dealings with the public; the 'doctrine of legitimate expectation' operates both in procedural and substantive matter. Where a public authority represents that it will act in a particular way, that representation may give rise to a legitimate expectation on the part of the represent that the public authority will so act, and the public authority may have to give effect to that expectation. Such legitimate expectations are commonly divided into two, procedural legitimate expectations where the expectation is of a procedural benefit such as notice or consultation before any change of tack on the part of the public authority, and substantive legitimate expectations, where the expectation is that the public authority will act in accordance with its representation as matter of substance. The application and the boundaries of the doctrine are still being explored. It is indicative of this ongoing exploration of the scope of the doctrine that the Courts have repeatedly found it necessary to re-visit it in order to find the path further up. It is also uncontroversial that the Courts will only give effect to legitimate expectation within the statutory context in which it has arisen and any expectation must yield to the terms of the statute under which the decision maker acts. Accordingly, where a public authority makes a representation that it has no power to honour or which would lead to a conflict with its statutory duty, absent a human rights element that representation will not generate an enforceable legitimate expectation, and if there is a change policy or the position is altered in public interest by a rule or by a legislation, no question of legitimate expectation would arise. Therefore, the person, who wants to invoke the power of judicial review of any administrative action of any public authority on the basis of legitimate expectation, must show that the claim is based on clear, unambiguous and reasonable representation and that the representations have been indeed by the decision maker and the representation must be one that it was competent for the decision maker to make without which reliance cannot be legitimated and the person who comes to Court for enforcement of a right arising out of legitimate expectation must establish that he had reasonable expectation in getting the things done by the concerned authority. The principle requires a substantive expectation on the part of the petitioner that he was entitled to get the reliefs for which he approached the Court. Along with this, we are also to remember that public authorities or statutory authorities always try to resile from 'legitimate expectation' of a party to fit in their own discretion.</u>

124. Keeping in view the above exposition of the doctrine of legitimate expectation' let us see whether the petitioners could make out any case of legitimate expectation for getting registrations and licences of their trawlers purchased in auction sale conducted by the Government functionaries, namely, the Directorate of Fisheries and whether the writ-respondents were justified in refusing not to issue licences for deep sea fishing to the petitioners' trawlers or in other words whether the writ-respondents could resile from the petitioners' legitimate expectation of getting registrations and licences in respect of their trawlers as directed by the High Court Division.

125. Admittedly, the writ-respondent-appellants did not file any affidavit-in-opposition in any of the writ petitions either controverting the case of the writ-petitioners as made out in the writ petitions or stating their own version on the claim of the writ-petitioners. In view of the above, we have tried to see the case of the writ-respondent-appellants from the civil petition for leave to appeal as well as from the concise statement filed before this Division, but we did not find any case of the writ-respondents. Although in the leave granting order, it appears that the learned Additional Attorney-General while making submissions referred to page-39 of the additional paper book filed in Leave Petition No. 1275 of 2005 (CA Appeal No. 127 of 2005) to point out that the Director of Sea Fisheries Department, Agrabad, Chittagong in his communication dated 22-9-2003 made it clear that the trawler was allowed to fish for two weeks at a time subject to various conditions and there was no stipulation that the trawler would be permitted to fish at its free will and that the High Court Division failed to appreciate that since Pakistan period, the exclusive economic territory for Marine Fisheries was utilised and after liberation some individual brought technology from abroad and the Government declared Marine sector as an industry, but the resources of the country being limited as per joint venture survey report made by Russia and Japan, the Government adopted some policies with regard to culturing, hatching (in the leave granting order it has wrongly been written as hedgering) and catching fishes within 200 nautical miles; that the High Court Division failed to consider that at a subsequent stage, a high powered technical committee of experts named as "Zaman Committee" was formed and its survey report was found to be in harmony with the survey report of the donors stating that without further survey number of trawlers except the existing 73 should not be increased, otherwise, it would create adverse effect on the Marine resources of the country and that the Government decided to increase the licences of fishing trawlers by another 40 for granting licences in 4 categories inviting by advertisement through paper on fulfillment of certain requirements, but the petitioners did not comply with such requirements, i.e. the body of the trawler must be steel body and the applicant must have bank solvency certificate to show that he/it was capable of spending taka 5 (five) crore for each trawler, but these facts have not been stated either in the leave petition or in the concise statement. To be precise, we are constrained to say that in the leave petition as well as in the concise statement, no fact whatsoever, on behalf of the writ-respondent-appellants has been stated. Therefore, the case of the writ-petitioner-respondents as stated in the writ petitions, particularly the fact that the trawlers of the petitioners are fishing trawlers which were seized by the Government of Bangladesh while they were fishing illegally within the Bangladesh territorial waters and subsequently those were sold in auction conducted by the concerned Government functionaries and were purchased by the petitioners with the expectation that those will be used for deep sea fishing and after purchase, the petitioners made necessary repair works and made all of them ready and fit for being used as fishing trawlers in the deep sea by spending huge amount of money and a technical committee formed by the authority to enquire as to the fitness of the trawlers of some of the petitioners found them fit for deep sea fishing and in other cases, fitness certificates were issued by the Mercantile Marine Department and Naval Architecture and Marine Engineer after due inspection of the trawlers and also, on their application, temporary fishing licences were given to some of them for fishing in the deep sea remained uncontroverted before the High Court Division as well as before this Division. It is true that the writ- petitioners have to succeed of their own, even the writ-respondents do not controvert their case, but when in the writ petitions, a positive case of 'legitimate expectation' was asserted and in support of the case, documents were annexed thereto, in the absence of any denial of the assertions of the writ-petitioner's case as well as the annexure annexed to the petitions, their case cannot altogether be rejected or ignored. In this regard, it is necessary to state that as regards the pleading of the parties in a writ petition, the principles of Order VI of the Code of the Civil Procedure will be applicable both in respect of writ petition as well as the affidavit-in-opposition; while in case of suits, the plaint and the written statement should contain only facts and not evidence, in the writ petition and in the affidavit-in-opposition not only facts, but also the evidence in proof of the facts stated therein need be pleaded and annexed. Facts stated in the writ petition are to be controverted by filing an affidavit-in-opposition and if any statement made in the writ petition is not controverted in the affidavit-in-opposition, the Court is to proceed as if such statements have been admitted by the respondent(s), similarly if facts asserted in the affidavit-in-opposition are not controverted by filing an affidavit-in-reply shall be deemed to have been admitted and therefore, the writ-respondents were required to state necessary facts in denial of the case of the writ-petitioners by filing affidavit-in-opposition before the High Court Division and at least in the concise statement. We like to observe further that the writ-respondents be it the Government and the other Government functionaries or a private individual cannot be allowed to argue or make submissions on fact unless they plead such fact by filing affidavit-in-opposition or in the concise statement.

126. In view of the admitted fact that the writ-respondents did not deny the assertions of the respective writ-petitioner made in the respective writ petition by filing affidavit-in-opposition as pointed out hereinbefore and also did not give any version of their own, we do not consider it necessary to examine each and every annexure annexed to the respective writ petition to see whether the respective writ-petitioner could make out a case of 'legitimate expectation' as found by the High Court Division and as argued by Mr. M Amir-ul Islam.

127. However, on perusal of the annexure of the respective writ petition, it appears that the respective writ-petitioner annexed the papers showing that the trawlers in respect of which they prayed for issuing registrations and licences for catching fish in the deep sea were Thai fishing trawlers and those were seized by the Government of Bangladesh when they were fishing illegally within the Bangladesh territorial waters and later on, were sold in open auction and were purchased by the respective writ-petitioner. In the respective writ petition, it has been categorically stated that the respective petitioner purchased the respective trawler sold in auction with the sole purpose and expectation to use that for fishing in deep sea. From the annexure annexed to the respective writ petition, it is apparent that. all trawlers were fishing trawlers and in the auction notice/Nilam Darpatra, as well it was clearly mentioned that the trawlers to be sold in auction were fishing trawlers. The Nilam Darpatra incorporated in the additional paper book filed in Civil Appeal No. 128 of 2005 very much relied upon by the learned Attorney-General also shows that the only embargo put against the auction sold trawlers was that those could not be registered as fishing trawlers and go for fishing without the permission of the Government of Bangladesh. Clause 8 of the Darpatra (only one Darpatra was filed as an example) further shows that an Angikamama was required to be filed on a 150 taka stamp to the said effect which was duly filed by the auction purchaser. And in the Angikarnama, it was stated as under:

“অঙ্গিকার করিতেছি যে নিলামকৃত ট্রলার FV RUKCHAI MONDKOL ট্রলারটি প্রাপ্ত হইলে বাংলাদেশ সরকারের অনুমতি ব্যতীত মতস্য ট্রলার হিসাবে ব্যবহার করিব না।”

128. It is not the case of the writ-respondents that the fishing trawlers sold in the auction could be used for any other purpose and definitely the writ-petitioners did not purchase those for using them as fire wood or as scrap. It is the writ-petitioners' case that they had repeatedly been asking the writ-respondents to give registrations and licences to their trawlers to go for deep see fishing and in support of their said case they have annexed their applications to the writ petitions. Moreso, when the writ-petitioners specifically asserted in the writ petitions that they being engaged in deep sea fishing, purchased the respective trawler in the auction conducted by the Government functionaries with the legitimate expectation to use them for deep sea fishing which was not denied by the writ-respondents, their said case has to be accepted. It is also very pertinent to state that the auction of each fishing trawler was done by the Directorate of Fisheries under the Ministry of the Government of Bangladesh. In one of the letters addressed to the auction purchaser issued by the customs authority (annexure-'A' to writ petition No. 433 of 1998 giving rise to CA No. 128 of 2005) asking it to take delivery of the same, it was clearly stated that the trawler could be used for fishing.

129. The learned Attorney-General by referring to the notification ( amfa) dated 19-4-2003 issued by the Director General, Fisheries Directorate which was published in "The Daily Protham Alo" dated 25-4-2003 (the notifications have been incorporated in the additional paper book filed in Civil Appeal No. 128 of 2005) by which applications were invited from Bangladeshi entrepreneurs for giving licences to 40 trawlers fitted with modern technology for fishing in deep sea on certain specified terms and conditions, two of the terms being "

“আবেদনকারীকে অবশ্যই আবেদনের সাথে প্রতিটি ট্রলারের জন্য ন্যূনপক্ষে ৫(পাচ) কোটি টাকা ব্যয় করিতে সক্ষম এই মর্মে কোন প্রতিষ্টিত ব্যাংক হতে ব্যাংক সলভেন্সী সাটিফিকেট দাখিল করিতে হইবে।

৬। আধুনিক প্রযুক্তির ষ্টীল বডির ট্রলার সংগ্রহ করিতে হইবে।”

submitted with all his force that it was a policy decision of the Government that only steel body trawlers with modern fittings would be allowed to go for deep-sea fishing, whereas the petitioners' trawlers are wooden body, so the 'doctrine of legitimate expectation' could not be applied to undo the said policy decision of the Government. But the High Court Division interfered with the said policy decision of the government by giving direction upon the writ respondent-appellants to give registrations and licences to the petitioners' trawlers in exercising the power of judicial review. The learned Attorney-General also submitted that the writ-petitioners involved in these 12 (twelve) appeals did not, at all, apply for giving them licences pursuant to the said notification and thus, did not avail the chance of getting licences for their trawlers for deep sea fishing. Therefore, they were not entitled to get any relief from the writ Court, the High Court Division erred in law in giving direction to the writ-respondents to give registrations and licences to the petitioners' trawlers. In support of his submission, the learned Attorney-General relied very much upon the cases of PTR Export (Madras) (P) Ltd vs Union of India, All India Ex-Emergency Commission Offices and short Commissioned officers welfare Association vs Union of India, Asif Hamded vs State of J&K, North South Property Development Ltd vs Ministry of Land, Chairman, BTTMC vs Nasir Ahmed, AR Shams-ud-Doha vs Bangladesh, Attorney-General vs Py A: Quaries, Brahmanbaria Pourashava vs Ministry of Land and Madras City Wine Merchants' Association vs State of TN (supra).

130. The notification as referred to by the learned Attorney-General was issued by the Director General of the Fisheries Directorate. The preamble of the notification reads as follows:

“বিজ্ঞপ্তি

বঙ্গোপসাগরে বাংলাদেশের একান্ত অর্থনৈতিক এলাকায় গভীর সমুদ্রে বিভিন্ন স্তরে বিভিন্ন পদ্ধতিতে মতস্য আহরণের নিমিত্তে নিস্নোক্ত ছক অনুযায়ী আধুনিক প্রযুক্তি সম্পন্ন ট্রলারের ফিশিং লাইসেন্স প্রদানের জন্য বাংলাদেশী উতসাহী উদোক্তাদের নিকট হইতে এত দ্বারা দরখাস্ত আহবান করা যাইতেছে।

131. Then in the body of the notification, the nature, the number and the conditions for filing application for licence of the trawler have been mentioned. A mere reading of the preamble of the notification shows that this had no reference of any policy decision of the Government. It was just a decision of the Director General, Fisheries Directorate. So naturally, a question arises whether the decision of the Director General could be termed to be a policy decision of the Government and what the status of this notification is. In other words, could the notification made by the Director General of the Fisheries Directoratd be said to be a policy decision of the government? The problem will be solved if we see the provisions of the Ordinance, 1983. Part II of the Ordinance, 1983 has dealt with "Administration". Section 7 of the Ordinance reads as follows:

"7. Having regard to the requirement of fisheries management and development plans, the Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, specify types, classes and number of fishing vessels that can be deployed in the Bangladesh fisheries waters:

Provided that the Government may exempt fishing vessels already permitted to operate prior to the coming into force of this ordinance."

<u>132. A mere reading of section 7 shows that the legislature has empowered the Government to specify types, classes and number of fishing vessels that can be deployed in the Bangladesh fisheries waters, but that has to be done by way of publication of a notification in the official Gazette. The learned Attorney-General failed to produce any official Gazette notification showing that the Government took a policy decision or decided to give licence only to steel body fishing trawler/vessel and not to any wooden body fishing trawler/vessel for fishing in the deep sea and that a person applying for such licence must file with his/its application a solvency certificate from any established bank that he/it was capable of spending taka 5 (five) crore for each trawler as stipulated in term Nos.4 and 6 of the said notification. Nowhere in the Ordinance, any power has been given to the Director General/Director to make any such notification. In this context, it is necessary to state that section 6 of the Ordinances, 1983 has dealt with delegation of power to the Director by the Government, all of its powers under the Ordinance or the Rules. The learned Attorney-General also failed to show that the delegation to exercise the powers as envisaged in section 9 of the Ordinance was delegated to the Director General of the Fisheries Directorate. Even assuming that the powers as envisaged in section 7 of the Ordinance were delegated to the Director General and if he, in exercise of such powers, took any policy decision to specify the types, classes and the number of fishing trawlers/vessels that can be deployed in the Bangladesh fisheries waters, that must be notified in the official gazette, but no such gazette notification has been produced by the learned Attorney-General. The notification, on which the learned Attorney-General relied, is just a paper signed by the Director General of the Fisheries Directorate and that too without any reference to the government's decision. We wondered how the learned Attorney-General could rely upon such a paper as a policy decision of the Government, The decisions relied upon by the learned Attorney-General as mentioned above for the legal proposition that in exercising the power of judicial review, the Court cannot interfere with the policy decision of the Government introduced by replacing the existing one/older one for public interest invoking the 'doctrine of legitimate expectation' have got no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of the cases in our hand. In the cases in our hand, we do not see any public interest in refusing the licences to the writ-petitioners' fishing trawlers for fishing in deep sea. In addition, as already found, there was no policy decision by the Government as to terms Nos.4 and 6 of the notification. More so, in the notification itself relied upon by the learned Attorney-General, there is nothing to show that clauses 4 and 6 therein were incorporated for public interest. It is noteworthy that when the writ petitions giving rise to these 12(twelve) appeals where Rules were issued calling upon the writ-respondent-appellants (including the Director General of fisheries) to show cause as to why they should not be directed to issue licences "to the respective trawler to the petitioners for catching fish in the deep sea" were pending before the High. Court Division, the Director General issued the said notification electing not to contest the Rule by filing affidavit-in-opposition. This shows the obstinate and defiant attitude of the Government functionaries to go with their own whims ignoring the proceedings pending in the apex Court. This move of the Director General of the 'Fisheries Directorate does not appear to us bona fide and as was resorted to thwart the result of the writ petitions. We deprecate this kind of attitude of the Government as well as its functionaries.</u>

133. Now, let us see the provisions of the two relevant laws, which have dealt with "fishing vessel" and the licence for such vessel, namely, the Ordinance, 1983 and the Bangladesh Merchant Shipping Ordinance, 1983.

134. Fishing vessel has been defined in section 2(f) of the Ordinance, 1983 as under: "fishing vessel" means any vessel used for fishing or for processing carriage or storage of fish, and includes any vessel used in support of, or ancillary to, fishing operations but does not include any vessel carrying fish as part of a general cargo unless that vessel is engaged in operations in support of, or ancillary to? fishing operation

" Fishing vessel has also been defined in clause (16) of section 2 of the Bangladesh Merchant Shipping Ordinance, 1983 as under:

"fishing vessel" means a vessel, of whatever size and by whatever means propelled, which is exclusively engaged in sea fishing for profit."

135. Besides the definition of "fishing vessel" given in clause (f) of section 2 of the Ordinance, 1983, in clauses (g) and (i) of the section, there are other definitions as well, namely: "foreign fishing vessel" and "Local fishing vessel" which are as under:

(g) "foreign fishing vessel" means any fishing vessel other than a local fishing vessel."

(i) "local fishing vessel" means any fishing vessel—

(i) wholly owned by one or more persons who are citizens of Bangladesh; or

(ii) wholly owned by any company, society or other association of persons established under the law of Bangladesh of which at least 51 per cent of the shares are held by citizens of Bangladesh and includes any fishing vessel registered in Bangladesh and operating under Bangladesh flag under joint venture or any other approved arrangements; or

(iii) wholly owned by the Government or by a statutory corporation established under a law of Bangladesh."

<u>136. From a reading of the definitions of fishing vessel (no separate definition of 'trawler' or 'fishing trawler' has been given in the two statutes) as quoted hereinbefore, it is apparent that trawlers used for fishing are "fishing vessel" and no distinction has been made by the legislature as to the wooden "fishing vessel" and "steel body fishing vessel". So the notification made by the Director General inviting applications for giving licence to steel body trawlers had/has no legal basis. Therefore, the submission of the learned Attorney-General that the Government changed its policy and decided to give licence to steel body trawler only in place of wooden body trawler is nothing but a myth and, as such, the same is not acceptable.</u>

137. Section 8 of the Ordinance, 1983 has .empowered the Director of the Fisheries for issuing licences in respect of all marine fishing in the Bangladesh Fisheries Waters; sections 17 and 18 of the Ordinance, 1983 have dealt with the provisions for granting licences to the local fishing vessels.

138. These sections read as follows:

"17. No licence shall be issued in respect of a local fishing vessel that is required to be registered under any law for the time being in force unless the vessel has been registered. 18. No licence shall be issued in respect of a local fishing vessel that is required to hold a valid certificate of inspection under any law for the time being in force unless such a certificate is issued in respect of that vessel."

139. A reading of sections 17 and 18 of the Ordinance shows that in order to have licence for a local fishing vessel, it has to fulfill 2(two) conditions, (i) the fishing vessel must have a valid certificate of inspection and (ii) to be registered if required under any law for the time being in force (under section 388 of the Bangladesh Merchant Shipping Ordinance, 1983, a fishing vessel has to be registered with the Registrar of Bangladesh Ships of the Mercantile Marine Department, Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh).

140. Another pertinent question arises whether the trawlers involved in the appeals are local fishing vessels or foreign fishing vessels. Admittedly the vessels in question were Thai fishing trawlers and were seized by the Bangladesh 'Government when they were fishing illegally in the Bangladesh territorial waters and subsequently, were forfeited and then were sold in auction by the Directorate of Fisheries and were purchased by the writ-petitioners who are either the Bangladeshi proprietor of proprietorship firm or Bangladeshi Company; so, by virtue of the definition of "local fishing vessel" as given in clause (i) of section 2 of the Ordinance, 1983 as quoted hereinbefore, are definitely "local fishing vessels." As stated hereinbefore, the fishing vessels/trawlers involved in these appeals were either inspected by the technical committee formed by the Government or inspected by the Mercantile Marine Department, Chittagong or inspected by the Naval Architecture and Marine Engineer and some were even registered under section 388 of the Bangladesh Merchant Shipping Ordinance, 1983 and such certificates of inspection and registrations have been annexed to the writ petitions and the writ-respondents did not, at all, deny their genuineness or otherwise, so the trawlers had valid certificates of inspection, the petitioners had a right to get them registered under the Bangladesh Merchant Shipping Ordinance, 1983 and also to get licences for deep sea fishing under section 8 read with sections 17 and 18 of the Ordinance, 1983.

141. Section 19 of the Ordinance, 1983 has spelt out the grounds on which the Director may, by order in writing refuse to issue a licence in respect of a local fishing vessel or suspend, cancel or refuse to renew any licence that has been issued in respect of a local fishing vessel, where he is satisfied that:

(a) it is necessary to do so in order to allow for the proper management, conservation and development of any particular fishery in accordance with any fisheries management, conservation and development plan; or

(b)it is otherwise in the best interest of marine fisheries industry to do so; or

(c) the vessel in respect of which the licence has been issued has been used in contravention of the provisions of this Ordinance or of any rules made there under or of any conditions or of any rules made there under or of any conditions of the licence; or

(d) the person applying for or holding the licence is unfit to hold a licence.

<u>142. We are not concerned with clauses (a)-(c) of section 19, we are concerned with the first part of clause (d) thereof that is, "the person applying for is unfit to hold a license". Unfit to hold a licence as contemplated in clause (d) of section 2 is referable to sections 17 and 18 of the Ordinance, 1983. We are of the view that the person mentioned in clause (d) of section 19 is the owner or the proprietor of the fishing trawler/ fishing vessel who applies for issuance of the licence and the expression "unfit to hold a licence" means who fails to fulfill the conditions as stipulated in sections 17 and 18 of the Ordinance, 1983. So, if the local fishing trawler/vessel for which the application for licence for fishing (here deep sea fishing) is filed fulfils the conditions as stipulated in the said two sections, the Director of the Marine Fisheries is legally obliged to issue licence. In this regard, it may be stated that some of the trawlers were also allowed to go for trial fishing by issuing "Sailing permission of fishing." It is also very relevant to mention that the Ministry refused to give licences to the petitioners' fishing trawlers not on the ground of their unfitness for deep sea fishing or for any other lacking within the meaning of sections 17, 18 and 19 of the Ordinance, 1983, but on the ground of non fixation of the number of trawlers for fishing by the Cabinet. The writ-petitioners having fulfilled the statutory requirements under sections 17 and 18 of the Ordinance, 1983 as discussed above, they could legitimately expect that their trawlers would be registered and licences for deep sea fishing under section 8 thereof read with section 19 thereof would also be given, because legitimate expectation may also arise within the statutory context and in case of such expectation, the Government and its functionaries are obliged to discharge their statutory obligation to that end. The refusal of the Government to give licences to the petitioners' fishing trawlers on the ground as stated hereinbefore also appears to us false and unfair, as during the pendency of the writ petitions, advertisement through notifications was made on 25-4-2003 in the daily newspaper by the Director General Fisheries inviting applications from Bangladesh entrepreneurs to give fishing licences to 40 trawlers in complete denial of the petitioners' expectation of being registered of their fishing trawlers, (in some case) and to get licences for fishing in the deep sea.</u>

<u>143. Here in these cases as discussed hereinbefore, it is clear that the writ-petitioner-respondents being engaged in deep sea fishing participated in the auctions conducted by the Government functionaries with the intention and expectation more than legitimate for using them for fishing in the deep sea. The State being the authority for both holding the auction of the fishing trawlers and granting licences, the writ-petitioners could legitimately and reasonably expect that if they fulfilled the requirements of law as envisaged in sections 17 and 18 of the Ordinance, 1983, they would get the necessary registrations of their fishing trawlers and licences to go for deep sea fishing. In fact, when they fulfilled all requirements for getting the fishing trawlers registered and to get licences as envisaged in the said two sections their expectations received the statutory backing as well. To establish a case of legitimate expectation it is not always necessary that the petitioners must show that the Government and its functionaries or any other public or statutory authority gave a promise to do a thing or to act in a particular way by making correspondences as submitted by the learned Attorney-General. 'Legitimate Expectation' may also arise from the express conduct of Government, its functionaries and other public or statutory authority as happened in the instant case. It is always expected that the Government and the other public and statutory functionaries shall act fairly and reasonably with a citizen or a person and the Court shall definitely interfere in a matter if it is found that the. Government and the other public and statutory functionaries failed to act fairly and reasonably as per the dictate of the statute in denial of the legitimate expectation of such citizen or person.</u>

<u>144. In the instant cases, the Government with the full knowledge and understanding that the sold fishing trawlers would be used for fishing, conducted the auction and sold them to the writ-petitioners, coupled with fact that undertaking was taken from the auction purchasers that such trawlers could be registered and used for fishing only with the permission of the Government show a clear representation from the Government to perform in a particular way which also constituted an element of legitimate expectation that if the petitioners could fulfill the requirements of law as provided in the Ordinance, 1983, they would get licences for fishing in the deep sea.</u>

145. The facts and circumstances of the cases decided in the cases of Syed Arif Niazi vs Bangladesh and Saya Protein Project Ltd. vs Bangladesh (supra), as cited by the learned Attorney-General on the question of legitimate expectation being completely different from the facts and circumstances of the instant cases, those do not help the learned Attorney-General to resist the case of legitimate expectation of the petitioners.

146. In view of our summing up on the 'Doctrine of legitimate expectation' and the finding given on the question hereinbefore, we do not consider it necessary to discuss the individual cases cited by Mr M Amir-ul Islam.

147. We conclude by saying that the writ-petitioner-respondents clearly established their case of legitimate expectation of getting registrations of their trawlers and licences for fishing in the deep sea and the High Court Division rightly gave directions in that respect in the impugned judgment and order while making the Rules absolute.

<u>148. Besides 'legitimate expectation', a new dimension has been added to the claim of the writ-petitioner-respondents to get their fishing trawlers registered and to get licences as well for deep-sea fishing pursuant to the directions given by the High Court Division. The new dimension is that a discriminatory treatment has been meted out to the writ-petitioner-respondents. In the concise statement filed by the writ-petitioner-respondents, it has been categorically stated that out of 36 writ petitions, in which Rules were made absolute, the writ-respondents have preferred appeal in respect of 12(twelve) writ petitions' only giving rise to these appeals, that is, no leave petition was preferred against the judgment and order passed in 22 (twenty two) other writ petitions and those 22 (twenty two) writ-petitioners have since been enjoying the benefit of the judgments and orders passed therein as the concerned authorities have already issued registrations, fitness certificates and licences for their trawlers; under similar facts and circumstances, the High Court Division made the Rule absolute in Writ Petition No. 5479 of 2003 on 27-8-2004 and in the name of the Government, Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1498 of 2004 was filed, but at the instance of the Government, the same was not pressed on 16-1-2007 by the learned Additional Attorney-General; in another case, a civil petition for leave to appeal being No. 110 of 2006 was filed, but the same was dismissed on 20-2-2008 for non-compliance of the Court's order. In support of the statements made in the concise statement as stated hereinbefore the respondents have filed the copies of the judgment and the orders passed in the respective writ petition and the leave petition and the copies of the licences filing an additional paper book in Civil Appeal No. 127 of 2005. The learned Attorney-General could not refute the submission of Mr. M Amir-ul Islam on the point of discriminatory treatment towards these 12 (twelve) writ-petitioner-respondents. Thus, it is clear that the writ-respondents made pick and choose in filing the leave petitions giving rise to these appeals and in doing so, the writ-petitioners have not been treated equally with 22 other writ-petitioners which is nothing but a clear violation of the provisions of article 27 of the Constitution. Therefore, we do not see any moral on the part of the writ-respondent-appellants to pursue these appeals.</u>

149. Leave was also granted with reference to a survey report submitted by a high powered technical committee of expert named as 'Zaman Committee' which was found to be in harmony with the survey report of the donors stating that without further survey, number of trawlers except the existing 73 should not be increased, otherwise, it would create adverse effect on our marine resources, but that report lost its factual impact when the Government set up another committee in 1997 headed by Dr Mahmudul Karim. From the additional paper book, in Civil Appeal No. 128 of 2005, it appears that the 'Zaman Committee' was headed by the then Cabinet Secretary, Mr MM Zaman as its Chairman and was formed for examining the provision of the Ordinance, 1983 and making recommendations for implementation of the provisions of the Ordinance. The Committee submitted its report on 12-3-1985. The term of reference of Dr Mahmudul Karim was to conduct a survey and to submit report as to the prospect of fishing in the deep sea with the necessary recommendations and the said committee after due survey submitted its report on 9-12-1997 recommending that the Government could increase the number of deep sea fishing trawler by about 20 in addition to the existing trawler already in the business. Therefore, the report earlier submitted by Mr MM Zaman, could not stand in the way in giving licences to the petitioners' fishing trawlers. In this regard, at the risk of repetition, it is necessary to further state that when the writ-respondents themselves made advertisement through the notification in the newspaper on 25-4-2003 for giving licences to 40 more trawlers for fishing in the Bay of Bengal the stand taken by the Government during the hearing of the leave petition on the basis of the report of 'Zaman Committee' as submitted by the learned Additional Attorney-General could not have any factual bearing in deciding the merits of the writ-petitioners' case, but the same lost sight of by this Division while granting leave. Therefore, we find no substance in the said point on which leave was granted.

150. For the discussions made herein-before, we find no merit in the appeals. Accordingly, the appeals are dismissed, however, without any order as to cost.

Nazmun Ara Sultana J: I have gone through the separate judgments prepared by my learned brother, Surendra Kumar Sinha, J and my learned brother, Md Abdul Wahhab Miah, J I agree with the judgment of Md Abdul Wahhab Miah, J

Syed Mahmud Hossain J : I have gone through the separate judgments prepared by my learned brother, Surendra Kumar Sinha, I and my learned brother, Md Abdul Wahhab Miah, J I agree with the judgment of Md Abdul Wahhab Miah; J

full_judgment:
Zafar Ahmed J: Delay of 20 days in filing the instant First Miscellaneous Appeal is condoned.

2. In the instant First Miscellaneous Appeal (FMA), the plaintiff as appellant has challenged the judgment and order dated 28-3-2012 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Chandpur in Title Suit No. 20 of 2012 by which the ad-interim order of injunction passed on 8-3- 2012 has been vacated.

3. Be it stated that during pendency of the instant FMA, the original plaintiff-appellant namely Abdul Hakim Gazi died on 1-1-2014. Thereafter, his wife, son and 3 daughters, who are his legal heirs, have been substituted in place of the deceased plaintiff-appellant by order dated 23-2-2014. One of the legal heirs of the deceased plaintiff namely Md Humayun Kabir Gazi, who was the proforma defendant No.3 in the original suit and also proforma opposite party No.3 in this FMA has been substituted as appellant No. 1 (b).

4. The case of the plaintiff, as averred in the plaint, in short, is that his son Md Humayun Kabir Gazi in 2003, obtained investment facility of Taka 1,00,000 for business purposes for his business enterprise M/s Sabbir Gazi Furniture from Islami Bank Bangladesh Limited, Chandpur branch as per sanction advice issued by the defendant No.1 (Manager Islami Bank Limited Bangladesh, Chandpur branch). Against the said sanction advice the plaintiff, as guarantor of the loan, mortgaged the (Ka) scheduled property owned by him comprising of 0.31 decimals of land and structures constructed thereon situated in Chandpur district by executing and registering a mortgage deed being No. 4923 on 7-10-2003 in favour of the bank. On the same day the plaintiff also executed and registered an irrevocable power of attorney being No. 4924 in favour of the bank. The plaintiff's son repaid the said investment facility with profit. On 22-1-2012 the plaintiff received a notice from Assistant Commissioner (Land), Chandpur Sadar and thereafter on inquiry he came to know that on 12-10-2011 the bank published an auction notice in the newspaper for sale of the (Ka) scheduled property on the ground that his son had defaulted in repaying the bank loan and on 9-1-2012 the bank executed and registered a sale deed being No.158 in respect of the said property in favour of the auction purchaser namely Chandpur Multipurpose Cooperative Society Ltd., Chandpur (defendant No.2).

5. Challenging the auction notice dated 12-10-2011, auction held on 26-10-2011 and registered sale deed No. 158 dated 9-1-2012 and also praying for a permanent injunction restraining the defendants from evicting the plaintiff from the (Ka) scheduled property or transferring the same, the plaintiff instituted the suit.

6. The plaintiff filed the suit on 8-3-2012 and on the same day filed an application for temporary injunction against the defendants. The court below vide order dated 8-3-2012 passed an ad-interim injunction restraining the defendants from evicting the plaintiff from the scheduled property or transferring the same till submission of written objection by the defendants and hearing of the same.

7. The defendants contested the injunction application by filing separate written objections on 27-3-2012. In the instant FMA, the written objection filed by the defendant No.1 i.e., the bank, has been produced before us by the plaintiff-appellant and although the FMA has been contested by both the defendants, the written objection filed by the defendant No. 2 has not been filed.

8. The case of the defendant No. 1, as stated in the written objection, is that the suit is not maintainable and barred by the principles of estoppel, waiver and acquiescence. The specific case of the defendant No.1 bank is that in 2003 the plaintiff's son obtained investment facility of Taka 1,00,000 as per sanction advice No. IBBL/CHAND/03 dated 4-10-2003. Against the said investment facility the plaintiff on 7-10-2003 executed and registered mortgage deed No.4923 and a deed of irrevocable power of attorney No.4924 in favour of the bank. Subsequently, upon prayer of the plaintiff's son the said investment facility was enhanced to Taka 4,00,000. Thereafter, vide another sanction advice dated 10-8-2009 the said investment facility was enhanced to Taka 8,00,000 and against the said additional investment facility the plaintiff on 9-9-2009 executed a deed of agreement and deposited the same with the bank. The plaintiff's- son availed investment facility of Taka 8,00,000 from the bank but defaulted in repaying the 'same within the stipulated period, The bank sent a legal notice under section 12 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 to the plaintiff's son who received the same on 17-8-2011, but did not repay the loan. Thereafter, under the provisions of section 12 of the Ain, the bank on 12-10-2011 published auction notices in the national Daily Sangram newspaper and in a local newspaper called Daily Chandpur Diganta. In response to the said auction notice the defendant No. 2 and two others submitted auction bids. Auction was held on 26-10-2011. The defendant No. 2 became the highest bidder which is Taka 65,41,000. On 9-1-2012 the bank executed and registered the sale deed No.158 in respect of the mortgaged property in favour of defendant. No.2. Out of the sale proceeds the bank adjusted its out- standing dues of Taka 10,29,359.74 and paid the rest amount of Taka 55,11,640.22 to the plaintiff in cash which was received. and acknowledged by the plaintiff.

9. After hearing the parties the court below vide the impugned judgment and order dated 28-3-2012 vacated the earlier order of ad-interim injunction dated 8-3-2012. Challenging the order dated 28-3-2012 the plaintiff preferred the instant FMA before this Court which has been admitted on 30-7-2012.

10. The defendant-respondent Nos:1 and 2 contested the FMA separately.

11. Mr Subrata Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-appellants, submits that at the time of the auction sale the market price of the (Ka) scheduled property was about Taka 6 crore, but in connivance between the defendants the same was sold at a shockingly low price at Taka 65,41,000 which amounts to fraud. He next submits the borrower i.e., the original plaintiff's son repaid the loan taken- in 2003 against which the plaintiff mortgaged the property and gave the power to the bank to sell the property in case of default by his son, but the bank fraudulently published the auction notice in 2011 for sale of the plaintiffs, mortgaged property for alleged non-payment, of the loan taken in 2009 and hence the auction sale is illegal and not binding upon the plaintiff.

12. Mr Chowdhury draws our attention to the power of attorney no. 4924 dated 7-10-2003 and the registered sale deed No. 158 dated 9-1-2012 (Annexure- X2 and Z respectively of the supplementary affidavit dated 22-10-2014 filed by the plaintiff-appellants) by which the bank transferred the property as attorney of the plaintiff (since deceased) to the auction purchaser (defendant No. 2) and submits that the bank had no legal right to sell the property on the basis of the said power of attorney inasmuch has the power of attorney ceased to be operative and became invalid for subsequent loan facility availed by the plaintiff's son in 2009 for which the plaintiff was neither a guarantor nor executed any power of attorney and since the bank had no legal right to sell the property both the auction notice and sale of the property to the defendant No.2 are void ab initio. He submits that the plaintiff-appellants have a good prima facie arguable case. "He submits that the substituted legal heirs of the deceased plaintiff reside at the (Ka) scheduled property and the building constructed thereon and as such the balance of convenience and inconvenience are in favour of the plaintiff-appellants and if an order of injunction is not granted the plaintiff-appellants would suffer irreparable loss and-injury which cannot be compensated in money.

13. On the other hand, Mr Md Kamrul Alam, the learned Advocate for the defendant-respondent No.1 bank, submits that following the auction sale, the bank, after deducting its outstanding liability, returned the balance amount to the plain- tiff which he received in cash and thus accepted and acknowledged the auction notice and auction sale and now he is estopped from denying the same. He submits that the plaintiff cannot approbate and reprobate at the same time. The learned advocate draws .our attention to memo No. 00. 293.027.08.27.010.2012-332 dated 4-4-2012 signed by the Executive Magistrate and Surveyor, Revenue Section, both of the office of Deputy Commissioner, Chandpur (Annexure-X series of the supplementary affidavit dated 27-10-2014 filed by the respondent No.1) by which the possession of the auction sold property was handed over to the defendant No.2. The learned advocate also refers to order dated 5-4-2012 passed by the court below in which the learned court referred to the submission of the learned advocate of the plaintiff that after vacating the order of injunction the defendants forcibly took possession of the property.

14. Mr Md Kamrul Alam submits that since the plaintiff received the sale proceeds and possession of the property has been handed over to defendant No.2 on 4-4-2012 prior to filing of the instant FMA, the same has become infructuous and order of injunction as prayed for by the appellants cannot be granted.

15. The learned Advocate then refers to section 12(8) of the Ain, 2003 and submits that in case of auction sale held illegally or with irregularity, the same cannot be challenged. However, the owner of the mortgaged property may sue the bank for any loss, if suffered because of such illegal or irregular auction sale or for sale the property at a shockingly low price as alleged by the plaintiff. In support of the argument the learned Advocate relies upon the case of Banesa Bibi vs Senior Vice President 8 LG (2011) AD 55 = 63 DLR (AD) 160.

16. Rebutting the argument of the learned Advocate of the plaintiff-appellants in respect of the bank's having no legal right to sell, Mr Alam the learned Advocate for the respondent No. 1 bank, submits that the guarantee given by the plaintiff against the loan taken by his son in 2003 is a continuing guarantee and as such the bank had the legal right to sell the property. The learned Advocate further submits that the plaintiff does not have any prima facie arguable case and since the application for injunction has become infructuous the instant FMA is liable to be dismissed.

17. In reply, Mr Chowdhury, the learned Advocate for the appellants, submits that so far as handing over of the possession of the property is concerned, the plaintiff-appellants are still in possession of the property and memo dated 4-4-2012 referred to by the learned Advocate for the bank is merely a paper transaction which was never acted upon.

18. Mr Md Fakhar Uddin, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant-respondent No.2 (auction purchaser) adopts the submissions of the learned Advocate for the defendant-respondent No.1.

19. During the course of hearing, the appellants and both the respondents filed series of various documents in support of their respective cases by filing several sets of affidavit.

20. We have heard the learned Advocates and perused the materials on record.

21. Admittedly, the plaintiff's son obtained investment facility of Taka 1,00,000 from the bank as per sanction advice dated 4-10-2003. Against the said loan, the plaintiff, as guarantor of the same, mortgaged the property by executing and registering a mortgage deed and the power of attorney on 7-10-2003 in favour of the bank. In the written statement filed by the bank it has been stated that the said loan was enhanced to Taka 4,00,000. Thereafter, vide another sanction advice dated 13-8-2009 (Annexure Z-3 of the supplementary affidavit dated 8-12-2014 filed by the respondent No.1) the existing loan was renewed and enhanced to Taka 8,00,000 which the plaintiff's son availed in full.

22. In the written statement filed by the bank it has further been stated that against the enhanced loan the plaintiff on 9-9-2009 executed a deed of agreement on Taka 150 stamped papers and deposited the same with the bank(মোঃ হুমাযুন কবির গাজীর অনুরোধে তাহার পিতা বিগত ৯-৯-২০০৯ইং তারিখে ১৫০ টাকার স্ট্যাপে বদ্ধকের অতিরিক্ত ৭,০০,০০০বিনিয়োগের (ঋণের) জন্য বদ্ধকের অতিরিক্ত বিনিয়োগের (ঋণের) অতিরিক্ত চুক্তিপত্র দলিল সম্পাদন করিয়া ব্যাংকে জমা প্রদান করিলে......). This document has not been produced before us. It appears that against the enhanced loan of Taka 8,00,000 the plaintiff neither executed any mortgage deed nor power of attorney.

23. In the legal notice dated 17-8-2011 given by the bank to the plaintiff's son, copy of which was given to the plaintiff (Annexure-Y of the supplementary affidavit dated 26-11-2013 filed the respondent No.1) it has been stated that between the period from 17-9-2009 to 9-6-2010 the plaintiff’s son availed investment facility of total Taka 8,00,000 in 10 installments, but he defaulted in repaying the same with profit.

24. The bank published auction notices in daily and local newspapers on 12-10-2011. The auction sale was held on 26-10-2011 in which the defendant No.2 became the highest bidder. On 9-1-2012 the bank executed and registered the sale deed No. 158 in respect of the mortgaged property to the defendant No.2 as attorney of the plaintiff by dint of registered power of attorney No. 4924 dated 7-10-2003.

25. The crux of the case of the appellants is that the bank had no legal power to sell the mortgaged property under section 12(1) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 (shortly 'the Ain'). Section 12(1) states,

১২। আর্থিক প্রতিষ্ঠান কর্তৃক কতিপয় জামানত বিক্রয়।-(১) উপ-ধারা (২) এর বিধান সাপেক্ষে, কোন আর্থিক প্রতিষ্ঠান, উহার নিজ দখল বা নিয়ন্ত্রণে থাকা বিবাদীর কোন সম্পত্তি যাহা পণ বা বন্ধক (lien or pledge) রাখিয়া ঋণ প্রদান করা হইয়াছে, এবং যাহা বিক্রিয় করিবার আইনগত অধিকার বাদীর রহিয়াছে বা বাদীকে অর্পণ করা হইয়াছে। উহা বিক্রয় না করিয়া এবং বিক্রয় লব্ধ অর্থঋণ পরিশোধ সমন্বয় না করিয়া, অর্থ ঋণ আদালতে কোন মামলা দায়ের করিবে না।

Section 12(2) of the Ain provides,

(২)উপ-ধারা (১) এর বিধান সত্ত্বেও, কোন আর্থিক প্রতিষ্ঠানে নিজ দখল বা নিয়ন্ত্রণে থাকা পণ বা বন্ধকী সম্পত্তি বিক্রয় না করিয়া মামলা দায়ের করিলে অনতিবিলম্বে উক্ত সম্পত্তি পূর্ব-বর্ণিত মতে বিক্রয় করিয়া বিক্রয়লব্ধ অর্থঋণের সহিত সমন্বয় করিবে এবং বিষয়টি আদালতকে লিখিতভাবে অবহিত করিবে।

26. It appears from a plain reading of section 12(1) of the Ain that the bank must have a legal right of sale (বিক্রয় করিবার আইনগত অধিকার বাদীর রহিয়াছে বা বাদীকে অর্পণ করা হইয়াছে) of the mortgaged property before it proceeds with the sale of the same.

Section 12(3) states,

"কোন আর্থিক প্রতিষ্ঠান, বিবাদীর নিকট হইতে কোন স্থাবর সম্পত্তি (Immovable Property) বন্ধক (Mortgage) রাখিয়া অথবা অস্থাবর সম্পত্তি (Movable Property) দায়বদ্ধ রাখিয়া (Hypothecated) ঋণ প্রদান করিলে এবং বন্ধক প্রদান বা দায়বদ্ধ রাখার সময় বন্ধক প্রদান বা দায়বদ্ধ রাখার সময় বন্ধকী বা দায়বদ্ধ সম্পত্তি বিক্রয়ের ক্ষমতা আর্থিক প্রতিষ্ঠানকে প্রদান করা হইয়া থাকিলে, উহা বিক্রয় না করিয়া এবং বিক্রয়লব্ধ অর্থ ঋণ পরিশোধ বাবদ সমন্বয় না করিয়া, অথবা বিক্রয়ের চেষ্টা করিয়া ব্যর্থ না হইয়া, অর্থ ঋণ আদালতে কোন মামলা দায়ের করিবে না।"

<u>27. The combined reading of sections 12(1) and 12(3) makes it crystal clear that the bank must have the power to sell the mortgaged property before it takes any step to proceed with the sale of the same under the section.</u>

28. The learned Advocate for the appellants submits that if the bank has no legal power to sell the mortgaged property or has not been given the power to sell the same, all the subsequent actions taken by the bank including publication of auction notice, the auction sale and transfer of the property to the auction purchaser becomes void ab initio. On the other hand, the learned Advocates for the respondents submit that section 12(8) of the Ain and the proviso thereof gives statutory protection to both the bank and the auction purchaser in respect of any illegality or irregularity committed in the process of the auction sale and inspite of such illegality or irregularity the auction purchaser acquires valid title. The remedy open to the owner of the mortgaged property is to file a suit for compensation and as such the instant suit not being maintainable, the plaintiff does not have prima facie arguable case.

29. For ready reference section 12(8) of the Ain is quoted below:

"আপাততঃ বলবৎ অন্য কোন আইনে ভিন্ন রুপ যাহা কিছুই থাকুক না কেন, এই ধারার অধীন আর্থিক প্রতিষ্ঠান কর্তৃক lien, pledge, hypothecation অথবা Mortgage এর অধীন প্রাপ্ত ক্ষমতা বলে কোন জামানতী স্থাবর বা অস্থাবর সম্পত্তি বিক্রয় করা হইলে, উক্ত বিক্রয় ক্রেতার অনুকূলে বৈধ স্বত্ব সৃষ্টি করিবে এবং ক্রেতার ক্রয়কে কোনভাবেই তকিত করা যাইবে নাঃ"

তবে শর্ত থাকে যে, আর্থিক প্রতিষ্ঠান কর্তৃক বিক্রয় কার্যক্রমে কোন রূপ অবৈধতা বা পদ্ধতিগত অনিয়ম থাকিলে, জামানত প্রদানকারী-ঋণ আর্থিক প্রতিষ্ঠানের বিরুদ্ধে ক্ষতিপূরণ দাবী করিতে পারিবেন।"

<u>30. The words “প্রাপ্ত ক্ষমতা বলে” (power derived) used in section 12(8) read with sections 12(1) and 12(3) also suggest that the bank must have the legal power to sell the mortgaged property which is the condition precedent to take subsequent actions .</u>

<u>31. The only conclusion that can be drawn from the above analysis of section 12 is that in the absence of bank's legal power to sell the mortgaged property, all the actions relating to sale of the same shall become void and will have no legal effect. In other words, every action in the absence of such power shall fall apart. The protection given to the bank and the auction purchaser in section 12(8) does not override sections 12(1) and 12(3). This protection is only available when the bank has the legal right to sell the mortgaged I property. The case of Banesa Bibi (supra), relied upon by the respondent No.1, has been decided on different facts and point of law. The issue raised in the instant case as to the bank's legal right to sell' was not raised in the said case. The case was decided solely on section 12(8) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 and as such the reported case has no manner of application in the case before hand.</u>

32. In the facts and circumstances of the case, as discussed above, now, the question before us for consideration is whether the bank had the legal right to seel the mortgaged property of the plaintiff as his attorney under the power of attorney dated 7-10-2003 executed against the loan taken by his son in 2003 for defaulting in repaying of the loan availed by his son in 2009-2010 as per sanction advice dated 13-8-2009 for which the plaintiff was neither a guarantor nor executed any power of attorney. It appears that this point was not raised before the court below and consequently, the same was not discussed.

33. The learned Advocate for the bank respondent No.1 draws our attention to both the registered mortgage deed No. 4923 dated 7-10-2003 executed by the plaintiff in favour of the bank as guarantor for his son's loan and the power of attorney No. 4924 dated 7-10-2003 and submits that the guarantee in question is a continuing guarantee and the loan taken in 2003 has been merged in the renewed and enhanced loan taken in 2009-2010 and therefore, the bank had the 'legal right to sell' the property.

<u>34. Section 129 of the Contract Act, 1872 defines continuing guarantee as a "guarantee which extends to the series of transactions". Section 133 of the same Act also provides that "any variance made without the surety's consent, in the terms of the contract between the principal debtor and the creditor, discharges the surety as to the transactions subsequent to the variance".</u>

<u>35. In the instant case, whether the loan taken in 2003 has been merged in the renewed and enhanced loan taken in 2009-2010, the guarantee given by the plaintiff in 2003 is a continuing guarantee and thus under section 12 of the Ain, 2003 the bank had the legal right to sell the mortgaged property as attorney of the plaintiff under the power of attorney dated 7-10-2003 which was executed against the loan taken in 2003 are to be determined by the trial Court upon taking evidence and scrutinising the terms of the relevant documents and transactions entered into between the parties. The instant case relates to an interlocutory matter of injunction. Therefore, we are not in a position to determine the issue without taking evidence. However, considering the facts and circumstances discussed above, we find a prima facie arguable case in favour of the plaintiff-appellants on this point.</u>

36. So far as the other principles governing the law of injunction i.e., the balance of convenience and inconvenience and irreparable loss are concerned, we note that the plaintiff received the sale proceeds of the auction sale from the bank. It is the case of the bank that according to the provisions of section 12 of the Ain, 2003 it took over the possession of the property on 4-4-2012 and handed over the same to the auction purchaser, which is evident from memo dated 4-4-2012 signed by the Executive Magistrate and Surveyor, Revenue Section, both of the office of Deputy Commissioner, Chandpur but the same has been denied by the appellants and their case is that the said memo is a paper transaction and was not acted upon. The appellants are still in possession of the suit property.

37. In the supplementary affidavit filed on behalf of the defendant No.2 auctioneer purchaser, it has been stated that the auction purchaser has been possessing the suit land and constructed a boundary wall surrounding the same. However, they did not file any document supporting the claim as to possession, So, we find a prima facie case in favour of the plaintiff-appellants in respect of the possession of the suit property.

38. Since we have already found a prima facie arguable case in favour of the plaintiff, it is our considered view that justice would be served by passing an order of status quo in respect of possession and position of the suit property in question.

39. In view of the facts, circumstances and laws discussed above, the parties are directed to maintain status quo in respect of the (Ka) scheduled property as described in the plaint till disposal of the Title Suit No. 20 of2012 now pending in the Court of Joint District Judge, Chandpur. With the above observations and direction the instant First Miscellaneous Appeal is disposed of. The connected Civil Rule No. 647(FM) of 2012 is accordingly disposed of.

40. The finding of facts made in this judgment will not be binding upon the court below. The trial court will come to its own finding, both on facts and law, upon evidences adduced by the parties.

Send down the copy of the judgment to the court below at once.

End.
